Malingering: intentional fake symptoms for an outside goal (money, avoiding work); not a psychiatric disorder

Not intentional: SSD and conversion

Tip: money or avoiding work = malingering

cards.prompt: Factitious disorder: signs and nursing care
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: dramatic tales (pseudologia fantastica), proper medical terms, new symptoms after negative tests, covert self-injury; common in health care workers

Nursing: treat injury first, nonjudgmental, avoid confrontation, centralize care, give a tactful way to stop

Imposed on another: protect the child; reporting is mandatory (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Dissociative amnesia and fugue
cards.answerHtml:
Amnesia: cannot recall important personal information, too much for forgetfulness; types: localized, selective, generalized, continuous, systematized

Fugue: sudden travel away from home with loss of identity or a new identity (a type of amnesia)

Cause: dissociation as a defense against trauma

cards.prompt: Dissociative identity disorder (DID)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: two or more distinct identities (alters) that take control, with memory gaps

Cause: early childhood trauma, often abuse

Nursing: safe calm setting, grounding, support decisions, do not push for memories

Therapy: CBT, psychodynamic; antidepressants for comorbid mood/anxiety

Caution: EMDR contraindicated with severe dissociation or active suicidal ideation

cards.prompt: Depersonalization/derealization disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: persistent detachment from self (depersonalization) or from surroundings (derealization); feels mechanical or unreal

Cause: defense against trauma

Nursing: grounding techniques, calm safe setting, do not push for memories

cards.prompt: Alcohol: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: disinhibition, slurred speech, ataxia, nystagmus; BAL 0.30 stupor, 0.40 coma, 0.50 respiratory failure

Withdrawal: usually within 12 h (ATI, Townsend: 4-12 h): tremor, sweating, tachycardia, high BP, anxiety, N/V; seizures within 48 h; DTs

Danger: withdrawal kills (seizures, DTs, MI); severe intoxication kills by respiratory failure

cards.prompt: Valium, Xanax, phenobarbital: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: looks like alcohol: slurred speech, ataxia, nystagmus, labile mood

Overdose: respiratory depression, coma, cardiac arrest (worse with alcohol or opioids)

Withdrawal: rebound anxiety, tachycardia, tremor, insomnia, seizures, delirium

Danger: both; abrupt withdrawal can be fatal, so taper

cards.prompt: Opioids: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication/overdose: euphoria, nodding, pinpoint pupils, slow pulse, constipation; overdose: respiratory depression, stupor, coma

Withdrawal: yawning, runny nose, dilated pupils, goose bumps, cramps, vomiting, diarrhea; onset 8-12 h (methadone 1-3 days), peak 48-72 h

Danger: overdose kills; withdrawal is miserable but rarely fatal (dehydration, suicidal thinking)

cards.prompt: Cocaine: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: euphoria, tachycardia, high BP, dilated pupils, rising temp, insomnia; rush lasts 10-20 min

Overdose: seizures, arrhythmia, MI, stroke, hyperthermia

Withdrawal (crash): sleeps 12-18 h, depression, anhedonia, hunger, craving

Danger: overdose (cardiac, seizures); crash carries suicide risk

cards.prompt: Amphetamines/meth/MDMA: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: like cocaine but longer: tachycardia, high BP, hyperthermia, insomnia, paranoia

Overdose: seizures, high fever, stroke, arrhythmia, psychosis; MDMA: rhabdomyolysis, kidney failure

Withdrawal: fatigue, hypersomnia, hunger, depression, craving (milder than cocaine)

Danger: intoxication (hyperthermia, seizures); crash needs suicide assessment

cards.prompt: Cannabis: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: relaxation, red eyes, dry mouth, time distortion, increased appetite

Overdose: anxiety/panic, tachycardia, paranoia, hallucinations

Withdrawal: irritability, restlessness, insomnia, low appetite, depressed mood (within about a week)

Danger: neither is usually fatal; risks are psychosis, impaired driving, hyperemesis; synthetic cannabinoids (Spice, K2) unpredictable

cards.prompt: Hallucinogens and PCP: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: distorted perception, dilated pupils, tachycardia, panic, paranoia

PCP: belligerent, nystagmus, numb to pain, rigidity, seizures; overdose: adrenergic crisis

Withdrawal: none; flashbacks (HPPD) can recur

Danger: intoxication (violence, injury, hyperthermia; PCP cardiovascular crisis)

cards.prompt: Inhalants: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: giddiness, dizziness, slurred speech, ataxia, nystagmus; fades in minutes

Overdose: sudden sniffing death (arrhythmia), stupor, coma, seizures

Withdrawal: none documented (Boyd: mild, alcohol-like)

Danger: intoxication, even the first use; long-term brain, liver, kidney damage

cards.prompt: Nicotine: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: alertness, concentration, appetite suppression; overdose: anxiety, nausea, palpitations

Withdrawal: craving, irritability, anxiety, low mood, poor concentration, insomnia, headache, hunger

Danger: neither acutely; chronic use is the killer (largest preventable cause of early death); 90% relapse within 1 year

cards.prompt: Caffeine: intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Intoxication: rambling speech, restlessness, insomnia, flushing, high BP/HR, anxiety

Overdose: arrhythmia, cardiac arrest (energy drinks, sensitive people)

Withdrawal: headache, drowsiness, fatigue, craving, poor concentration

Danger: intoxication, rarely (arrhythmia)

cards.prompt: Which withdrawals can kill?
cards.answerHtml:
Can kill: alcohol and sedatives (seizures, DTs, autonomic collapse)

Rarely fatal: opioids

Suicide risk: stimulant crash (cocaine, meth)

No real withdrawal: hallucinogens, PCP, inhalants

Highest priority: the patient withdrawing from alcohol or a sedative, or with respiratory depression

cards.prompt: Stimulus clues: which substance?
cards.answerHtml:
• pinpoint pupils + slow breathing = opioid
  • dilated pupils + tachycardia = stimulant
  • seizures after stopping = alcohol or sedative withdrawal
  • yawning, runny nose, goose bumps = opioid withdrawal
  • sleeping 14 h, depressed, hungry = cocaine crash
  • red eyes, dry mouth, paranoid = cannabis

cards.prompt: Opioid overdose: what does the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: Opioid overdose: what does the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Signs: RR below 10-12, pinpoint pupils, hard to rouse

Priority: support breathing AND give naloxone together; never let either delay the other

  • call for help, open airway, support ventilation
  • give naloxone (IM, SQ, IV, intranasal, inhalation); IV effect in about 2 min

Watch: naloxone lasts 30-81 min, opioid lasts longer: re-sedation; repeat dose; reassess breathing

Also: may precipitate withdrawal; does not reverse xylazine, but still give it (fentanyl)

cards.prompt: Alcohol: antidote and priority care
cards.answerHtml:
Antidote: none

Thiamine: give before or with any glucose, never after (verify); prevents or treats Wernicke

Withdrawal: benzodiazepine taper per CIWA-Ar; add folate, magnesium

Safety: seizure precautions, airway, fluids
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Cocaine, meth, MDMA overdose: antidote and care
cards.promptHtml: Cocaine, meth, MDMA overdose: antidote and care
cards.answerHtml:
Antidote: none

Care: ABCs, cooling, seizure precautions

  • benzodiazepines for agitation, as ordered (verify)
  • ECG, notify provider
  • check CK for rhabdomyolysis

Also: suicide precautions during crash
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Which substances have an antidote?
cards.answerHtml:
Opioids: naloxone

Benzodiazepines: flumazenil

None: alcohol, barbiturates, stimulants, cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids, hallucinogens, PCP, inhalants, nicotine, caffeine, xylazine (supportive care)

cards.prompt: ABCs or antidote first?
cards.answerHtml:
Always: airway, breathing, circulation first

Opioid: ventilate and give naloxone together; airway wins if both are listed, naloxone wins over history or labs

Others: no antidote-first rule; ABC and supportive care are the treatment

After naloxone: reassess breathing every few minutes

cards.prompt: Naloxone vs Narcan vs naltrexone
cards.answerHtml:
Naloxone = Narcan: same drug; rescue for opioid overdose; 30-81 min; re-sedation, precipitated withdrawal

Naltrexone (ReVia; Vivitrol monthly shot): maintenance to prevent relapse (alcohol, opioid)

Naltrexone needs: 7-10 opioid-free days; check LFTs; medical ID

cards.prompt: When is naloxone appropriate vs naltrexone?
cards.answerHtml:
Naloxone: unresponsive or slow-breathing person with suspected opioid use (RR 6 after heroin)

Naltrexone: detoxified, motivated patient preventing relapse to opioids or alcohol

Not appropriate: naltrexone 2 days after heroin (needs 7-10 days opioid-free); naltrexone does not treat withdrawal or overdose

cards.prompt: Cannabis withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
When: within about a week after stopping heavy, prolonged use

Looks like: irritability, anger or aggression, restlessness, insomnia, disturbing dreams, low appetite, weight loss, anxiety, depressed mood, headache, sweating, abdominal pain, tremor

Care: no antidote; supportive care; not usually fatal

cards.prompt: Cannabis overdose/toxicity
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: anxiety or panic, tachycardia, paranoia, delusions and hallucinations at high doses, red eyes, dry mouth

Care: calm quiet room, reassurance, monitor vitals; benzodiazepine for severe agitation (verify)

Teach: no driving for 8-12 h; edibles act slower and longer (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome
cards.answerHtml:
Cause: long-term heavy cannabis use

Looks like: cycles of severe nausea, repeated vomiting, abdominal pain; relieved by hot showers or baths

Care: IV fluids, electrolytes, antiemetics as ordered; stopping cannabis is the cure

Risk: dehydration, electrolyte loss, kidney injury

Whole card is general knowledge; not in lecture or Boyd (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Cannabis: other exam facts
cards.answerHtml:
• addictive: about 30% develop use disorder; starting before 18 raises risk 4-7 times
  • THC stored in fat and brain for weeks
  • urine screen: 7-10 days casual, 2-4 weeks heavy (syllabus); lecture says 4-6 weeks
  • Spice/K2: unpredictable, no antidote
  • no approved drug for the disorder (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Wernicke vs Korsakoff
cards.answerHtml:
Cause: thiamine (B1) deficiency in chronic alcohol use

Wernicke (acute): ataxia, confusion, abnormal eye movements; treat with thiamine

Korsakoff (chronic): memory loss with confabulation

Nursing: thiamine now

cards.prompt: Alcohol withdrawal timeline
cards.answerHtml:
Onset: usually within 12 h (ATI, Townsend: 4-12 h)

Seizures: usually within 48 h

DTs: 2-3 days after last drink (ATI); peak 48-72 h (Saunders)

Over: uncomplicated withdrawal 48-96 h

Ask first: last drink and amount

cards.prompt: Delirium tremens (DTs)
cards.answerHtml:
When: 2-3 days after last drink

Looks like: disorientation, hallucinations, fever, HR 120-140, severe hypertension, arrhythmia, seizures

Nursing: medical emergency: rapid response, one-to-one, benzodiazepines, seizure precautions, low stimulation

cards.prompt: CIWA-Ar
cards.answerHtml:
Use: scores alcohol withdrawal severity; guides benzodiazepine dosing

Max score: 67; under 10 usually needs no added medication

Report: rising score

Related: COWS scores opioid withdrawal

cards.prompt: Substance use disorder: education for patient and family
cards.promptHtml: Substance use disorder: education for patient and family
cards.answerHtml:
• addiction is a chronic relapsing brain disease; relapse is expected, not failure
  • never stop alcohol or sedatives abruptly at home
  • know signs of overdose; call 911; keep naloxone at home
  • never mix alcohol with sedatives or opioids; cocaine plus alcohol makes cocaethylene
  • AA, NA, SMART, Al-Anon; HALT (hungry, angry, lonely, tired)

cards.prompt: Substance use disorder: what are we looking for? (red flags)
cards.promptHtml: Substance use disorder: what are we looking for? (red flags)
cards.answerHtml:
• RR under 10-12, pinpoint pupils, hard to rouse: opioid overdose
  • tremor, sweating, rising HR within hours of last drink: early withdrawal
  • confusion, hallucinations, fever, HR over 120: DTs
  • ataxia, confusion, eye changes: Wernicke
  • hyperthermia, seizures after stimulant: toxicity
  • suicidal statements during detox or crash

cards.prompt: Nursing role in substance use disorder
cards.answerHtml:
1. Safety: airway, seizure precautions, low stimulation, one-to-one if withdrawing

2. Monitor: vitals, CIWA-Ar/COWS, fluids, electrolytes

3. Give ordered meds and teach

4. Assess whole person: nutrition, suicide, violence, co-occurring disorders

5. Therapeutic relationship: motivational interviewing, SBIRT/FRAMES

6. Refer, harm reduction, report impaired colleagues

Order: safety, then assess, then motivate

cards.prompt: Assessment of a patient with substance use disorder
cards.promptHtml: Assessment of a patient with substance use disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Screen: CAGE, AUDIT (alcohol); DAST (drugs)

Ask first: substance, amount, route, last use, prior withdrawal

Check: nutrition, track marks, suicide risk, denial, motivation

Priority: will this patient withdraw?

cards.prompt: DSM criteria: substance use disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Syllabus (DSM-IV): abuse = 1 or more of 4 consequence criteria; dependence = 3 or more of 7 (tolerance, withdrawal...)

DSM-5-TR: one SUD, 2 or more of 11 criteria in 12 months

  • mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe 6+

Not counted: tolerance/withdrawal from medication taken as prescribed

cards.prompt: Impaired nurse
cards.answerHtml:
Warning signs: mood swings, implausible absences, errors, alcohol on breath, volunteering to give meds

Duty: patient safety first; notify supervisor now; report through proper channels; remove from patient care

Help: peer assistance programs; confidential if the nurse accepts treatment

Not OK: covering up (enabling)

cards.prompt: Co-occurring disorders (dual diagnosis)
cards.answerHtml:
Fact: about half of patients with a mental disorder have an SUD

Treat: both disorders at the same time

Stages: engagement, motivation, active treatment, relapse prevention

Watch: suicide risk; antidepressants for depression fueling use

cards.prompt: Enabling behaviors
cards.answerHtml:
Enabling: shielding the user from consequences

Examples: excuses, covering, paying debts, rescuing

Nursing: teach it comes from love and fear; set boundaries, allow natural consequences; refer to Al-Anon, Nar-Anon

Staff: accepting rationalization or extra PRN is enabling

cards.prompt: Signs of successful recovery
cards.answerHtml:
• acknowledges problem; stops rationalizing
  • names triggers; has relapse prevention plan
  • uses coping skills, attends groups, takes meds
  • changes people, places, routines
  • handles a lapse by re-engaging

Best plan: concrete trigger-and-support plan

cards.prompt: Substance use disorder: what is OK vs not OK?
cards.promptHtml: Substance use disorder: what is OK vs not OK?
cards.answerHtml:
OK: voicing cravings or shame; medication-assisted treatment; groups; honest disclosure; harm-reduction teaching; refusing treatment (right to decline)

Not OK: using or hiding substances on the unit; manipulating, demanding extra doses; punishing or shaming; labels; enabling; opioids to a naltrexone user; disulfiram without consent

cards.prompt: Limit setting and the nurse's stance with substance use
cards.promptHtml: Limit setting and the nurse's stance with substance use
cards.answerHtml:
Stance: caring, matter-of-fact, direct; never punitive

Limits: state the rule, apply fair and consistent consequences

Do not: argue against denial, lecture, accept rationalization or leave a withdrawing patient alone

Therapeutic: open-ended, nonjudgmental questions

cards.prompt: Substance use: labs to monitor
cards.answerHtml:
• BAL, urine drug screen
  • AST, GGT; ALT (verify) (liver; disulfiram, naltrexone)
  • MCV, CBC
  • K, Mg, glucose; phosphate, Na (verify)
  • BUN/creatinine
  • CK if unconscious or stimulant/PCP toxicity
  • ECG (cocaine, meth); QT with methadone (verify)
  • HIV, hepatitis B/C, TB, pregnancy

Report: rising CIWA, low K or Mg, high CK
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Urine drug screen windows
cards.answerHtml:
Opioids: 12-24 h

Amphetamine: 1-3 days

Cocaine: 1-3 days (up to 7-12 days heavy)

Cannabis: 7-10 days casual, 2-4 weeks heavy (lecture: 4-6 weeks)

cards.prompt: Organs and electrolytes affected: alcohol
cards.answerHtml:
Brain: Wernicke-Korsakoff, atrophy, neuropathy

Heart: cardiomyopathy, hypertension, arrhythmia

Liver/GI: fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, varices

Blood: anemia, high MCV

Electrolytes: low Mg, K, thiamine, folate; low phosphate (verify); hypoglycemia (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Organs affected: cocaine, meth and other drugs
cards.promptHtml: Organs affected: cocaine, meth and other drugs
cards.answerHtml:
Stimulants: heart (MI, arrhythmia), brain (stroke), kidneys (rhabdomyolysis); meth: teeth, skin sores

Smoked drugs: lungs (COPD, cancer)

Injection: HIV, hepatitis, endocarditis

Inhalants: brain, kidney, liver

Opioids: respiratory depression, constipation

cards.prompt: Personality disorder: definition
cards.answerHtml:
Definition (six features):

  • enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior
  • deviates markedly from cultural expectations
  • pervasive and inflexible
  • begins in adolescence or early adulthood
  • stable over time
  • causes distress or impairment

Also: usually egosyntonic (patient does not see it as a problem)

Not a PD if: it starts after adulthood, comes and goes, or is caused by substances or a medical condition

cards.prompt: Cluster A overview
cards.answerHtml:
Theme: odd or eccentric

Disorders: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal

Hook: suspicious, detached or strange; rarely seek care; genetic link to schizophrenia

cards.prompt: Cluster B overview
cards.answerHtml:
Theme: dramatic, emotional, erratic

Disorders: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic (4)

Hook: impulsive, intense, boundary-testing; the most self-harm, aggression and staff splitting, so the highest safety priority

cards.prompt: Cluster C overview
cards.answerHtml:
Theme: anxious or fearful

Disorders: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive (OCPD)

Hook: fear of rejection (avoidant), of being left to cope alone (dependent), of losing control (OCPD); most likely to seek and stay in therapy

cards.prompt: Which cluster? (sorting card)
cards.answerHtml:
A (odd): paranoid = distrust; schizoid = loner; schizotypal = magical thinking

B (dramatic): antisocial = no remorse; borderline = splitting, self-harm; histrionic = attention-seeking; narcissistic = grandiose

C (anxious): avoidant = fears rejection; dependent = clings; OCPD = perfectionist, controlling

Count: 3 + 4 + 3 = 10

Not in a cluster: passive-aggressive PD (syllabus key term; not one of the 10 DSM-5-TR PDs)

cards.prompt: Personality development theories
cards.answerHtml:
Biologic: heritable temperament, limbic and frontal dysfunction (BPD)

Psychoanalytic: failed separation-individuation, projective identification

Cognitive: early maladaptive schemata

Linehan biosocial: emotional vulnerability + invalidating environment (basis of DBT)

ASPD: difficult temperament, poor attachment

cards.prompt: Paranoid personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: pervasive distrust, hypervigilant, holds grudges, hostile; violence and stalking risk

Example: "You're writing things down about me."

Nursing care:

  • honest, consistent, calm; keep every promise
  • never whisper or laugh within earshot
  • respect space; assess violence risk
  • once trust forms: acceptance, confrontation and reflection

Therapy: techniques to change thought patterns; antipsychotic only if psychotic

cards.prompt: Schizoid personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: detached loner, flat affect, indifferent to praise, criticism and relationships

Example: "I don't mind living alone; I don't need visitors."

Nursing care:

  • balance social activity (Boyd, the course answer): enough to prevent retreat, not so much it is intolerable
  • ATI: respect the need to isolate; its key marks "increase socialization" wrong
  • do not take lack of response personally

Therapy: social skills training; supportive psychotherapy

cards.prompt: Schizotypal personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: magical thinking, ideas of reference, odd dress and speech, paranoia; brief psychosis under stress

Example: "The radio is sending me messages."

Nursing care:

  • screen for depression and suicide
  • reinforce appropriate dress; teach cognitive skills
  • if psychotic, care as for schizophrenia

Therapy: social skills training; antipsychotic for paranoia

cards.prompt: Antisocial personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: disregard for others' rights, deceit, no remorse, aggression; age 18+ with conduct disorder before 15

Example: "That loser was in my way."

Nursing care:

  • high-alert safety for patient and staff first, then withdrawal
  • firm, consistent limits by all staff
  • no bargaining, lecturing or arguing; short-term agreed goals

Therapy: motivational interviewing, group, milieu, anger management

cards.prompt: Borderline personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: fear of abandonment, splitting, unstable self-image and mood, self-harm, emptiness

Example: "You're my favorite nurse; the night nurse is terrible."

Nursing care:

  • self-harm precautions: remove sharps, check pill hoarding, ask directly
  • consistent staff and boundaries; team meetings expose splitting
  • treat wounds matter-of-factly, then explore triggers
  • written safety plan + commitment to treatment, not a no-harm contract

Therapy: DBT (central); MBT

cards.prompt: Histrionic personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: attention-seeking, dramatic, seductive, shallow shifting emotions

Example: "You're the only nurse who understands me."

Nursing care:

  • keep professional boundaries with flirtation
  • build autonomy and problem solving
  • praise non-attention-seeking behavior

Therapy: psychotherapy, assertiveness groups

cards.prompt: Narcissistic personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: grandiose, needs admiration, lacks empathy; rage at criticism

Example: "This unit is beneath me; get the chief."

Nursing care:

  • no power struggles; stay respectful and consistent
  • concrete goals the patient owns

Therapy: long-term psychotherapy; treat comorbid depression or anxiety

cards.prompt: Borderline vs histrionic
cards.answerHtml:
Borderline: unstable self and mood, frantic fear of abandonment, splitting, self-harm and suicide risk; care = safety, consistency, DBT

Histrionic: attention-seeking, seductive, shallow emotion; care = boundaries, autonomy, assertiveness

Both: Cluster B, dramatic, emotional

cards.prompt: Antisocial vs borderline vs narcissistic
cards.answerHtml:
BPD: hurts self; needs closeness, fears abandonment

ASPD: hurts others; uses people, no remorse; conduct disorder before 15, law-breaking

Narcissistic: lacks empathy but not conduct disorder or law-breaking

cards.prompt: Avoidant personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: avoids people from fear of rejection and inadequacy; hypersensitive to criticism; wants closeness

Example: "They would find out I'm not good enough."

Nursing care:

  • no criticism; slow, patient trust
  • build self-esteem; point out past successes
  • screen for depression and suicide

Therapy: social skills training; long-term psychotherapy

cards.prompt: Dependent personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: clinging, submissive, cannot decide alone, urgently seeks a new relationship

Example: "Which gown should I wear? I can't go home alone."

Nursing care:

  • do not decide for the patient; support small decisions
  • teach adult skills and assertiveness
  • self-check for countertransference

Therapy: psychotherapy, assertiveness training; antidepressant or anxiolytic if anxiety blocks progress

cards.prompt: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: orderliness, perfectionism, control, workaholic, rigid; does not see it as a problem

Example: "I haven't taken a vacation in 8 years."

Nursing care:

  • treat physical symptoms first (insomnia, fatigue)
  • accept the need for order, then examine beliefs
  • avoid power struggles

Therapy: psychotherapy; SSRIs for comorbid anxiety and mood

cards.prompt: Avoidant vs schizoid
cards.answerHtml:
Avoidant: wants closeness but fears rejection; hypersensitive to criticism; care = no criticism, build self-esteem, reduce isolation

Schizoid: does not want closeness; indifferent to praise or criticism; care = respect solitude, balance activity

cards.prompt: OCPD vs OCD
cards.answerHtml:
OCPD: personality style of order and control; no true obsessions or compulsions; patient sees it as right (egosyntonic)

OCD: intrusive obsessions and compulsions that rise with anxiety; patient finds them excessive and distressing

cards.prompt: Fear of abandonment (borderline) vs fear of rejection (avoidant)
cards.promptHtml: Fear of abandonment (borderline) vs fear of rejection (avoidant)
cards.answerHtml:
Borderline: frantic fear of abandonment (DSM criterion 1; syllabus, Boyd, ATI text p.91)

Avoidant: fear of rejection and criticism

Dependent: fear of being left alone to care for self

Conflicting sources:

  • ATI answer key (ch 16, p.93-94) keys "I'm scared you're going to leave me" as avoidant
  • lecture slide 2 graphic prints abandonment in the avoidant box

Learn: borderline; recognize the quote as ATI's key only

cards.prompt: Impulse-control disorders: shared pattern
cards.answerHtml:
Core cycle: tension builds, the act brings pleasure or relief, remorse follows

Care: safety first, nonjudgmental, long-term outpatient and group therapy

Meds: depend on the target symptom; treat comorbid conditions

Includes: IED, kleptomania, pyromania

cards.prompt: Intermittent explosive disorder (IED)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: aggressive outbursts out of proportion to provocation; diagnosis of exclusion

Example: punches a wall after a minor tease, then sobs with shame

Nursing care: safety first, de-escalate, low stimulation, teach triggers and a stop-and-think plan; assess suicide risk

Therapy: anger management, group

Meds: SSRIs, GABAergic mood stabilizers, anxiolytics; medication alone is insufficient

cards.prompt: Kleptomania
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: irresistible urge to steal items not needed or wanted; tension then relief, then guilt

Example: a well-paid woman takes pens she later throws away

Nursing care: nonjudgmental; screen for depression, eating disorder, OCD; explore the tension-relief cycle

Therapy: behavior therapy

Meds: SSRIs, mood stabilizers, naltrexone (more research needed)

cards.prompt: Pyromania
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: irresistible urge to set fires, fascination with fire, gratification; not for anger, profit or politics

Example: sets dumpster fires and watches calmly, then helps afterward

Nursing care: safety first, protect others and property; screen for ASPD, substance use, depression

Therapy: CBT

Meds: none named in the lecture or Boyd; treat comorbid conditions

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: patient education
cards.answerHtml:
Teach:

  • a PD is a long-standing pattern, not a character flaw; it is treatable
  • coping skills at the moment of urge (pause, five senses, "I" statements)
  • self-harm warning signs, who to call, no pill hoarding
  • meds for target symptoms only; no OTC or street drugs
  • sleep, nutrition; alcohol raises overdose risk

Families: boundaries; stop covering for ASPD behavior

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: what we look for (red flags)
cards.promptHtml: Personality disorders: what we look for (red flags)
cards.answerHtml:
Act now:

  • suicidal talk, cutting, burning, swallowed objects, long sleeves in warm weather
  • threats, stalking, aggression
  • substance use or withdrawal
  • depression (schizotypal, avoidant)

Team alert: splitting

Also: impulsivity, dissociation, eating or purging signs, your own reaction

Rule: pick the answer that asks directly about self-harm

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: OK vs not OK
cards.answerHtml:
OK: talking about urges in words; coping skills; a standing time each shift; real choices; respectful disagreement; ignore harmless irritating behavior

Not OK: self-harm, violence, contraband, exploiting others, bargaining over rules, gifts or calls off shift, splitting

How to limit: name behavior, state expectation and consequence; same for every staff; calm, nonpunitive

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: nursing role
cards.answerHtml:
Role: support the therapist and model healthy interaction (not the primary therapist)

  • keep patient safe
  • therapeutic relationship
  • team-wide boundaries
  • teach and reinforce skills
  • manage meds for target symptoms
  • self-assess; use supervision
  • plan termination openly

Setting: hospital only for acute self-harm or violence

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: medications
cards.answerHtml:
Rule: target symptom, short duration, adjunct to therapy; choice depends on the root cause

No drug is FDA-approved for any PD (verify)

  • mood swings: mood stabilizers or atypical antipsychotics
  • depression: SSRIs, SNRIs
  • anxiety: buspirone; avoid benzodiazepines in BPD
  • paranoia or psychosis: low-dose antipsychotic
  • ASPD aggression: atypicals, lithium, anticonvulsants, stimulants; no drug treats ASPD itself
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: labs
cards.answerHtml:
No lab diagnoses a PD (verify); labs follow the drug or comorbidity

  • lithium: trough level (0.6-1.2 mEq/L), BUN/creatinine, thyroid, sodium
  • valproate: LFTs, CBC and platelets
  • atypicals: weight, glucose, lipids
  • substance use: urine drug screen
  • purging: potassium (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Personality disorders: organs and electrolytes affected
cards.answerHtml:
Not organ diseases; harm comes through behavior and drugs

  • self-harm: skin, GI tract (swallowed objects), bleeding, infection
  • alcohol and drugs: liver, pancreas
  • binge, purge: low potassium, low magnesium (verify)
  • weight-gaining drugs: glucose, lipids
  • lithium: low sodium or dehydration raises level
  • impulsive sex: STIs
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Splitting
cards.answerHtml:
Splitting: seeing people as all good or all bad; idealizes one nurse, devalues another (BPD)

Nursing:

  • consistent staff, same rules
  • share information in team meetings
  • do not take sides; redirect to feelings and the plan
  • validate the feeling without accepting the distortion

cards.prompt: Manipulation in personality disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: lying, charm, playing staff against each other, special requests

Nursing:

  • name the specific behavior; chart it objectively, not as "manipulative"
  • consistent limits and consequences, no punishment
  • no bargaining or special rules
  • do not take it personally

cards.prompt: Countertransference with personality disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Definition: the nurse's own emotional reaction to the patient (irritation, flattery, rescuing)

Why it matters: it can mirror how others react to the patient

Nursing:

  • self-assess before and during care
  • use supervision and team meetings
  • keep boundaries and professional role

cards.prompt: BPD self-cutting: what does the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: BPD self-cutting: what does the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Do:

  • treat the wound matter-of-factly, no punishment or extra attention
  • assess suicide intent and safety
  • afterward explore trigger, feelings and urge
  • teach alternatives (five senses, delay, DBT skills)
  • tell all staff; raise observation as needed

Use: a written safety plan + commitment to treatment, not a no-harm contract (syllabus and Pearson list one; Boyd: not effective)

cards.prompt: BPD patient asks for sessions after discharge
cards.promptHtml: BPD patient asks for sessions after discharge
cards.answerHtml:
Meaning: fear of abandonment

Do:

  • do not agree to extra sessions
  • acknowledge the fear; review progress
  • explore feelings about the ending
  • keep the professional role; do not extend the relationship
  • confirm the therapist's coverage, a crisis plan and follow-up (verify)

Prevent: state the end date early and count down sessions
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Anorexia nervosa (AN)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: restricted intake, intense fear of weight gain, body-image distortion, denial of seriousness

Weight: significantly low

Types:

  • restricting (diet, fast, exercise)
  • binge-eating/purging

Severity (BMI): mild 17+, moderate 16-16.99, severe 15-15.99, extreme under 15

cards.prompt: AN without low weight (OSFED)
cards.answerHtml:
Also called: atypical AN

Looks like: all AN criteria except low weight; weight normal or high

Key point: can still have full AN complications (bradycardia, electrolyte loss)

Nursing: treat like AN; weight alone never rules out an emergency

cards.prompt: Bulimia nervosa (BN)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: binge (within about 2 h) plus compensation (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, exercise), at least once a week for 3 months; secretive, shame

Weight: usually normal

Signs: Russell sign, enamel erosion, parotid swelling

Setting: usually outpatient

cards.prompt: Binge-eating disorder (BED)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: binges with loss of control, distress, guilt; eats until uncomfortably full

No purging or compensation

Weight: often overweight

Setting: outpatient

cards.prompt: Purging disorder (OSFED)
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics) after normal amounts of food, at least weekly, fear of weight gain

No binge (key difference from BN)

Weight: variable

Check: potassium, orthostatics, ECG, as for anyone who purges

cards.prompt: ARFID
cards.answerHtml:
Looks like: food avoidance from low interest, sensory issues, or fear of choking/vomiting

Weight: often low, or growth failure

Not like AN: no body-image distortion (verify)

Setting: outpatient; inpatient if unstable
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Other feeding/eating disorders: night eating, pica, rumination
cards.promptHtml: Other feeding/eating disorders: night eating, pica, rumination
cards.answerHtml:
Night eating syndrome (OSFED): eating after waking from sleep or excess after the evening meal; morning anorexia

Pica: eating non-food items (dirt, starch, ice) 1+ month

Rumination: repeated regurgitation, rechewing, reswallowing 1+ month

Diabulimia (not DSM): type 1 diabetic cuts insulin to lose weight, risk of DKA

cards.prompt: AN vs BN vs BED: assessment findings
cards.promptHtml: AN vs BN vs BED: assessment findings
cards.answerHtml:
AN: low weight, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo, amenorrhea

BN: normal weight, Russell sign, enamel erosion, parotid swelling, irregular periods

BED: overweight, hypertension possible, guilt

Exam tip: normal weight does not rule out a dangerous disorder

cards.prompt: Eating disorder risk factors and who to screen
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorder risk factors and who to screen
cards.answerHtml:
Risk: first-degree relative (3-5x risk), perfectionism, trauma, lean-sport athletes, LGBTQ/transgender, social media, bullying

Screen everyone: boys (males present at 16-24), older adults, any body size

Onset: AN 14-16; BN 15-24

Tools: EDE-Q, EAT-26 (over 20 needs follow-up), CHEAT

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: nursing priorities
cards.answerHtml:
Order:

  • 1. medical stability (cardiac, electrolytes) and suicide risk
  • 2. fluids, electrolytes, nutrition
  • 3. therapeutic relationship
  • 4. cognitive/behavioral work
  • 5. teaching, family, relapse prevention

Exam tip: cardiac monitoring comes before psychotherapy or weight contracts

cards.prompt: Patient admitted with AN: first nursing actions
cards.promptHtml: Patient admitted with AN: first nursing actions
cards.answerHtml:
Do:

  • vitals with orthostatic BP/pulse, temp; continuous cardiac monitoring
  • labs (K, Mg, Phos, glucose, Na, Ca, BUN, creatinine) and ECG
  • suicide and self-harm screen, set observation level
  • fluids/electrolytes and refeeding plan with dietitian
  • gown weight after voiding
  • start a firm, non-reactive relationship

cards.prompt: Therapeutic relationship with eating disorder patients
cards.answerHtml:
AN: mistrusts staff; be firm, accepting, patient, consistent, non-reactive; give a reason for every intervention

BN: wants to please, ashamed; stay nonjudgmental

Avoid: power struggles, arguing about body size, "why" questions

Also: check your own frustration

cards.prompt: Eating disorder patient education
cards.answerHtml:
Teach after medically stable and eating again.

  • starvation harms every organ; restriction drives binges
  • regular meals, correct food myths
  • realistic small goals (+300 kcal/day)
  • triggers, food/mood diary
  • privileges tied to weight are not punishment
  • BN: laxatives cause water loss only; K loss, dental, cardiac damage
  • support groups do not replace therapy

cards.prompt: Teaching family and friends
cards.answerHtml:
Do: say you care and are concerned; encourage professional help

Don't:

  • discuss weight, calories, eating habits
  • comment on appearance ("you look healthy" sounds like "fat")
  • power struggle; you cannot force eating

Therapy: family-based therapy starts even while inpatient

cards.prompt: Weight and intake monitoring
cards.answerHtml:
Weigh: same time (on arising, after voiding), same scale, same gown

Record: all intake and output

Goal: 1-2 lb/week (ATI: 2-3 lb/week)

Discharge from hospital: at least 85% of ideal weight, then partial hospitalization or intensive outpatient

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: what the nurse allows and encourages (OK)
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorders: what the nurse allows and encourages (OK)
cards.answerHtml:
OK:

  • expressing fear, anger, shame about food and body
  • calm meals with set time limit (about 30 min) and staff present
  • questions about the plan, with a reason for each rule
  • earned privileges tied to intake or weight goals
  • small goals, journaling, relaxation, imagery
  • family visits and groups that follow the unit plan

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: what the nurse stops or limits (not OK)
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorders: what the nurse stops or limits (not OK)
cards.answerHtml:
Not OK:

  • skipping meals, hiding or discarding food, cutting food tiny
  • bargaining or negotiating portions and menus
  • purging, secret exercise
  • falsifying weights (water loading, hidden weights)
  • self-harm
  • long talks about food, calories, weight
  • power struggles; nurse never argues, pleads, or punishes

cards.prompt: Meal supervision and bathroom after meals
cards.answerHtml:
Meals: sit with patient, set time limit (about 30 min), no bargaining

After meals: observe about 1 hour; accompany to the bathroom if purging is suspected

Why: prevents vomiting and hidden food disposal

If refuses: offer liquid supplement; NG tube if life-threatening malnutrition

State limits calmly and non-punitively

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: labs to monitor
cards.answerHtml:
Routine: CBC, K, Na, Cl/bicarb, Mg, Phos, Ca, vitamin D, BUN, creatinine, glucose, LFTs and albumin, TSH, ECG

Also: amylase (purging), stool occult blood, DEXA bone scan, abdominal x-ray

Findings: low K/Mg/Phos, low glucose, anemia, leukopenia, high BUN, high cholesterol

Recheck often during refeeding

cards.prompt: Potassium (K) in eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Low from: vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, dehydration

Organ effect: heart (arrhythmia, flat T/U waves (verify), sudden death) and muscle (weakness, cramps)

Risk: highest in BN/purging

Nurse: ECG, replace K as ordered; low Mg keeps K hard to correct (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Sodium (Na) in eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Low from: water loading, laxatives, diuretics

High from: dehydration (verify)

Organ effect: brain (confusion, seizures if severe)

Nurse: neuro checks, seizure precautions, watch I&O and water loading before weigh-ins
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Chloride and acid-base: vomiting vs laxatives
cards.answerHtml:
Vomiting: loses stomach HCl, so hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis (tetany possible (verify))

Laxatives: lose bicarbonate, so metabolic acidosis

Why it matters: the pattern shows the purging method

Note: lecture slide says "hyperchloremic", likely a typo
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Magnesium (Mg) in eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Low from: malnutrition; falls further in refeeding

Organ effect: heart (arrhythmia, prolonged QT (verify)), muscle weakness, seizures (verify)

Nurse: replace as ordered; Mg must be fixed for K to correct (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Phosphate (Phos) in eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Low from: malnutrition; drops further when refeeding begins

Organ effect: heart and lungs (cardiac and respiratory failure in refeeding)

Key: hypophosphatemia is the precursor to refeeding syndrome and can cause sudden death

Nurse: recheck often early in refeeding; replace as ordered

cards.prompt: Cardiac effects and ECG in eating disorders
cards.promptHtml: Cardiac effects and ECG in eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Heart: muscle shrinks; bradycardia, hypotension, orthostasis, sudden death

ECG: sinus bradycardia, prolonged QT/QTc, PACs/PVCs, V-tach

Ipecac: cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias

Nurse: continuous monitoring, repeat ECG during refeeding and when a psychotropic is added (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Eating disorders: bone, teeth, GI, kidney, endocrine effects
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorders: bone, teeth, GI, kidney, endocrine effects
cards.answerHtml:
Bone: osteopenia/osteoporosis (low estrogen, Ca, vitamin D), sarcopenia; fall precautions, PT

Teeth: enamel erosion of front teeth, caries; parotid swelling; rinse, don't brush right after vomiting (verify)

GI: slow emptying, constipation, SMA syndrome, esophageal tears

Kidney: dehydration, high BUN

Endocrine: amenorrhea, low estrogen, hypothyroid pattern, hypoglycemia
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Refeeding syndrome: what and why
cards.answerHtml:
What: dangerous shift when nutrition restarts after starvation; insulin rises and Phos, K, Mg move into cells

Result: low Phos/K/Mg, thiamine deficiency, fluid overload, respiratory and cardiac failure

When: within about 5 days (guidelines: 3-7)

Key: hypophosphatemia first, can cause sudden death

cards.prompt: Refeeding syndrome: who is at risk and what to report
cards.promptHtml: Refeeding syndrome: who is at risk and what to report
cards.answerHtml:
At risk (verify): very low BMI, little intake for days, rapid weight loss, low baseline K/Phos/Mg, purging, alcohol

Report now:

  • tachycardia, arrhythmia, new edema
  • dyspnea, crackles
  • confusion, weakness, seizures
  • falling Phos/K/Mg, glucose swings
  • sudden weight gain from fluid
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Refeeding syndrome: nursing actions
cards.answerHtml:
Prevent: feed in hospital; gradual calories, +300 kcal/day (range 1,000-3,500; high-calorie start 1,500); thiamine and electrolyte correction (verify)

Monitor: electrolytes, vitals, I&O, weights, edema

If suspected: report to provider now, expect cardiac monitoring, slowed feeding (verify), electrolyte replacement

Also: no exercise, constant supervision, bathroom monitoring
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Hospital admission criteria: AN
cards.answerHtml:
Boyd (ATI value in parentheses):

  • heart rate near 40 (below 40)
  • BP below 80/50 (SBP below 70)
  • temp below 36.1 C / 97 F (below 36 C / 96.8 F)
  • weight below 85% of ideal (or over 30% loss in 6 months)
  • low K, Phos, or Mg

Psychiatric: suicide risk, severe depression, failed outpatient care

Use Boyd's values.

cards.prompt: Hospital admission criteria: BN
cards.answerHtml:
Admit for:

  • extreme dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
  • depression and suicidality
  • symptoms that did not remit with outpatient care

Otherwise: BN is usually outpatient

Exam tip: pick the patient with bradycardia, hypotension, low K/Phos, or suicidal ideation, not one refusing breakfast

cards.prompt: Medications for eating disorders: depend on the disorder and target
cards.promptHtml: Medications for eating disorders: depend on the disorder and target
cards.answerHtml:
AN: no FDA-approved drug; olanzapine for weight, anxiety, ED thoughts; SSRIs only for comorbid depression/OCD; short-term anxiolytic for meal panic (verify)

BN: fluoxetine

BED: lisdexamfetamine

Never replaces nutrition and psychotherapy

Avoid: bupropion (seizures)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Eating disorder therapies: which works for what
cards.promptHtml: Eating disorder therapies: which works for what
cards.answerHtml:
Family-based: AN in adolescents (enmeshment)

CBT: BN, BED (distorted thoughts, cues, food rules)

DBT: AN, BN (emotional dysregulation, self-harm)

IPT: AN, BN (role transitions)

Support groups: maintenance, never a substitute

cards.prompt: Naloxone (Narcan)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: opioid antagonist (rescue drug)

Use: suspected opioid overdose: slow breathing, pinpoint pupils, unresponsive

Monitor:

  • IV works in about 2 min but lasts only 30–81 min
  • reassess breathing often; repeat doses are common (re-sedation)

Stop & report: precipitated withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, tachycardia)

Teach:

  • airway and ventilation first, naloxone with them
  • Narcan is naloxone; routes IM, SQ, IV, intranasal (inhalation)
  • does not reverse xylazine, but still give it (fentanyl is usually present)

cards.prompt: Naltrexone (Vivitrol; ReVia)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: opioid antagonist (maintenance; blocks reward)

Use: preventing relapse in alcohol or opioid use disorder; 50 mg PO daily or 380 mg IM monthly

Monitor:

  • opioid-free 7–10 days first (negative urine screen)
  • LFTs (liver injury)

Stop & report: precipitated withdrawal if opioids are on board

Teach:

  • wear a medical ID: opioid pain medicine won't work
  • big opioid doses to override it can kill
  • does not treat withdrawal; not for pregnancy

cards.prompt: Flumazenil (Romazicon)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: benzodiazepine receptor antagonist (IV)

Use: reverses sedation and toxicity of a benzodiazepine overdose, on provider order

Monitor:

  • airway and breathing first, then the antidote
  • re-sedation can follow (verify)

Stop & report: seizures: risk in benzodiazepine-dependent patients and mixed overdoses (verify)

Teach:

  • no antidote for barbiturates or alcohol
  • supportive care is often chosen instead (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Disulfiram (Antabuse)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: aldehyde dehydrogenase blocker (aversion therapy)

Use: motivated, abstinent patient with alcohol use disorder; informed consent required

Monitor: LFTs (hepatotoxicity); first dose at least 12 h after last drink

Stop & report: reaction to any alcohol: flushing, vomiting, sweating, palpitations, hypotension, then respiratory depression, seizures, collapse

Teach:

  • avoid hidden alcohol: mouthwash, cough syrup, aftershave, hand sanitizer
  • reaction possible up to 2 weeks after stopping
  • medical alert ID; it does not reduce craving

cards.prompt: Acamprosate (Campral)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: glutamate modulator (reduces craving and abstinence discomfort)

Use: maintaining alcohol abstinence; start only after the patient is abstinent

Monitor: BUN and creatinine; avoid in kidney impairment

Stop & report: diarrhea (keep fluids up)

Teach:

  • 333–666 mg three times a day with meals (hard for adherence)
  • eases dysphoria, anxiety, restlessness of abstinence
  • join a 12-step or self-help group

cards.prompt: Methadone (Dolophine)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: full opioid agonist (substitution therapy)

Use: opioid detox and long-term maintenance; prevents withdrawal without a high

Monitor: respiratory depression, sedation; QT on ECG (verify)

Stop & report: slow breathing, extreme drowsiness

Teach:

  • daily oral dose, only from a federally approved clinic
  • long half-life, 15–30 h (syllabus says "low"; long is correct)
  • pair with a 12-step program

Taper/withdrawal: taper slowly; withdrawal starts in 1–3 days and can last weeks
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Buprenorphine (Subutex)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: partial opioid agonist (schedule III)

Use: opioid withdrawal and maintenance; can be started during active withdrawal

Monitor: craving and adherence

Stop & report: precipitated withdrawal if started too soon after a full agonist (verify)

Teach:

  • given sublingually (tablet or buccal film)
  • a primary care provider can prescribe it (methadone needs a clinic)
  • buprenorphine-only is the preferred product in pregnancy
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: partial opioid agonist plus opioid antagonist (combination)

Use: opioid detox and long-term maintenance, office-based

Monitor: craving and adherence

Teach:

  • sublingual tablet or buccal film
  • lecture and Boyd: the naloxone protects against overdose if opioids are misused; in practice it deters injecting (verify)
  • in pregnancy use buprenorphine-only (Subutex) instead
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Methadone (Dolophine) vs buprenorphine (Subutex, Suboxone) vs naltrexone (Vivitrol)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: full agonist vs partial agonist vs antagonist

  • Methadone: daily, approved clinic only; respiratory depression
  • Buprenorphine: sublingual; primary care can prescribe; can start during withdrawal; buprenorphine-only in pregnancy
  • Naltrexone: blocks opioids; needs 7–10 opioid-free days; monthly IM option

Teach: these are real treatment, not "swapping one drug for another"; pair with counseling or a 12-step group

cards.prompt: Thiamine (vitamin B1)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: vitamin B1

Use: every heavy drinker in detox; prevents and treats Wernicke encephalopathy (and Korsakoff); also part of refeeding care

Monitor: confusion, ataxia, abnormal eye movements = Wernicke: give thiamine now, notify provider

Teach:

  • 100 mg PO 3–4 times daily, or IM/IV
  • give before or with IV glucose (verify)
  • given with folate, magnesium, multivitamin
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Chlordiazepoxide (Librium) and lorazepam (Ativan) for alcohol withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Class: benzodiazepines (substitution therapy; cross-tolerant with alcohol)

Use: alcohol withdrawal: CIWA-Ar-guided, around the clock or PRN, short-term

Monitor:

  • VS and neuro checks; CIWA-Ar (under 10 usually needs no added dose)
  • seizure precautions (seizures within 48 h; DTs 48–72 h)

Taper/withdrawal: taper over several days; long-acting chlordiazepoxide tapers smoothest; lorazepam for older adults and liver disease

cards.prompt: Clonidine (Catapres) / lofexidine (Lucemyra) for opioid withdrawal
cards.answerHtml:
Class: alpha-2 agonists

Use: autonomic opioid-withdrawal symptoms (sweating, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, runny nose, goose bumps); do not reduce craving

Monitor: baseline and ongoing BP and HR (hypotension, bradycardia (verify))

Teach:

  • drowsy: avoid tasks needing alertness
  • dry mouth: sugarless gum, hard candy, sips of water

Taper/withdrawal: taper, don't stop abruptly: rebound hypertension (verify); lofexidine is approved for up to 14 days (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Varenicline (Chantix)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: nicotinic receptor partial agonist (ATI: agonist)

Use: smoking cessation; cuts craving and withdrawal, blocks nicotine's reward

Monitor: BP; glucose control in diabetes; mood

Stop & report: new depression, suicidal thoughts, unpredictable behavior; chest pain: seek care now

Teach:

  • take after a meal (nausea common); follow the titration
  • banned for truck and bus drivers, pilots, air traffic controllers: ask the patient's occupation

cards.prompt: Nicotine replacement (patch, gum, lozenge)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: nicotine replacement therapy

Use: tobacco cessation; nearly doubles the quit rate

Stop & report: skin reaction under the patch: remove it

Teach:

  • patch: clean dry skin each morning, off at bedtime (16 h); rotate sites; remove before MRI; no other nicotine
  • gum: chew slowly over 30 min; nothing by mouth 15 min before/during; max 6 months
  • lozenge: dissolves 20–30 min; max 5 per 6 h, 20/day

cards.prompt: Fluoxetine (Prozac) in eating disorders
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI

Use:

  • bulimia: FDA-approved; cuts binge and purge episodes even without depression; usually 60 mg/day, with CBT
  • anorexia: treats comorbid depression or OCD only, after weight is restored; weaker at low weight

Monitor: suicidal thoughts (boxed warning in youth), agitation, behavior change

Teach: take in the morning; full effect up to 4 weeks; report sexual dysfunction

cards.prompt: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: CNS stimulant (ADHD drug)

Use: binge-eating disorder: reduces binges by regulating appetite; FDA-approved for moderate to severe BED in adults (verify)

Monitor: HR, BP, sleep

Stop & report: misuse: habit-forming, may not suit a patient with substance use disorder

Teach: last dose before 4 p.m.; not a weight-loss drug (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Olanzapine (Zyprexa) in anorexia nervosa
cards.answerHtml:
Class: second-generation antipsychotic (off-label in anorexia)

Use: helps weight gain; lowers anxiety and the intensity of eating-disorder thoughts

Monitor:

  • weight, glucose, lipids (diabetes, dyslipidemia)
  • ECG: starvation already prolongs QT

Teach: she may fear weight gain, so explain the purpose honestly; medication never replaces nutrition and therapy

cards.prompt: Anorexia nervosa: is there an FDA-approved drug?
cards.promptHtml: Anorexia nervosa: is there an FDA-approved drug?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: none; no drug is FDA-approved for anorexia (Lecture; Boyd p.1516 says fluoxetine, but that approval is for bulimia)

Use: drugs target the root cause:

  • olanzapine: weight, anxiety, eating-disorder thoughts
  • SSRIs: comorbid depression or OCD
  • anxiolytics: mealtime panic

Stop & report: bupropion is contraindicated (seizure risk with purging, low electrolytes)

Teach: nutrition and psychotherapy come first

cards.prompt: Which drug types target BPD symptoms, and which to avoid?
cards.promptHtml: Which drug types target BPD symptoms, and which to avoid?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: mood stabilizers, atypical antipsychotics, SSRIs, for target symptoms only

Use:

  • mood swings: lithium, valproate, lamotrigine; low-dose aripiprazole, quetiapine
  • depression: SSRIs, SNRIs (weak evidence)
  • anxiety: buspirone, the safer choice

Stop & report: avoid benzodiazepines (habituation, misuse); question a lorazepam or alprazolam order

Teach: short-term adjunct to DBT; limit supply if suicidal; ask about OTC drugs and herbals

cards.prompt: Lithium carbonate (Lithobid; syllabus: Eskalith)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Drug of choice for acute mania and maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder; also lowers suicide risk and has a mild antidepressant effect in bipolar depression.
  • Onset is slow (5–7 days, up to 2 weeks), so an antipsychotic or short-term benzodiazepine is often added until it takes effect.
  • Narrow therapeutic range; never stopped abruptly (see level and monitoring cards).

cards.prompt: What is lithium's therapeutic serum range during acute mania, and for maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder?
cards.promptHtml: What is lithium's therapeutic serum range during acute mania, and for maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Therapeutic level: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (lecture).
  • Acute mania may be run higher: about 0.8–1.4 mEq/L (Boyd Ch12). (Townsend/Psych Notes/ATI: 1.0–1.5.)
  • Levels above 1.5 mEq/L are treated as toxic.

cards.prompt: A patient started on lithium for acute mania has a serum level of 1.2 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: A patient started on lithium for acute mania has a serum level of 1.2 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Administer the next dose as scheduled.
  • 1.2 mEq/L is an expected level during acute mania — not a reason to withhold the dose or request a stat repeat level.

cards.prompt: What are the signs of mild lithium toxicity, roughly under 1.5 mEq/L?
cards.promptHtml: What are the signs of mild lithium toxicity, roughly under 1.5 mEq/L?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Metallic taste, fine hand tremor, nausea, polyuria/polydipsia, loose stools, muscle weakness, fatigue, weight gain, edema, memory problems.
  • These often overlap with expected early side effects and tend to improve over time.

cards.prompt: What are the signs of moderate lithium toxicity, roughly 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, and what should the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: What are the signs of moderate lithium toxicity, roughly 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, and what should the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Severe diarrhea/vomiting, drowsiness/sedation, muscle weakness, ataxia/poor coordination, coarse tremor, slurred speech, tinnitus, blurred vision, confusion, muscle twitching, asymmetric reflexes.
  • Withhold the dose, notify the provider, and obtain a repeat level.
  • ATI splits this band into early (1.5–2.0, withhold/notify) and advanced (2.0–2.5, acute care); Boyd treats 1.5–2.5 as one moderate band.

cards.prompt: What are the signs of severe, life-threatening lithium toxicity, above about 2.5 mEq/L, and how is it treated?
cards.promptHtml: What are the signs of severe, life-threatening lithium toxicity, above about 2.5 mEq/L, and how is it treated?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Cardiac arrhythmias, nystagmus, coarse tremor/fasciculations, visual or tactile hallucinations, oliguria progressing to renal failure, seizures, coma, death.
  • Hemodialysis is the definitive treatment; there is no antidote (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: A patient on lithium has a level of 3.0 mEq/L. What does the nurse see, and what are the priority actions?
cards.promptHtml: A patient on lithium has a level of 3.0 mEq/L. What does the nurse see, and what are the priority actions?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Severe, life-threatening toxicity: above 2.5 mEq/L in both the ATI and Boyd bands.
  • Expect arrhythmias, nystagmus, coarse tremor/fasciculations, visual/tactile hallucinations, oliguria progressing to renal failure, seizures, rapid progression to coma and death.
  • Hold the next dose immediately; notify the provider; obtain a stat repeat level plus electrolytes/creatinine.
  • Assess airway/LOC, start seizure precautions (fall precautions and cardiac monitoring, verify), and push fluids (oral, or IV isotonic saline if the patient can't drink).
  • Severe toxicity is treated with hemodialysis.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What definitive treatment is used for a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L, and at what thresholds is it typically started?
cards.promptHtml: What definitive treatment is used for a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L, and at what thresholds is it typically started?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Hemodialysis — the definitive treatment for severe lithium toxicity; there is no antidote (verify).
  • Boyd: may be necessary in severe toxicity; ATI: can be warranted above 2.5 mEq/L.
  • Common triggers: a level above 4.0 mEq/L, or above 2.5 mEq/L with seizures, dysrhythmias, decreased consciousness, or kidney impairment (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Why doesn't activated charcoal help treat a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L?
cards.promptHtml: Why doesn't activated charcoal help treat a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Activated charcoal does not bind lithium (verify).
  • Management is supportive: IV fluids, possible gastric lavage after an acute ingestion, and hemodialysis for severe cases.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: How long does it take for lithium toxicity to resolve once the drug is stopped, and what permanent damage can severe toxicity cause?
cards.promptHtml: How long does it take for lithium toxicity to resolve once the drug is stopped, and what permanent damage can severe toxicity cause?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Mild toxicity usually resolves within 24–48 hours of stopping lithium.
  • Severe toxicity can leave permanent neurologic (cerebellar) damage (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: When should a trough lithium level be drawn relative to the last dose?
cards.promptHtml: When should a trough lithium level be drawn relative to the last dose?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • 10–12 hours after the last dose, in the morning, before the next (morning) dose.
  • In the hospital, the morning dose is held until the blood is drawn, to avoid a falsely high level.

cards.prompt: How often are lithium levels checked during initiation/acute treatment versus stable maintenance?
cards.promptHtml: How often are lithium levels checked during initiation/acute treatment versus stable maintenance?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Initiation/acute phase: twice weekly (Boyd Ch26, Townsend) until the therapeutic level is reached.
  • Stable maintenance: every 2 months (lecture). (Boyd Ch26: every 2–3 months.)
  • Recheck closely after any dose change (ATI), and after a new interacting drug or illness (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What baseline and ongoing lab work is needed for a patient starting lithium?
cards.promptHtml: What baseline and ongoing lab work is needed for a patient starting lithium?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Renal function (BUN, creatinine) and thyroid function (TSH) — baseline, then every 6 months (ATI: thyroid annually).
  • Electrolytes (especially sodium), calcium, CBC every 6 months; ECG if over 40 or with cardiac history (verify); pregnancy test (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Why do low sodium intake, dehydration, or fluid loss (vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating) raise lithium toxicity risk, and what should the nurse teach?
cards.promptHtml: Why do low sodium intake, dehydration, or fluid loss (vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating) raise lithium toxicity risk, and what should the nurse teach?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • The kidney handles lithium like sodium — when sodium or fluid is low, it reabsorbs more lithium, raising the blood level.
  • Teach: keep sodium intake normal and consistent (never start a low-salt diet without the prescriber; add salt with heavy sweating or exercise); drink 6–8 glasses of water a day (Townsend); limit caffeine.
  • Hold the next dose and call the provider for vomiting, diarrhea, or heavy sweating — fluid loss raises the level.

cards.prompt: Which drugs raise lithium levels or add to its toxicity risk?
cards.promptHtml: Which drugs raise lithium levels or add to its toxicity risk?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) can raise levels 30–60% within days — recommend aspirin instead for pain relief; thiazide diuretics (the most dangerous diuretic), loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), and ACE inhibitors also raise levels; ARBs too (verify). Fluoxetine and alcohol may too.
  • Carbamazepine, haloperidol, and methyldopa can cause neurotoxicity even when the lithium level itself looks normal.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What common (expected) side effects does lithium cause, and how does the nurse tell them apart from early toxicity?
cards.promptHtml: What common (expected) side effects does lithium cause, and how does the nurse tell them apart from early toxicity?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Expected: fine hand tremor, metallic taste, nausea, polyuria/polydipsia, mild diarrhea, drowsiness, muscle weakness, weight gain, edema — follow peak levels and fade over the first few weeks.
  • Toxicity signals: a tremor turning coarse, or mild nausea/loose stools progressing to severe diarrhea, vomiting, ataxia, or slurred speech.

cards.prompt: What long-term thyroid and kidney effects can lithium cause?
cards.promptHtml: What long-term thyroid and kidney effects can lithium cause?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Hypothyroidism/goiter after 6–18 months (more common in women): dry skin, constipation, bradycardia, hair loss, cold intolerance, weight gain; treated with levothyroxine while lithium continues.
  • Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: lithium blunts the kidney's response to ADH (verify), causing large dilute-urine volumes and thirst; monitor intake/output; ATI lists a potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone) for polyuria.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What should the nurse teach a woman of childbearing age about lithium and pregnancy?
cards.promptHtml: What should the nurse teach a woman of childbearing age about lithium and pregnancy?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Crosses the placenta: first-trimester birth defects (classically cardiac, Ebstein anomaly, verify) and third-trimester neonatal toxicity (hypotonia, cyanosis, diabetes insipidus).
  • Do not breastfeed; plan pregnancy with the prescriber before stopping birth control (Case 6).
  • Thyroid monitoring is especially important in women, since lithium-induced hypothyroidism is more common in them.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Why must adherence to lithium be especially consistent, and what is the most common reason patients stop taking it?
cards.promptHtml: Why must adherence to lithium be especially consistent, and what is the most common reason patients stop taking it?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Abrupt discontinuation causes relapse of mania/depression in almost half of patients within weeks, and lithium may work less well if restarted; short half-life also means immediate-release forms need 2–3 consistent doses/day.
  • Most often stopped due to mental slowness, poor concentration, and memory problems; onset of effect is 5–7 days, up to 2 weeks.

cards.prompt: What are the overall nursing implications for a patient on lithium therapy — what should they be taught to report?
cards.promptHtml: What are the overall nursing implications for a patient on lithium therapy — what should they be taught to report?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Draw trough levels correctly; hold the morning dose until drawn.
  • Report a tremor turning coarse, severe GI symptoms, confusion, or illness causing fluid loss — all can signal a rising level.
  • Keep sodium/fluids consistent; avoid NSAIDs, thiazides, and ACE inhibitors unless monitored; never stop abruptly; attend renal/thyroid/pregnancy monitoring.

cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol); haloperidol decanoate (Haldol Decanoate)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic, high potency (butyrophenone).

  • Use: schizophrenia, acute psychosis/agitation, mania, Tourette disorder
  • Stop & report: haloperidol + lithium can cause encephalopathy — report confusion, new EPS, fever, or high WBC
  • Teach: decanoate is a deep IM Z-track depot with a dry ≥21-gauge needle; never give it IV; don't massage the site

cards.prompt: Fluphenazine (formerly Prolixin); fluphenazine decanoate
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic, high potency (phenothiazine).

  • Use: psychotic disorders; long-term maintenance by decanoate depot
  • Teach: decanoate is usually given every 2–3 weeks (Boyd lists every 3 weeks); the oral concentrate can cause contact dermatitis — avoid skin contact

cards.prompt: Chlorpromazine (formerly Thorazine)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic, low potency (phenothiazine).

  • Use: schizophrenia, mania, severe nausea/vomiting, intractable hiccups
  • Stop & report: strong alpha-1 blockade causes severe orthostatic hypotension, worst after IM doses — keep the patient lying down ~30 min (verify) and check BP before ambulating
  • Teach: photosensitivity and skin pigmentation (orange to blue-gray) — use sunscreen; avoid skin contact with the liquid concentrate
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril; Versacloz)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic — reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

  • Use: used last, when other antipsychotics have not worked; also reduces recurrent suicidal behavior
  • Stop & report (boxed warnings): myocarditis in months 1–2 (verify) (fever, tachycardia, chest pain, dyspnea); dose-related seizures, highest risk with rapid titration
  • Teach: GI hypomotility can progress to bowel obstruction (verify) — start a bowel regimen day one (verify); nighttime sialorrhea — sugar-free gum
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Risperidone (Risperdal); paliperidone (Invega)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics (paliperidone is risperidone's active metabolite (verify)).

  • Use: schizophrenia; acute mania; autism-related irritability (risperidone)
  • Monitor: paliperidone is excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys — few liver interactions; use cautiously in renal impairment
  • Teach: starting Risperdal Consta (LAI) — continue oral risperidone the first 3 weeks while blood levels build (verify). Invega Sustenna: monthly; Trinza: every 3 months; Hafyera: every 6 months

(Hyperprolactinemia is its own card)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Olanzapine (Zyprexa)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Use: schizophrenia; bipolar mania/maintenance; IM for acute agitation
  • Stop & report: high risk of weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia — tied with clozapine for the worst
  • Teach: smoking induces CYP1A2 and lowers olanzapine levels; quitting raises levels and can cause sedation, hypotension, or seizures — report any change in smoking

(Zyprexa Relprevv post-injection monitoring is its own card)

cards.prompt: Quetiapine (Seroquel; Seroquel XR)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Use: schizophrenia; acute mania; bipolar depression; adjunct for major depression (XR)
  • Monitor: cataract risk — eye (lens) exam at baseline and about every 6 months (verify)
  • Teach: marked sedation, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, constipation; CYP3A4 substrate — avoid grapefruit; ketoconazole/erythromycin/fluconazole raise its level
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Ziprasidone (Geodon)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Use: schizophrenia; acute mania
  • Stop & report: QTc prolongation — the most of the second-generation drugs, risk of torsades de pointes; baseline ECG, correct potassium/magnesium first; report palpitations, fainting, or dizziness
  • Teach: take with a meal of at least 500 kcal (Boyd) — food roughly doubles absorption (lecture: ~350 — likely lurasidone's figure)

cards.prompt: Aripiprazole (Abilify)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic — dopamine D2/5-HT1A partial agonist (ATI calls it third-generation).

  • Use: schizophrenia; bipolar mania; adjunct for major depression; autism irritability
  • Stop & report: akathisia is the leading reason patients stop it — ask, "Is the restlessness in your muscles or in your mind?"
  • Teach: Abilify Maintena (LAI) — continue oral aripiprazole for 14 days after the first injection

cards.prompt: Lurasidone (Latuda)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Use: schizophrenia; bipolar I depression (alone or with lithium/valproate)
  • Monitor: low risk of weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia; no anticholinergic effects
  • Teach: take with food, at least 350 kcal — roughly doubles absorption; avoid grapefruit (CYP3A4)

cards.prompt: Xanomeline–trospium (Cobenfy)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Antipsychotic — central muscarinic M1/M4 agonist (xanomeline) with a peripheral antimuscarinic (trospium); no dopamine D2 blockade.

  • Use: schizophrenia — newest approved agent; no EPS or weight gain from D2 blockade (verify)
  • Teach: take with food (course lecture) (label: 1 h before or 2 h after a meal)
  • Monitor: fast heart rate, liver impairment, anticholinergic effects (constipation, urinary retention), nausea, dyspepsia, vomiting, diarrhea
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril): which blood counts must be monitored, and what values require holding or stopping the drug?
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine (Clozaril): which blood counts must be monitored, and what values require holding or stopping the drug?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Monitor ANC: baseline ANC ≥1,500/µL to start; weekly × 6 months, then every 2 weeks, and for 4 weeks after stopping
  • ANC <1,000 → interrupt (verify); ANC <500 = severe neutropenia → stop; watch for infection
  • Sore throat or fever → hold the dose until a count is drawn

(Boyd: WBC <3,500 / granulocytes <1,500 — older rule)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril): what should the nurse do if the patient develops a fever or sore throat, and why?
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine (Clozaril): what should the nurse do if the patient develops a fever or sore throat, and why?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Hold the dose and obtain a WBC/ANC before the next dose
  • Notify the prescriber — this may be early agranulocytosis (fever, sore throat, malaise, mouth sores are the warning signs)

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril), olanzapine (Zyprexa), risperidone (Risperdal), and quetiapine (Seroquel): what metabolic labs are checked, and on what schedule?
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine (Clozaril), olanzapine (Zyprexa), risperidone (Risperdal), and quetiapine (Seroquel): what metabolic labs are checked, and on what schedule?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics.

  • Weight/BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose/HbA1c, fasting lipids, blood pressure
  • Baseline, then weight monthly x3 then quarterly; glucose and lipids within 3 months then annually
  • >5% weight gain → more frequent labs, consider switching drugs

cards.prompt: Risperidone (Risperdal): what hormonal side effect is it most strongly linked to, and what are its signs?
cards.promptHtml: Risperidone (Risperdal): what hormonal side effect is it most strongly linked to, and what are its signs?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Hyperprolactinemia — risperidone is the second-generation drug most linked to it
  • Gynecomastia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, sexual dysfunction
  • Check prolactin level if these symptoms appear

cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol) and risperidone (Risperdal): what mechanism of action produces their effect on psychotic symptoms?
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol (Haldol) and risperidone (Risperdal): what mechanism of action produces their effect on psychotic symptoms?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (haloperidol) and second-generation (risperidone) antipsychotics.

  • Both block dopamine D2 receptors, which reduces psychotic symptoms
  • Second-generation drugs like risperidone also block serotonin 5-HT2A receptors

cards.prompt: Syllabus quiz Q15: name two drugs in the same chemical family as chlorpromazine (Thorazine). Is that family still the most commonly used group?
cards.promptHtml: Syllabus quiz Q15: name two drugs in the same chemical family as chlorpromazine (Thorazine). Is that family still the most commonly used group?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Phenothiazines (a first-generation antipsychotic chemical family) — e.g., chlorpromazine (Thorazine), fluphenazine (Prolixin); also perphenazine (Trilafon), trifluoperazine (Stelazine), thioridazine (Mellaril).

  • No longer: second-generation drugs are now first-line and the most used; first-generation only when those fail or cannot be used (course lecture)
  • (Syllabus Q15 answer: phenothiazines, the most commonly used group)

cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol), risperidone (Risperdal), olanzapine (Zyprexa), and quetiapine (Seroquel): what boxed warning applies when they are used for dementia-related psychosis in older adults?
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol (Haldol), risperidone (Risperdal), olanzapine (Zyprexa), and quetiapine (Seroquel): what boxed warning applies when they are used for dementia-related psychosis in older adults?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First- and second-generation antipsychotics.

  • Boxed warning: increased death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis (mostly infection and cardiovascular events)
  • Not approved for this use

cards.prompt: Zyprexa Relprevv (long-acting olanzapine): what reaction requires a 3-hour observation period after every injection?
cards.promptHtml: Zyprexa Relprevv (long-acting olanzapine): what reaction requires a 3-hour observation period after every injection?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • Post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome (PDSS): sedation up to coma, and/or delirium
  • Give only at a registered facility; observe at least 3 hours; patient must be alert before leaving and should be accompanied home

cards.prompt: Trifluoperazine (Stelazine), thiothixene (Navane), pimozide (Orap), and molindone (Moban)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotics on the syllabus drug table.

  • Trifluoperazine: schizophrenia; short-term anxiety only — max 6 mg/day, ≤12 weeks
  • Thiothixene: schizophrenia; contraindicated in Parkinson disease, circulatory collapse, children <12
  • Pimozide: Tourette tics; one of the worst QTc-prolongation risks — baseline ECG/QTc
  • Molindone: schizophrenia; start older adults at a reduced dose

cards.prompt: Thioridazine (Mellaril), loxapine (Loxitane; Adasuve), and mesoridazine (Serentil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotics on the syllabus drug table.

  • Thioridazine: boxed warning (verify) — dose-related QTc prolongation/torsades de pointes; max 800 mg/day; also causes pigmentary retinopathy at high doses
  • Loxapine: oral for schizophrenia; inhaled (Adasuve) carries a bronchospasm boxed warning — only given at an enrolled facility (verify)
  • Mesoridazine: listed on the syllabus table but has been withdrawn from the U.S. market (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Perphenazine (formerly Trilafon): in an ATI practice scenario, which of a client's findings are the EPS, not NMS or a drying/urinary-retention side effect?
cards.promptHtml: Perphenazine (formerly Trilafon): in an ATI practice scenario, which of a client's findings are the EPS, not NMS or a drying/urinary-retention side effect?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic, medium potency (phenothiazine).

  • EPS: drooling, continual pacing, involuntary arm movements
  • Not EPS: decreased consciousness (suggests NMS); urinary retention (anticholinergic)
