cards.prompt: Haloperidol (Haldol) and risperidone (Risperdal): what happens if these medications are stopped abruptly instead of tapered?
cards.promptHtml: Haloperidol (Haldol) and risperidone (Risperdal): what happens if these medications are stopped abruptly instead of tapered?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First- and second-generation antipsychotics.

  • Rebound nausea, vomiting, dizziness, insomnia, tremulousness
  • Relapse of psychotic symptoms
  • Not addictive, but must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly

cards.prompt: Risperidone (Risperdal) and olanzapine (Zyprexa) compared with haloperidol (Haldol) and chlorpromazine (Thorazine): which symptom type does each group treat better?
cards.promptHtml: Risperidone (Risperdal) and olanzapine (Zyprexa) compared with haloperidol (Haldol) and chlorpromazine (Thorazine): which symptom type does each group treat better?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation vs. first-generation antipsychotics.

  • Haloperidol/chlorpromazine: effective for positive symptoms only (minimal effect on negative symptoms)
  • Risperidone/olanzapine: effective for both positive and negative symptoms

cards.prompt: What should the nurse do immediately if a patient on haloperidol (Haldol) develops sudden muscle rigidity and a high fever?
cards.promptHtml: What should the nurse do immediately if a patient on haloperidol (Haldol) develops sudden muscle rigidity and a high fever?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic.

  • Treat fever plus rigidity as a possible emergency (NMS) until proven otherwise
  • Hold the medication and notify the provider immediately
  • Report any new rigidity, confusion, or temperature change right away

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril): what is the Clozapine REMS program, and is it still in effect?
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine (Clozaril): what is the Clozapine REMS program, and is it still in effect?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

  • REMS was eliminated (2025, verify) (Townsend 2017: dispensed only through the Clozapine REMS — certified prescribers and pharmacies, 1-week supplies tied to ANC results)
  • ANC monitoring still applies (weekly for the first 6 months); follow current labeling and facility policy
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Acute dystonia: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.promptHtml: Acute dystonia: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.answerHtml:
• Signs: sudden muscle spasm — twisted neck, eyes rolled back (oculogyric crisis), trouble breathing (laryngospasm) = airway emergency
  • Onset: 1–5 days; usually the first EPS to appear (Boyd)
  • Treat with: benztropine (Cogentin) or diphenhydramine (Benadryl) IM/IV; relief usually within minutes; airway first if breathing is affected

cards.prompt: Pseudoparkinsonism: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.promptHtml: Pseudoparkinsonism: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.answerHtml:
• Signs: resting tremor (pill-rolling), rigidity, bradykinesia, shuffling gait, mask-like face, drooling
  • Onset: 5–30 days (Boyd) (Townsend: 1–5 days)
  • Treat with: benztropine (Cogentin) or trihexyphenidyl (Artane); amantadine (Symmetrel), a dopamine agonist (Boyd); also lower the dose or switch drugs

cards.prompt: Akathisia: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.promptHtml: Akathisia: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.answerHtml:
• Signs: inner restlessness, pacing, can't sit still — felt "in the muscles/legs," not "in the mind" (distinguishes it from anxiety)
  • Onset: 1–30 days (Boyd) (Townsend: 50–60 days, mostly in women)
  • Treat: first reduce the antipsychotic dose (lecture); sometimes propranolol (Inderal) — check apical pulse/BP before each dose, never stop abruptly; or benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam); anticholinergics help little

cards.prompt: Tardive dyskinesia: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.promptHtml: Tardive dyskinesia: what are the signs, usual onset, and which drugs treat it?
cards.answerHtml:
• Signs: involuntary oral-buccal movements (lip smacking, tongue thrusting, worm-like tongue movements); involuntary arm, leg, and trunk movements
  • Onset: months to years (usually ≥6 months, or when the dose is lowered)
  • Treat with: valbenazine (Ingrezza) or deutetrabenazine (Austedo) — VMAT2 inhibitors; anticholinergics do NOT help and can worsen TD

cards.prompt: What classification of medication is commonly prescribed for drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions, and what are two examples?
cards.promptHtml: What classification of medication is commonly prescribed for drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions, and what are two examples?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticholinergic (antiparkinsonism) agents.

  • Benztropine (Cogentin)
  • Trihexyphenidyl (Artane)
  • Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) is also used

cards.prompt: What does the AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) assess, how is it scored, and how often should it be performed?
cards.promptHtml: What does the AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) assess, how is it scored, and how often should it be performed?
cards.answerHtml:
• A 5–10 minute clinician-rated exam of face, lips, jaw, tongue, extremities, and trunk movements
  • Scored 0 (none) to 4 (severe), plus global severity and patient awareness
  • When: baseline before starting the drug (course lecture), then at least every 3–6 months (Boyd) (ATI: after 12 months of therapy, then every 3 months)

cards.prompt: Benztropine (Cogentin), trihexyphenidyl (Artane), and diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticholinergic antiparkinsonism agents (diphenhydramine is an antihistamine with anticholinergic action).

  • Use: acute dystonia (IM/IV) and pseudoparkinsonism; not for tardive dyskinesia — they don't help and can worsen it
  • Max dose: benztropine 6 mg/day; diphenhydramine 400 mg/day
  • Teach: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary hesitancy, drowsiness — sugarless gum, fluids/fiber; older adults are most prone to confusion/delirium

cards.prompt: Valbenazine (Ingrezza) and deutetrabenazine (Austedo)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: VMAT2 inhibitors.

  • Use: tardive dyskinesia
  • Valbenazine: once daily, with or without food
  • Deutetrabenazine: twice daily, with food, swallowed whole

cards.prompt: Amantadine (Symmetrel)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Dopaminergic antiparkinsonian agent (raises dopamine at the receptor); also an influenza A antiviral.

Use: drug-induced EPS, especially pseudoparkinsonism (rigidity, akinesia, tremor).

Stop & report: hallucinations or worsening psychiatric symptoms (it raises dopamine).

Contraindicated: angle-closure glaucoma.

cards.prompt: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI.

Use: Depression, OCD, bulimia, panic disorder; pediatric depression (age 8+); Sarafem brand for PMDD.

Monitor: Mood, suicide risk; sodium in older adults on diuretics.

Stop & report: Serotonin syndrome signs; new or worsening suicidal thoughts.

Teach: Longest half-life of any antidepressant (2-9 days, Boyd; Psych Notes: parent 1-3 d, metabolite 5-7 d); strong CYP2D6 inhibitor; take in the morning.

Taper/withdrawal: Self-tapers - least discontinuation trouble. Wait 5 weeks before starting an MAOI.

cards.prompt: Sertraline (Zoloft)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI.

Use: Depression, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, PMDD; among the safest in breastfeeding (Boyd); often preferred in cardiac disease (verify).

Monitor: Mood, suicide risk; sodium in older adults.

Stop & report: Serotonin syndrome signs; bruising or bleeding if also on an NSAID or warfarin.

Teach: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea), sexual dysfunction; oral concentrate contains alcohol - avoid with disulfiram; take with food.

Taper/withdrawal: Taper - do not stop abruptly.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Paroxetine (Paxil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI.

Use: Depression, social anxiety, panic disorder, OCD, GAD, PTSD.

Monitor: Mood, suicide risk.

Stop & report: First-trimester cardiac defects in pregnancy (verify) - report pregnancy.

Teach: Most anticholinergic SSRI (verify); sedating; potent CYP2D6 inhibitor; short half-life (~21 h), no active metabolite; avoid in older adults (Beers) (verify).

Taper/withdrawal: Caution: withdrawal syndrome (Psych Notes); worst SSRI discontinuation syndrome (verify) - never stop abruptly, always taper.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Citalopram (Celexa) / Escitalopram (Lexapro)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI (escitalopram is the active S-isomer of citalopram).

Use: Depression; escitalopram also treats GAD.

Monitor: Baseline ECG; potassium, magnesium if cardiac risk (verify).

Stop & report: Citalopram causes dose-dependent QT prolongation - report palpitations or fainting; contraindicated in congenital long QT.

Teach: Citalopram max 40 mg/day (20 mg if over 60; also if hepatic impairment (verify)). Escitalopram 10 mg/day, up to 20 mg after 1 week; 10 mg in older adults. Never combine the two.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Fluvoxamine (Luvox)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI.

Use: OCD (primary indication).

Monitor: Mood, suicide risk; caffeine intake.

Stop & report: Serotonin syndrome signs; contraindicated with alosetron, thioridazine, pimozide, tizanidine.

Teach: Potent CYP1A2 inhibitor (also 2C9, 2C19, 3A4) - raises clozapine, theophylline, warfarin, and caffeine (verify) levels. Split doses above 100 mg/day; larger dose at bedtime.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Venlafaxine (Effexor) / Desvenlafaxine (Pristiq)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SNRI (desvenlafaxine is venlafaxine's active metabolite (verify)).

Use: Depression, GAD, social anxiety; good when the patient sleeps excessively with little energy.

Monitor: BP regularly - rise is dose-dependent.

Stop & report: Sustained hypertension; bruising; seizures.

Teach: Take with food. Desvenlafaxine usual dose 50 mg/day.

Taper/withdrawal: Short half-life (5-11 h, Boyd; Psych Notes: parent 3-5 h) - severe discontinuation symptoms after even one missed dose (verify); always taper.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Duloxetine (Cymbalta)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SNRI.

Use: Depression, GAD, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain.

Monitor: BP; LFTs if liver symptoms or heavy alcohol use (verify).

Stop & report: Liver injury, worse with alcohol - jaundice, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant pain (verify). Do not use in hepatic disease, heavy alcohol use, or severe renal impairment.

Teach: Levels rise with CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, cimetidine) and 2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine); limit alcohol.

Taper/withdrawal: Taper gradually.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Amitriptyline (Elavil) / Imipramine (Tofranil) / Nortriptyline (Pamelor)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: TCA.

Use: Amitriptyline - depression, migraine prevention. Imipramine - depression, enuresis in children 6+. Nortriptyline - depression, often chosen for older adults (verify).

Monitor: Levels - amitriptyline 110-250 ng/mL (includes nortriptyline); imipramine 200-350 ng/mL; nortriptyline 50-150 ng/mL - above or below this window both give a poorer response (verify).

Stop & report: Adding paroxetine raises nortriptyline into toxicity (narrow therapeutic index).

Teach: Give at bedtime; rise slowly; anticholinergic self-care.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Clomipramine (Anafranil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: TCA (syllabus lists it as SSRI).

Use: OCD (labeled indication).

Monitor: Plasma level 80-100 ng/mL.

Stop & report: Dose-related seizures above 250 mg/day (verify) (max 250 mg/day); never combine with an MAOI.

Teach: Primarily increases serotonin (syllabus) - carries the full TCA profile of sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, and high overdose lethality.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Phenelzine (Nardil) / Tranylcypromine (Parnate) / Isocarboxazid (Marplan)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: MAOI.

Use: Depression resistant to other drugs, especially atypical depression; also panic disorder, social anxiety.

Monitor: Lying/standing BP every visit - hold and notify for a significant drop; glucose in diabetics.

Stop & report: Hypertensive crisis - the most life-threatening MAOI effect (severe occipital headache, stiff neck, palpitations).

Teach: Full tyramine diet for all three; tranylcypromine is most stimulating, highest crisis risk (verify); tell every provider about MAOI use.

Taper/withdrawal: Taper - abrupt stop causes flu-like symptoms, worsening depression.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Selegiline transdermal (Emsam)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: MAOI - the only transdermal antidepressant.

Use: Major depression.

Monitor: Application site for rash/irritation; BP.

Stop & report: Hypertensive crisis at higher doses; contraindicated with carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine.

Teach: No diet restriction at 6 mg/24h; tyramine restriction required at 9 and 12 mg/24h. Apply to dry skin on torso/thigh/upper arm, rotate sites, keep away from heat. Start 6 mg/24h; increase no more often than every 2 weeks; older adults stay at 6 mg.

cards.prompt: Bupropion (Wellbutrin; Zyban)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: NDRI - an atypical antidepressant.

Use: Depression, especially when SSRI sexual side effects are intolerable; smoking cessation (Zyban); unlabeled adult ADHD.

Monitor: Weight/intake; seizure history before starting.

Stop & report: Dose-related seizures - contraindicated in seizure disorders, bulimia/anorexia nervosa, and abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal.

Teach: No sexual dysfunction; appetite suppression/weight loss. Never combine Wellbutrin and Zyban (same drug). Max 450 mg/day; no single IR dose over 150 mg; do not double up a missed dose.

cards.prompt: Mirtazapine (Remeron)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Atypical antidepressant (alpha-2 antagonist) - the course lecture misplaces it under tricyclics.

Use: Depression with insomnia, anxiety, or poor appetite/weight loss; use with caution and at a reduced dose in older adults.

Monitor: Lipids, weight, LFTs; CBC if signs of infection.

Stop & report: Agranulocytosis (rare) - fever, sore throat, flulike symptoms, weakness.

Teach: Sedation is greater at the lower 15 mg dose; increased appetite/weight gain. Take once daily at bedtime; avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants.

cards.prompt: Trazodone (Desyrel)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SARI - an atypical antidepressant.

Use: Depression, but mostly low-dose for insomnia, often added to an activating antidepressant.

Monitor: Cardiac status in cardiac disease (use with caution); QT (verify).

Stop & report: Priapism - a prolonged, painful erection; if it lasts more than 4 hours, go to the emergency department (untreated, can cause permanent impotence). Orthostatic hypotension and falls.

Teach: Very sedating - give at bedtime; avoid grapefruit (raises levels).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Esketamine (Spravato)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: NMDA antagonist (S-enantiomer of ketamine) - the only approved ketamine-based antidepressant.

Use: Treatment-resistant depression and depression with acute suicidal ideation (verify), given with an oral antidepressant; gives rapid effects.

Monitor: BP before and after each dose.

Stop & report: Sedation, dissociation, increased BP; boxed warning for abuse/misuse and suicidal thoughts.

Teach: Certified REMS setting only (verify); self-administered under direct supervision with post-dose observation, at least 2 hours (verify); no driving until the next day.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Other syllabus-list drugs: amoxapine (Ascendin), trimipramine (Surmontil), maprotiline (Ludiomil), protriptyline (Vivactil), desipramine (Norpramin), doxepin (Sinequan), nefazodone (Serzone)
cards.promptHtml: Other syllabus-list drugs: amoxapine (Ascendin), trimipramine (Surmontil), maprotiline (Ludiomil), protriptyline (Vivactil), desipramine (Norpramin), doxepin (Sinequan), nefazodone (Serzone)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: TCAs (maprotiline: tetracyclic), including trimipramine - TCA (syllabus: 'Other'); nefazodone - SARI, like trazodone (syllabus: SSRI/'Other'; lecture & Boyd: SNRI). The lecture lists protriptyline under both TCAs and MAOIs.

Stop & report: Amoxapine - unusually for a TCA, can cause EPS/NMS. Maprotiline - QT prolongation, seizures. Nefazodone - boxed warning for hepatic failure; report jaundice, malaise (LFTs).

Teach: Desipramine is least sedating (verify) (level 125-300 ng/mL); doxepin is strongly sedating (level 100-200 ng/mL, avoid after MI).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: By what general mechanism do medications prescribed for depression produce their effect, regardless of the specific drug?
cards.promptHtml: By what general mechanism do medications prescribed for depression produce their effect, regardless of the specific drug?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Applies across all classes used for depression (TCA, SSRI, SNRI, MAOI, atypical).

Mechanism:

  • Block reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and/or serotonin into the presynaptic neuron (TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion).
  • Block the MAO enzyme that breaks the monoamines down (MAOIs).
  • Block presynaptic receptors that act as release brakes (mirtazapine).

All raise synaptic monoamine levels.

cards.prompt: As the nurse, when should you expect a patient to begin showing symptomatic relief after starting therapy for depression?
cards.promptHtml: As the nurse, when should you expect a patient to begin showing symptomatic relief after starting therapy for depression?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Applies across all classes used for depression.

Teach:

  • Course lecture: relief begins in about 2 weeks (Boyd: some improvement by day 7; Townsend: optimum effect 4-6 weeks).
  • An 'adequate trial' is at least 6 weeks at a therapeutic dose.
  • Teach the patient not to stop early because relief feels slow.

cards.prompt: For what must the nurse be especially alert in a patient who has just started therapy for depression?
cards.promptHtml: For what must the nurse be especially alert in a patient who has just started therapy for depression?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Boxed warning applies across all classes used for depression.

Stop & report:

  • Suicidal thoughts/behavior - energy, sleep, and activity often improve before mood lifts, so risk can rise in the first weeks, and after dose changes (verify). Boxed warning covers children, adolescents, and young adults under 25.
  • Serotonin syndrome.
  • A manic switch if bipolar disorder is undiagnosed.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Which foods must a patient taking phenelzine (Nardil), tranylcypromine (Parnate), or isocarboxazid (Marplan) avoid due to their tyramine content?
cards.promptHtml: Which foods must a patient taking phenelzine (Nardil), tranylcypromine (Parnate), or isocarboxazid (Marplan) avoid due to their tyramine content?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: MAOI diet teaching.

Teach - avoid:

  • Aged cheese, salami, sauerkraut
  • Beer, wine
  • Yeast extracts
  • Avocados, caviar
  • Fava beans, overripe/fermented aged foods
  • Pickled herring, beef/chicken livers, preserved sausages
  • Sour cream, yogurt, soy sauce

Continue the diet for 2 weeks after stopping the drug. (Lecture also lists cured/smoked meats, dried fruit, snow peas, broad beans, miso/fish/teriyaki sauces, caffeine with tyramine.)

cards.prompt: A patient is stopping fluoxetine (Prozac) to start phenelzine (Nardil). How long must she wait, and why?
cards.promptHtml: A patient is stopping fluoxetine (Prozac) to start phenelzine (Nardil). How long must she wait, and why?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: SSRI-to-MAOI switch teaching.

Teach:

  • Wait at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI (its long half-life needs time to clear).
  • For other SSRIs, SNRIs, or TCAs switching to or from an MAOI, the washout is 14 days (2 weeks) in both directions.
  • Starting early risks serotonin syndrome.

cards.prompt: What withdrawal symptoms should the nurse expect if a patient abruptly stops a medication taken for weeks to treat depression, and which drugs cause the worst symptoms?
cards.promptHtml: What withdrawal symptoms should the nurse expect if a patient abruptly stops a medication taken for weeks to treat depression, and which drugs cause the worst symptoms?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Applies across all classes used for depression; worst with short-half-life SSRIs/SNRIs.

FINISH mnemonic (verify):

  • Flu-like symptoms
  • Insomnia, vivid dreams
  • Nausea
  • Imbalance (dizziness)
  • Sensory disturbances ('brain zaps')
  • Hyperarousal (anxiety, irritability)

Taper/withdrawal: Onset within 1-3 days (verify); worst with paroxetine and venlafaxine (shortest half-lives) (verify). Fluoxetine self-tapers. Never stop abruptly.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What is the most potentially life-threatening adverse effect of phenelzine (Nardil), tranylcypromine (Parnate), or isocarboxazid (Marplan), and what symptoms should the nurse and patient watch for?
cards.promptHtml: What is the most potentially life-threatening adverse effect of phenelzine (Nardil), tranylcypromine (Parnate), or isocarboxazid (Marplan), and what symptoms should the nurse and patient watch for?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: MAOI.

Stop & report: Hypertensive crisis - the most life-threatening MAOI effect.

Teach - report immediately:

  • Sudden, severe pounding occipital/temporal headache
  • Stiff or sore neck
  • Palpitations/racing pulse
  • Sweating, nausea/vomiting, chest pain

Caused by tyramine or sympathomimetic drugs; prevented by the tyramine diet and avoiding interacting drugs.

cards.prompt: Why must the nurse limit the medication supply given to a suicidal patient taking amitriptyline (Elavil) or imipramine (Tofranil)?
cards.promptHtml: Why must the nurse limit the medication supply given to a suicidal patient taking amitriptyline (Elavil) or imipramine (Tofranil)?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: TCA.

Stop & report: High overdose lethality - the lethal dose is only 3-5 times the therapeutic dose; more than 1 g is often fatal.

Teach: Give no more than a 1-week supply to an acutely ill patient, then no more than 1 month at a time.

Monitor: Baseline ECG and plasma levels; a widening QRS, dysrhythmia, or seizure signals toxicity.

cards.prompt: Which other drugs or supplements raise the risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with a medication prescribed for depression?
cards.promptHtml: Which other drugs or supplements raise the risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with a medication prescribed for depression?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Risk applies across classes used for depression, especially when combined.

Stop & report: Risk of serotonin syndrome (confusion, agitation, fever, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, diarrhea) with:

  • St. John's wort
  • Triptans
  • Linezolid
  • Tramadol, meperidine, dextromethorphan
  • Other antidepressants (especially MAOIs), lithium, trazodone

Teach: Check every OTC/herbal product before adding it; report these symptoms right away.

cards.prompt: Valproate/Divalproex (Depakote, Depakene)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • Use: acute mania; bipolar maintenance.
  • Monitor: LFTs + CBC/platelets baseline & periodic; ammonia if lethargy/confusion/vomiting (hyperammonemia); level 50–100 mcg/mL (lecture; Boyd: 50–150).
  • Stop & report: anorexia/nausea/vomiting/jaundice (hepatotoxicity); abdominal pain radiating to back (pancreatitis — check amylase/lipase); bruising/bleeding gums (thrombocytopenia).
  • Teach: avoid in pregnancy — birth defects (neural tube defects, lower IQ, autism risk, verify); folic acid and reliable contraception (verify); never stop abruptly, taper only.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • Use: acute mania and mixed episodes; rapid cycling; lithium nonresponders.
  • Monitor: level 8–12 mcg/mL (Boyd) (Townsend/Psych Notes/ATI: 4–12), monthly until stable; CBC with differential; sodium (SIADH/hyponatremia risk).
  • Stop & report: fever/sore throat/bruising (agranulocytosis); fever + mucosal lesions + spreading rash (possible Stevens-Johnson, higher risk with HLA-B*1502 allele, more common in Asian ancestry) (verify).
  • Teach: avoid grapefruit juice (raises level); decreases hormonal contraceptive efficacy; never stop abruptly.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Oxcarbazepine (Trileptal)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • Use: off-label for bipolar disorder (approved for epilepsy); cross-sensitivity with carbamazepine.
  • Monitor: serum sodium at baseline and periodically (verify) — causes hyponatremia/SIADH even more often than carbamazepine (verify).
  • Stop & report: headache, confusion, nausea, lethargy, or seizures (signs of hyponatremia).
  • Teach: decreases hormonal contraceptive efficacy — use an alternate method.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • Use: bipolar depression and maintenance.
  • Monitor: no routine therapeutic blood level established; monitor skin for rash at every contact during titration.
  • Stop & report: any new rash (see dedicated rash/Stevens-Johnson card).
  • Teach: valproate (Depakote) roughly doubles lamotrigine's level/half-life — started at about half the usual dose when combined with valproate.

cards.prompt: Topiramate (Topamax)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer (adjunct).

  • Use: off-label adjunct in bipolar disorder.
  • Stop & report: sudden eye pain/blurred vision (acute angle-closure glaucoma), signs of metabolic acidosis, or flank pain (kidney stones — encourage fluids) (verify).
  • Teach: decreases hormonal contraceptive efficacy; can cause weight loss and word-finding difficulty.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Valproate/divalproex (Depakote, Depakene): what is the therapeutic serum level, and how often is it checked?
cards.promptHtml: Valproate/divalproex (Depakote, Depakene): what is the therapeutic serum level, and how often is it checked?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • 50–100 mcg/mL (lecture; Psych Notes agrees). (Boyd Ch26: 50–150.)
  • Levels weekly until stable, then every 6 months; the routine follow-up lab is AST/ALT (liver).

cards.prompt: Carbamazepine (Tegretol): what is the therapeutic serum level, and how often is it checked?
cards.promptHtml: Carbamazepine (Tegretol): what is the therapeutic serum level, and how often is it checked?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • 8–12 mcg/mL (Boyd, unit misprinted as ng/mL). (Townsend/Psych Notes/ATI: 4–12.)
  • Checked monthly until the dose is stable.

cards.prompt: Lamotrigine (Lamictal): what serious adverse reaction requires stopping the drug, and what is the rule about starting dose and any new rash?
cards.promptHtml: Lamotrigine (Lamictal): what serious adverse reaction requires stopping the drug, and what is the rule about starting dose and any new rash?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome (boxed warning), usually within 2–8 weeks of starting — any new rash = stop and notify the provider immediately; a benign rash can't be told apart from a dangerous one at onset.
  • Started at a very low dose and titrated up slowly over weeks; a dose started too high or raised too fast raises the risk, as does valproate co-use.
  • Missing about 5+ days of doses means restarting the slow titration from the beginning, not the prior dose (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Which drugs — carbamazepine (Tegretol), oxcarbazepine (Trileptal), and topiramate (Topamax) — decrease the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives?
cards.promptHtml: Which drugs — carbamazepine (Tegretol), oxcarbazepine (Trileptal), and topiramate (Topamax) — decrease the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • All three reduce hormonal (oral) contraceptive effectiveness.
  • Teach patients on any of these to use an alternate or non-hormonal method of birth control.

cards.prompt: What should patients on valproate (Depakote) or carbamazepine (Tegretol) be taught about stopping the drug?
cards.promptHtml: What should patients on valproate (Depakote) or carbamazepine (Tegretol) be taught about stopping the drug?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizer.

  • Never stop abruptly — both are tapered under the prescriber's direction.
  • Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal seizures and relapse of mood symptoms.

cards.prompt: Valproate (Depakote), carbamazepine (Tegretol), oxcarbazepine (Trileptal), lamotrigine (Lamictal): how do they stabilize mood?
cards.promptHtml: Valproate (Depakote), carbamazepine (Tegretol), oxcarbazepine (Trileptal), lamotrigine (Lamictal): how do they stabilize mood?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsant mood stabilizers.

Action:

  • Act on ion channels, reducing repetitive firing of nerve action potentials; this most directly decreases manic symptoms
  • Valproate is also thought to raise GABA (inhibitory) levels
  • No single action explains the mood-stabilizing effect; the exact mechanism is unknown

cards.prompt: Lorazepam (Ativan): what is the mechanism of action behind its calming effect?
cards.promptHtml: Lorazepam (Ativan): what is the mechanism of action behind its calming effect?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

  • Enhances the inhibitory effect of GABA at the GABA-A/chloride-channel complex, producing calming, sedation, muscle relaxation, and a higher seizure threshold.
  • Relief of anxiety occurs rapidly after a dose.

cards.prompt: What are two examples of the most commonly used group of antianxiety medications?
cards.promptHtml: What are two examples of the most commonly used group of antianxiety medications?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepines (the most widely used antianxiety drug group).

  • Examples: lorazepam (Ativan), alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium) (also chlordiazepoxide/Librium, clonazepam/Klonopin).
  • Generic names mostly end in "-am"; chlordiazepoxide is the exception.

cards.prompt: Diazepam (Valium): what must a patient on long-term therapy be taught to prevent a potentially life-threatening situation?
cards.promptHtml: Diazepam (Valium): what must a patient on long-term therapy be taught to prevent a potentially life-threatening situation?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

Taper/withdrawal:

  • Never stop abruptly after regular or high-dose use - taper over several weeks under the prescriber's direction (may switch to a long-acting drug first).
  • Abrupt withdrawal after long-term use is potentially life threatening: anxiety, insomnia, tremors, diaphoresis, palpitations, lightheadedness, light sensitivity, abdominal pain, rising systolic BP, delirium and seizures.
  • Also avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants.

cards.prompt: Alprazolam (Xanax) vs. diazepam (Valium) or clonazepam (Klonopin): which causes withdrawal symptoms sooner, and why?
cards.promptHtml: Alprazolam (Xanax) vs. diazepam (Valium) or clonazepam (Klonopin): which causes withdrawal symptoms sooner, and why?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

Taper/withdrawal:

  • Alprazolam (shorter half-life, 12-15 h; Townsend 6.3-26.9 h): levels drop between doses - interdose rebound anxiety; withdrawal starts sooner and is more pronounced.
  • Diazepam/clonazepam (long half-lives; clonazepam 18-50 h): withdrawal is milder and delayed.
  • Onset: several hours to a few days after stopping, depending on the half-life (Townsend).
  • Signs: rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, palpitations, light sensitivity, cramps, vomiting, seizures, delirium.
  • Never stop abruptly; taper.

cards.prompt: Lorazepam (Ativan): what is the antidote for overdose, and why can giving it be risky in a patient who takes it regularly?
cards.promptHtml: Lorazepam (Ativan): what is the antidote for overdose, and why can giving it be risky in a patient who takes it regularly?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

Antidote:

  • Flumazenil - an IV competitive benzodiazepine-receptor antagonist that reverses sedation and toxicity. Keep resuscitation equipment available and maintain a patent airway.
  • In a patient physically dependent on benzodiazepines it can precipitate seizures, and because its half-life is shorter than many benzodiazepines, resedation can occur after it wears off - keep monitoring (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Lorazepam (Ativan): why is combining it with alcohol or an opioid dangerous?
cards.promptHtml: Lorazepam (Ativan): why is combining it with alcohol or an opioid dangerous?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

Stop & report:

  • Additive CNS and respiratory depression - this combination is contraindicated.
  • FDA boxed warning (2016): profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death when combined with opioids (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Lorazepam (Ativan)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

Use: anxiety and sedation; the only benzodiazepine reliably absorbed IM (diazepam/chlordiazepoxide IM absorption is slow and erratic, so those are given IV or PO instead).

Monitor: give IV no faster than 2 mg/min - rapid push can cause apnea, cardiac arrest, bradycardia, hypotension.

Teach: not recommended for PTSD; SSRIs are first-line for PTSD, prazosin for nightmares.

cards.prompt: Alprazolam (Xanax)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine.

Use: panic disorder and anxiety disorders, with or without agoraphobia; also anxiety with depression.

Monitor: avoid grapefruit juice - raises alprazolam levels (also triazolam, midazolam), increasing sedation risk (verify).

Stop & report: new confusion (possible toxicity), persistent dizziness, rash, palpitations, edema, trouble voiding, or worsening depression/self-harm thoughts; no driving until effects are known; avoid alcohol.

Teach: causes drowsiness, ataxia, memory dulling, morning "hangover," headache, dry mouth, nausea. Per ATI, the nursing priority with overdose toxicity is data collection first (general emergency teaching: airway first).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Diazepam (Valium) / Chlordiazepoxide (Librium) / Clonazepam (Klonopin)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine (long-acting group).

Use: diazepam - anxiety; chlordiazepoxide - classic exam answer for acute alcohol withdrawal (CIWA-Ar-guided dosing), also anxiety/preop sedation; clonazepam - panic disorder and seizure disorders.

Monitor: diazepam's long half-life (30-100 h; Townsend 20-80 h) with active metabolites accumulates, causing sedation, confusion, and falls in older adults; clonazepam's long half-life (18-50 h) gives lower rebound-anxiety risk than alprazolam.

cards.prompt: Oxazepam (Serax)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine (Boyd pairs it with lorazepam).

Use: anxiety.

Teach: no active metabolites - cleared by glucuronidation only, so it doesn't accumulate; the safer choice for an older adult or a patient with liver disease/abnormal liver function tests.

cards.prompt: Buspirone (BuSpar)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic (azapirone).

Use: anxiety - acts at serotonin 5-HT1A (and dopamine) receptors, not GABA; no sedation, muscle relaxation, abuse potential, or CNS-depressant potentiation.

Teach: fixed schedule only, never PRN - no immediate effect; takes 2-4 weeks of continual use for relief (Boyd; Townsend: 7-10 days).

Stop & report: combining with an MAOI (e.g., phenelzine/Nardil) or within 14 days of one causes a hypertensive crisis; grapefruit juice also raises levels.

cards.prompt: Hydroxyzine (Vistaril, Atarax)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: First-generation antihistamine (H1 blocker) used as an anxiolytic.

Use: anxiety, pruritus, and perioperative sedation - a non-habit-forming substitute for benzodiazepines; indicated for temporary relief of anxiety symptoms (Townsend).

Teach: avoid in older adults (Boyd) - anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation); also causes sedation, dizziness, and possible QTc prolongation.

cards.prompt: Propranolol (Inderal) / Prazosin (Minipress)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Propranolol - nonselective beta blocker; prazosin - alpha-1 blocker.

Use: propranolol - performance/situational anxiety; blocks peripheral norepinephrine effects (tachycardia, tremor, sweating) without sedation; single dose 30-60 min before the event (verify). Prazosin - PTSD nightmares (off-label).

Monitor: propranolol - hypotension/bradycardia: check pulse and BP; hold for HR under 50 (ATI; many references use 60) or SBP under 90 (verify); can worsen asthma (Psych Notes). Prazosin - first-dose orthostatic hypotension/syncope: first dose at bedtime, start low, rise slowly (verify).

Taper/withdrawal: if propranolol is taken daily, never stop abruptly - rebound tachycardia.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Zolpidem (Ambien) / Eszopiclone (Lunesta) / Zaleplon (Sonata)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Non-benzodiazepine sleep agents ("Z-drugs").

Stop & report: complex sleep behaviors (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating with amnesia) - stop and notify the prescriber at once (FDA boxed warning (verify)). Flumazenil reverses Z-drug overdose.

Teach: zolpidem's recommended IR dose is 5 mg, CR 6.25 mg (Boyd; Townsend: 10 mg adults, 5 mg older adults); eszopiclone causes an unpleasant taste, start 2 mg, 1 mg in older adults (Townsend); zaleplon has the shortest half-life (~1 h) and may be taken after a nighttime awakening only if at least 4 hours remain before rising.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Suvorexant (Belsomra) / Ramelteon (Rozerem)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Suvorexant - dual orexin receptor antagonist; ramelteon - melatonin receptor agonist.

Use: both for insomnia. Suvorexant - contraindicated in narcolepsy (blocks the wakefulness neuropeptide orexin); give within 30 min of bedtime with at least 7 h available for sleep (Townsend; Boyd general hypnotic teaching: 8 h).

Teach: ramelteon is not controlled and has low abuse potential, good for a substance-use history; contraindicated with fluvoxamine (raises levels) and severe hepatic impairment.

cards.prompt: Older syllabus-list drugs: meprobamate (Equanil), clorazepate (Tranxene), butabarbital (Butisol), phenobarbital (Luminal), chloral hydrate (Somnote), flurazepam (Dalmane), quazepam (Doral), estazolam (ProSom), temazepam (Restoril), triazolam (Halcion)
cards.promptHtml: Older syllabus-list drugs: meprobamate (Equanil), clorazepate (Tranxene), butabarbital (Butisol), phenobarbital (Luminal), chloral hydrate (Somnote), flurazepam (Dalmane), quazepam (Doral), estazolam (ProSom), temazepam (Restoril), triazolam (Halcion)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Older antianxiety/sleep agents: meprobamate, barbiturates (butabarbital, phenobarbital), chloral hydrate, benzodiazepine sleep agents.

Use: meprobamate - anxiety and chloral hydrate - sleep (syllabus table only); clorazepate - anxiety/alcohol withdrawal (tapered ~4 days)/partial-seizure adjunct; butabarbital - sedation/insomnia/preop; temazepam - sleep maintenance.

Monitor: flurazepam/quazepam active metabolites accumulate - poor choice for older adults; quazepam contraindicated in sleep apnea; estazolam 0.5-1 mg in older adults; triazolam - never with ketoconazole/itraconazole.

Antidote: barbiturate overdose has none (flumazenil doesn't work) - supportive care; lethal with alcohol/opioids.

cards.prompt: Herbal supplements used for anxiety/sleep: St. John's wort, kava, valerian, ginkgo biloba
cards.promptHtml: Herbal supplements used for anxiety/sleep: St. John's wort, kava, valerian, ginkgo biloba
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Herbal supplements.

Use: St. John's wort - mild-moderate depression/anxiety/insomnia; kava - anxiety; valerian - nervousness/insomnia; ginkgo - memory/cerebral blood flow.

Stop & report:

  • St. John's wort: serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs/MAOIs (or any other serotonergic drug); CYP3A4 inducer - lowers oral contraceptive, digoxin, warfarin levels.
  • Kava: FDA hepatotoxicity warning; added sedation with benzodiazepines/alcohol.
  • Valerian: added CNS depression with benzodiazepines/alcohol/barbiturates/opioids ; some reports of hepatotoxicity (Boyd; Townsend: generally safe).
  • Ginkgo: bleeding with aspirin/warfarin/anticoagulants; stop ~2 weeks before surgery (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Low-dose doxepin (Silenor) / Trazodone (Desyrel) for sleep
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Doxepin - TCA (selective H1 antagonist at the low 3-6 mg Silenor dose (verify)); trazodone - sedating antidepressant (5-HT2A antagonist), often used off-label for insomnia (Boyd). The syllabus lists doxepin (Sinequan) under antianxiety drugs, but at Silenor's dose it's a sleep aid.

Use: sleep-maintenance insomnia; TCA effects only at full doxepin antidepressant doses.

Teach: doxepin - not within 3 h of a meal; no MAOIs within 2 weeks.

Stop & report: trazodone - priapism (erection over 4 h) is an emergency; orthostatic hypotension; QT prolongation (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Pregabalin (Lyrica) and gabapentin (Neurontin)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anticonvulsants (calcium-channel modulators).

Use: other agents that may be used for anxiety disorders (ATI); not GABA agonists - bind the alpha-2-delta calcium-channel subunit to reduce excitatory transmitter release (verify).

Stop & report: respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants, especially in older adults or COPD (FDA warning 2019) (verify); misuse (pregabalin Schedule V).

Taper/withdrawal: taper over at least a week - abrupt stop risks withdrawal and seizures (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Clonazepam (Klonopin): why must it be tapered slowly, especially in a patient taking it for seizures?
cards.promptHtml: Clonazepam (Klonopin): why must it be tapered slowly, especially in a patient taking it for seizures?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Benzodiazepine (long half-life, 18–50 h).

Use: seizure disorders; panic disorder.

Taper/withdrawal:

  • Abrupt stop after long-term use can be life-threatening: withdrawal convulsions (lecture: seizure risk), plus anxiety, insomnia, tremor, delirium
  • Taper slowly over several weeks, on the prescriber's orders

cards.prompt: Donepezil (Aricept)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Cholinesterase inhibitor (prevents breakdown of acetylcholine).

Use: mild, moderate, severe Alzheimer disease - delays decline but doesn't restore function or cure the disease; start as soon as diagnosed.

Monitor: check pulse - acetylcholine excess can cause bradycardia/syncope, report a slow/irregular pulse or fainting; prolonged NSAID (incl. OTC aspirin) use raises GI ulcer/bleed risk; also nausea, diarrhea, vomiting.

Teach: give once daily at bedtime (long half-life) - a "morning vs. bedtime" question should answer bedtime.

Taper/withdrawal: titrate up slowly; taper, don't stop abruptly - can cause rapid worsening.

cards.prompt: Rivastigmine (Exelon)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Cholinesterase inhibitor (also inhibits butyrylcholine breakdown).

Teach: patch - rotate application sites; remove the old patch before applying a new one to avoid double-patching and overdose (verify); take oral form with food.

Monitor: causes nausea, vomiting, upset stomach, muscle weakness, and weight loss - watch closely in a patient who is already undernourished. Titrated slowly from 1.5 mg BID to a maximum of 24 mg/day.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Galantamine (Razadyne)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Cholinesterase inhibitor (also modulates nicotinic receptors).

Monitor: paroxetine, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, amitriptyline, and anticholinergic drugs raise galantamine levels - check for these before adding new medications.

Teach: titrate 4 mg BID up to 16-24 mg/day over 8 weeks; build the titration schedule with the family to limit side effects.

cards.prompt: Memantine (Namenda); Namzaric (memantine ER + donepezil)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: NMDA receptor antagonist (blocks toxic excess-glutamate effects); Namzaric adds the cholinesterase inhibitor donepezil.

Use: moderate to severe Alzheimer disease (not mild, unlike cholinesterase inhibitors); slows decline but doesn't alter the disease course or cure it.

Monitor: about 174 known drug interactions - check every new prescription first; report new/worsening confusion, dizziness, falls.

Teach: Namzaric - once daily evening; swallow whole or sprinkle on applesauce, never crush/chew; don't double a missed dose.

cards.prompt: Lecanemab (Leqembi) and donanemab (Kisunla)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies - disease-modifying therapy that removes amyloid-beta plaque, given by IV infusion in mild (early) Alzheimer disease. Aducanumab (Aduhelm) — discontinued 2024; lecture still lists it (Boyd profiles only aducanumab).

Monitor: baseline and periodic MRI to screen for ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities: brain edema or microhemorrhage) (verify).

Stop & report: new headache, confusion, or seizure during therapy - possible signs of ARIA.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), galantamine (Razadyne), and memantine (Namenda): what should a family be taught to expect from these drugs for Alzheimer disease?
cards.promptHtml: Donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), galantamine (Razadyne), and memantine (Namenda): what should a family be taught to expect from these drugs for Alzheimer disease?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) and an NMDA receptor antagonist (memantine).

Teach: these drugs delay cognitive decline and can slow symptom progression, but they do not restore lost function, halt, or cure the underlying disease - benefit is modest and the family should expect gradual decline to continue, just more slowly. Start therapy as soon as the diagnosis is made. None should be stopped abruptly; doses are titrated up slowly and tapered down, not stopped suddenly, to avoid rapid clinical worsening.

cards.prompt: NMS: recognizing it
cards.answerHtml:
Caused by: dopamine-blocking drugs (e.g., haloperidol, fluphenazine).

Signs (3 syllabus categories):

  • EPS: rigidity, tremors, dystonia, drooling, dysphagia, mutism
  • Stupor (hard to arouse/assess)
  • Autonomic instability: hyperthermia (up to 107°F rectally), diaphoresis, tachycardia, swinging BP, urinary retention → renal failure

Labs: ↑WBC, ↑CPK (rhabdomyolysis, often in the thousands — key lab), ↑liver enzymes.

cards.prompt: NMS: who's at risk, and what precipitates it
cards.promptHtml: NMS: who's at risk, and what precipitates it
cards.answerHtml:
• Thought to result from dopamine blockade in the basal ganglia.
  • Precipitated by rapid, massive loading of a dopamine-blocking drug, or sudden withdrawal of a dopamine agonist (e.g., levodopa).
  • Predisposing conditions: exhaustion, dehydration, agitation.
  • Typically appears within the 1st week of therapy (lecture); 80% of cases are under age 40; twice as common in men; higher risk with long-acting IM drugs (Haldol, Prolixin).
  • Incidence 0.05–1.0% (lecture: 0.01–3.2%); mortality 5–15% (lecture).

cards.prompt: NMS: nursing priorities
cards.answerHtml:
• Stop the dopamine-blocking drug immediately and notify the provider.
  • Assess vital signs (especially temperature) and level of consciousness.
  • Transfer to ICU for cardiopulmonary support.
  • Maintain renal function: IV fluids, strict intake and output.
  • Cooling measures for fever; monitor closely for 1–3 weeks.

cards.prompt: NMS: treatment drugs
cards.answerHtml:
• Dantrium (dantrolene) — a direct skeletal muscle relaxant.
  • Parlodel (bromocriptine) — a dopamine receptor agonist that reverses EPS.
  • Dialysis does NOT work: the causative drug is protein- and lipid-bound (unlike lithium toxicity, where dialysis IS the definitive treatment).

cards.prompt: Serotonin syndrome: recognizing it
cards.answerHtml:
Caused by excess serotonin activity from combining two or more serotonergic drugs; an MAOI plus an SSRI, SNRI, or clomipramine is the most dangerous combination (can be fatal — always confirm a full washout period before switching).

Classic triad:

  • Mental status changes (agitation, confusion)
  • Autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhea)
  • Neuromuscular hyperactivity (tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus)

Clonus plus hyperreflexia after a serotonergic drug is the giveaway sign.

cards.prompt: Serotonin syndrome: nursing priorities
cards.answerHtml:
• Withhold all serotonergic drugs, including PRNs (tramadol, ondansetron, dextromethorphan); notify the provider immediately.
  • Assess ABCs and vitals (especially temperature); check for myoclonus and hyperreflexia.
  • Cool the client: cooling blanket, tepid baths (Boyd lists antipyretics — current guidance: they don't help; fever is muscle-driven (verify)).
  • IV fluids; monitor I&O; benzodiazepines (lorazepam) as ordered for agitation/muscle activity.
  • Seizure/fall precautions; safety measures to prevent injury (Townsend).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Serotonin syndrome: antidote
cards.answerHtml: • Cyproheptadine — an antihistamine that blocks the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor.

cards.prompt: NMS vs. serotonin syndrome vs. anticholinergic toxicity
cards.promptHtml: NMS vs. serotonin syndrome vs. anticholinergic toxicity
cards.answerHtml:
All three can cause fever and altered mental status — differentiate by onset and the rest of the picture:

  • Serotonin syndrome: onset in hours; hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor, diarrhea, dilated pupils, sweating.
  • NMS: onset over days; lead-pipe rigidity, slow/normal reflexes, no clonus (verify), no diarrhea.
  • Anticholinergic toxicity: hot, dry, flushed skin, absent/decreased bowel sounds, urinary retention, normal reflexes (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Phenelzine (Nardil)-type hypertensive crisis: recognizing it
cards.answerHtml:
Trigger: tyramine-rich food/drink or an interacting drug causes a surge of norepinephrine.

Trigger foods: aged cheese, salami/preserved sausages, sauerkraut, pickled herring, liver, beer/wine, yeast extracts, soy sauce, avocados, caviar, sour cream, yogurt, fava beans, overripe/fermented foods; also OTC decongestants/diet pills.

Signs: severe occipital headache, marked hypertension, stiff neck, palpitations, sweating, nausea/vomiting, chest pain, nosebleeds; can cause hemorrhagic stroke.

Onset: sudden (Boyd).

cards.prompt: Phenelzine (Nardil)-type hypertensive crisis: nursing priorities
cards.answerHtml:
• Hold the MAOI (discontinue immediately) and notify the provider.
  • Monitor vital signs, BP every 5–15 minutes (verify); continuous cardiac monitoring and respiratory support.
  • Keep the client upright (head of bed elevated), quiet, low stimulation (verify).
  • Assist with a short-acting IV antihypertensive as ordered; external cooling for fever.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Phenelzine (Nardil)-type hypertensive crisis: treatment drug
cards.answerHtml:
• Phentolamine IV — a rapid-acting alpha-adrenergic blocker — or another short-acting IV antihypertensive as ordered (Townsend).
  • (ATI also lists nifedipine — no longer recommended.)

cards.prompt: Isocarboxazid (Marplan): how long to continue the tyramine-restricted diet after stopping
cards.promptHtml: Isocarboxazid (Marplan): how long to continue the tyramine-restricted diet after stopping
cards.answerHtml:
• For 2 weeks after stopping the drug.
  • MAO enzyme inhibition takes at least 2 weeks to resolve after the drug is stopped, so the dietary restriction and interacting-drug precautions continue that long (wait 2 weeks before starting another antidepressant).

cards.prompt: Lithium toxicity: emergency nursing priorities
cards.answerHtml:
A patient develops ataxia, slurred speech, and persistent vomiting on lithium (Lithobid):

  • Withhold the next dose; notify the provider; obtain a stat lithium level plus electrolytes/creatinine.
  • Assess airway and level of consciousness; implement seizure precautions.
  • Push fluids (or give IV isotonic saline): low sodium/fluid volume makes the kidney reabsorb more lithium, so restoring volume helps the kidney excrete it and protects renal function.

cards.prompt: Lithium toxicity: which clinical signs mean the nurse should anticipate hemodialysis?
cards.promptHtml: Lithium toxicity: which clinical signs mean the nurse should anticipate hemodialysis?
cards.answerHtml:
Escalate past fluids/monitoring to hemodialysis (there is no antidote) when severe-toxicity signs appear:

  • Cardiac arrhythmias, coarse tremor with fasciculations, confusion
  • Oliguria/renal failure
  • Seizures or coma — the most severe, life-threatening signs.
  • (Numeric dialysis thresholds are on the Lithium level cards.)

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril) agranulocytosis: what must the patient report immediately
cards.promptHtml: Clozapine (Clozaril) agranulocytosis: what must the patient report immediately
cards.answerHtml:
• Sore throat (pharyngitis), fever, and mouth sores — the classic early warning signs.
  • Also malaise, weakness, lethargy, and flu-like symptoms.

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril): nursing actions for severe neutropenia
cards.answerHtml:
• Stop clozapine at ANC <500/µL = severe neutropenia (Townsend); ANC <1,000 → interrupt (verify) (Boyd: WBC <3,500 / granulocytes <1,500 — older rule).
  • If fever or sore throat develops, withhold until a CBC with differential is back; notify the provider immediately.
  • Monitor for infection; hospitalization with reverse isolation is usually required.
  • Daily ANC until recovery; usually not restarted (verify).
  • (Monitoring schedule is on the Medications › Clozapine blood-count card.)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Clozapine (Clozaril): neutropenic precautions once severe
cards.answerHtml:
• Protective (reverse) isolation, usually in hospital; reduce exposure to infection — avoid crowds and ill visitors.
  • Report any fever or sore throat at once (no fever goes uninvestigated); temperature every 4 hours, report ≥38.0°C (100.4°F) (verify).
  • Strict hand hygiene; avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories, enemas; soft toothbrush; daily skin/mouth checks (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: A patient started on clozapine (Clozaril) a few weeks ago develops resting tachycardia, fever, and chest pain. What reaction is suspected, and what does the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: A patient started on clozapine (Clozaril) a few weeks ago develops resting tachycardia, fever, and chest pain. What reaction is suspected, and what does the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Myocarditis, a clozapine boxed warning.

  • Stop clozapine and notify the provider
  • Monitor vital signs; watch for palpitations, dyspnea, edema; ECG
  • Labs: troponin and CRP (elevated); echocardiogram (verify)
  • Usually appears in the first 1–2 months of therapy (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: SJS: recognizing it
cards.answerHtml:
• Rash with fever, cough and mucosal lesions — stop the drug and get immediate care.
  • A positive Nikolsky sign (skin slides off with light pressure) (verify).
  • Large flaccid blisters, sheets of skin peeling (verify).
  • Pain out of proportion to the rash (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: SJS: what to do at the first sign of a rash
cards.promptHtml: SJS: what to do at the first sign of a rash
cards.answerHtml:
• Hold the drug (e.g., lamotrigine, carbamazepine) at the first sign of any rash and notify the provider immediately.
  • Any rash can be SJS — it cannot be predicted which rash is benign.

cards.prompt: SJS: nursing priorities once suspected
cards.answerHtml:
• Serious rashes require hospitalization and stopping the drug.
  • Assess airway/breathing (mucosal sloughing can involve the airway) (verify).
  • Document extent of skin/mucosal involvement; prepare for transfer to a burn unit or ICU (verify).
  • IV fluid/electrolyte replacement; protective isolation; nonadhesive wound care; eye and mouth care (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Carbamazepine (Tegretol): what genetic screen is done before the first dose, and what does a positive result mean?
cards.promptHtml: Carbamazepine (Tegretol): what genetic screen is done before the first dose, and what does a positive result mean?
cards.answerHtml:
• HLA-B*1502 testing in patients of Asian ancestry (verify)
  • Carriers have a much higher risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so carbamazepine is generally not started (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Anticholinergic toxicity: recognizing it
cards.answerHtml:
• Hot as a hare (fever)
  • Blind as a bat (dilated pupils, blurred vision)
  • Dry as a bone (dry skin/mouth, no sweat)
  • Red as a beet (flushed skin)
  • Mad as a hatter (delirium); full as a flask (urinary retention)

cards.prompt: Anticholinergic toxicity: nursing priorities
cards.answerHtml:
Risk rises sharply when several anticholinergic drugs are combined (e.g., benztropine + diphenhydramine; also trihexyphenidyl, clozapine, olanzapine, TCAs, OTC antihistamines/sleep aids), especially in older adults:

  • Stop the offending drugs; notify the provider immediately.
  • ABCs, vitals with temperature, continuous cardiac monitoring (verify).
  • Safety: reorient, low-stimulation room, fall/seizure precautions, 1:1 if agitated (verify).
  • Cooling measures, fluids; check the bladder (scan/catheterize per order) (verify).
  • Usually self-limited (~3 days).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Anticholinergic toxicity: antidote
cards.answerHtml:
• Physostigmine — a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor; 1–2 mg IV given slowly over 5 minutes (fast push can cause seizures, bradycardia, heart block).
  • Short-acting (relief 2–3 hours); may repeat after 20–30 minutes.
  • Never give in a TCA overdose or when the QRS is widened (risk of asystole) (verify).
  • Keep atropine at the bedside to reverse cholinergic excess if it occurs (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Benzodiazepine overdose: recognizing it
cards.answerHtml:
• Early signs: drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech, ataxia, diminished reflexes.
  • Progresses to slow/shallow respirations, falling SpO2, stupor, coma, apnea, and cardiac arrest.

cards.prompt: Benzodiazepine overdose: the nurse's first action
cards.answerHtml:
• Clinical first action: protect the airway and breathing — maintain a patent airway, monitor vital signs, give fluids to maintain BP, keep resuscitation equipment ready; flumazenil reverses sedation.
  • An ATI-style question instead frames the nursing-process priority action as data collection — identifying the client's level of orientation — over flumazenil, IV fluids, or gastric lavage.

cards.prompt: Benzodiazepine overdose: antidote
cards.answerHtml:
• Flumazenil IV (ATI).
  • Can precipitate seizures in long-term benzodiazepine dependence, a seizure disorder, or a mixed TCA overdose; short half-life means resedation can follow (verify).
  • If opioids are also involved (e.g., with alcohol, pinpoint pupils), support ventilation and give naloxone together — it reverses the respiratory-depressing opioid component; naloxone does NOT reverse benzodiazepines.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Why alprazolam (Xanax) or diazepam (Valium) must never be stopped abruptly after long-term use
cards.promptHtml: Why alprazolam (Xanax) or diazepam (Valium) must never be stopped abruptly after long-term use
cards.answerHtml:
• Abrupt discontinuation after long-term use can cause life-threatening withdrawal seizures.
  • The dose must be tapered gradually under the prescriber's direction.
  • Teach the patient never to stop or skip doses without consulting the provider, and to avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants during treatment.

cards.prompt: Why is a phenobarbital (Luminal) overdose more dangerous than a lorazepam (Ativan) overdose alone?
cards.promptHtml: Why is a phenobarbital (Luminal) overdose more dangerous than a lorazepam (Ativan) overdose alone?
cards.answerHtml:
• Phenobarbital depresses the CNS at every level as the dose rises: sedation, hypnosis, coma, death; respiratory depression
  • Lorazepam works by enhancing GABA at the GABA-chloride channel complex
  • Phenobarbital can open the chloride channel directly with no ceiling effect, so it can be lethal alone (verify)
  • No antidote for barbiturate toxicity (flumazenil reverses only benzodiazepines)
  • Treat: supportive care, airway and ventilation (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Amitriptyline (Elavil) overdose: treating cardiotoxicity
cards.answerHtml:
A patient who overdosed on amitriptyline (Elavil) has a 12-lead ECG showing a widened QRS:

  • Sodium bicarbonate IV for QRS widening (verify).
  • Death comes from arrhythmia, hypotension or seizures; check a serum TCA level; gastric lavage, cardiorespiratory support.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Acute laryngeal dystonia: a drug-induced airway emergency
cards.promptHtml: Acute laryngeal dystonia: a drug-induced airway emergency
cards.answerHtml:
A patient on haloperidol (Haldol) suddenly develops a stiff neck, difficulty swallowing, and stridor:

  • Airway first: assess for stridor, have oxygen/suction ready, call a rapid response if breathing is compromised.
  • Then give IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine as ordered; stay with the client until spasms resolve.

cards.prompt: A client in a California facility has been held on a 72-hour (5150) hold. On the third day the treatment team still believes the client is a danger to others and refuses voluntary treatment. Which statement about the next legal step is correct? A. The client must be released at 72 hours because the hold cannot be extended. B. The facility may certify the client for up to 14 days of intensive treatment, and a certification review hearing will follow. C. A 30-day temporary conservatorship is automatically placed. D. A 180-day post-certification order is entered without a hearing.
cards.promptHtml:
A client in a California facility has been held on a 72-hour (5150) hold. On the third day the treatment team still believes the client is a danger to others and refuses voluntary treatment. Which statement about the next legal step is correct?

  • A. The client must be released at 72 hours because the hold cannot be extended.
  • B. The facility may certify the client for up to 14 days of intensive treatment, and a certification review hearing will follow.
  • C. A 30-day temporary conservatorship is automatically placed.
  • D. A 180-day post-certification order is entered without a hearing.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

After a 5150 evaluation, staff may certify the client for up to 14 days (5250) if the client is a danger to self or others or gravely disabled, was advised about voluntary treatment, and refuses it. A certification review hearing follows within about 4 days, and the client may ask for a writ of habeas corpus. Release is not required (A). A temporary conservatorship (C) is for grave disability and needs a court process. The 180-day order (D) is only for dangerousness to others and gives the right to a jury trial.

cards.prompt: A nurse helps the team judge whether a client has the capacity to consent to treatment. Which abilities does the assessment of competency include? Select all that apply. A. Ability to communicate a choice B. Ability to understand the relevant information C. Agreeing with the clinician's recommendation D. Ability to appreciate the situation and its consequences E. Using a logical thought process to compare risks and benefits
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse helps the team judge whether a client has the capacity to consent to treatment. Which abilities does the assessment of competency include? Select all that apply.

  • A. Ability to communicate a choice
  • B. Ability to understand the relevant information
  • C. Agreeing with the clinician's recommendation
  • D. Ability to appreciate the situation and its consequences
  • E. Using a logical thought process to compare risks and benefits
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D, E

Competency is the ability to understand and appreciate consent information at a specific time. It includes communicating a choice, understanding information, appreciating consequences, and reasoning about risks and benefits. It is not the same as rationality: a competent client may make a choice the team thinks is unwise, and disagreeing with the recommendation (C) is not evidence of incapacity. Only a court determines incompetence.

cards.prompt: In an outpatient session a client says, "I am going to hurt my brother tonight. I know where he lives. Don't tell anyone." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate? A. Promise to keep the statement confidential and encourage the client to keep talking. B. Document the statement and bring it to the next team meeting. C. Notify the provider and follow agency policy right away so the brother and authorities can be warned, and tell the client the limits of confidentiality. D. Telephone the client's family to ask whether the client is serious.
cards.promptHtml:
In an outpatient session a client says, "I am going to hurt my brother tonight. I know where he lives. Don't tell anyone." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

  • A. Promise to keep the statement confidential and encourage the client to keep talking.
  • B. Document the statement and bring it to the next team meeting.
  • C. Notify the provider and follow agency policy right away so the brother and authorities can be warned, and tell the client the limits of confidentiality.
  • D. Telephone the client's family to ask whether the client is serious.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

A threat of violence toward an identifiable person creates a legal duty to warn and protect (Tarasoff). Disclosure is mandated and overrides confidentiality. The nurse acts now, because delay risks the victim's life, and follows policy through the provider. Promising secrecy (A) is dishonest and unsafe. Waiting (B) delays protection. Calling the family (D) is itself a breach of confidentiality that is not legally required.

cards.prompt: A nursing student asks about seclusion and restraint on the unit. Which statement by the student shows correct understanding? A. "They are used only after less restrictive measures have failed, and the client is observed continuously." B. "Restraint is allowed when staff are short so the unit stays safe." C. "A PRN order lets us restrain a client whenever the behavior returns." D. "Medication given to calm a client is not a form of restraint."
cards.promptHtml:
A nursing student asks about seclusion and restraint on the unit. Which statement by the student shows correct understanding?

  • A. "They are used only after less restrictive measures have failed, and the client is observed continuously."
  • B. "Restraint is allowed when staff are short so the unit stays safe."
  • C. "A PRN order lets us restrain a client whenever the behavior returns."
  • D. "Medication given to calm a client is not a form of restraint."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Seclusion and restraint are last-resort measures. Use the least restrictive option first, apply them for the shortest time with a provider order, and observe constantly. They are never for staff convenience (B) or punishment. Once a restraint ends, a new order is needed before restraining again, so a standing PRN order (C) is not allowed (ATI ch 2, p.11). Medication used to control behavior or restrict movement, and not part of standard treatment, is a chemical restraint (D).

cards.prompt: During a unit on bias, a nursing student lists personal strategies to reduce the effect of implicit bias on patient care. Which strategies are consistent with the course teaching? Select all that apply. A. Pausing to reflect before caring for a patient from a group about which the student holds stereotypes B. Assuming that clinical training removes all unconscious bias C. Evaluating the patient by personal characteristics, such as shared interests, rather than group membership D. Considering the experience from the point of view of the person who is stereotyped E. Using terms like "I'm so OCD" to build rapport with patients
cards.promptHtml:
During a unit on bias, a nursing student lists personal strategies to reduce the effect of implicit bias on patient care. Which strategies are consistent with the course teaching? Select all that apply.

  • A. Pausing to reflect before caring for a patient from a group about which the student holds stereotypes
  • B. Assuming that clinical training removes all unconscious bias
  • C. Evaluating the patient by personal characteristics, such as shared interests, rather than group membership
  • D. Considering the experience from the point of view of the person who is stereotyped
  • E. Using terms like "I'm so OCD" to build rapport with patients
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

The lecture's tool kit includes slowing down and reflecting, individuation (seeing the person, not the group), perspective-taking, introspection, mindfulness, and cultural humility. Health care providers hold the same level of implicit bias as the general public, so training does not remove it (B). Casual use of diagnoses (E) feeds stigma and makes patients hide symptoms.

cards.prompt: A client on a voluntary unit says, "I'm not taking that pill. I'm not crazy." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "You have to take it, or the doctor will be upset." B. "Everyone here takes medication. It's part of the program." C. "You are not crazy, so there is nothing to worry about." D. "Tell me more about what concerns you about this medication."
cards.promptHtml:
A client on a voluntary unit says, "I'm not taking that pill. I'm not crazy." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "You have to take it, or the doctor will be upset."
  • B. "Everyone here takes medication. It's part of the program."
  • C. "You are not crazy, so there is nothing to worry about."
  • D. "Tell me more about what concerns you about this medication."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

An open-ended, nonjudgmental response explores the client's concern, which may involve side effects, fear of the label (self-stigma), or loss of control. It respects the right to refuse and keeps the relationship open. The nurse then reports the refusal to the provider. Threats and pressure (A, B) are coercive and ignore self-determination. False reassurance (C) closes the discussion and avoids the real concern.

cards.prompt: A client recently left the hospital, is back at work and living at home, and needs structured help with stress management and relapse prevention for about 3 hours a day, 3 days a week. Which setting best fits these needs? A. Partial hospitalization program B. Intensive outpatient program C. Crisis stabilization unit D. Residential treatment
cards.promptHtml:
A client recently left the hospital, is back at work and living at home, and needs structured help with stress management and relapse prevention for about 3 hours a day, 3 days a week. Which setting best fits these needs?

  • A. Partial hospitalization program
  • B. Intensive outpatient program
  • C. Crisis stabilization unit
  • D. Residential treatment
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Intensive outpatient programs serve highly vulnerable clients who function independently and have resumed work, school, or family life. Sessions run 3 to 4 hours per day, 2 to 3 days per week, and teach stress management, illness, medication, and relapse prevention. Partial hospitalization (A) is a longer day program for clients with poorer functioning and emphasizes social skills. Crisis stabilization (C) lasts under 7 days for acute symptoms. Residential care (D) provides housing and 24-hour support.

cards.prompt: The daughter of an 82-year-old woman reports that her mother became confused and withdrawn over the last 3 days and says, "I think she is just depressed." Which action should the nurse take first? A. Ask the provider to start an antidepressant. B. Prepare for transfer to a memory care unit. C. Assess for physical causes, including vital signs, hydration, signs of infection, and recent medication changes. D. Give a standard intelligence test to measure cognition.
cards.promptHtml:
The daughter of an 82-year-old woman reports that her mother became confused and withdrawn over the last 3 days and says, "I think she is just depressed." Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Ask the provider to start an antidepressant.
  • B. Prepare for transfer to a memory care unit.
  • C. Assess for physical causes, including vital signs, hydration, signs of infection, and recent medication changes.
  • D. Give a standard intelligence test to measure cognition.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Sudden change in mental status in an older adult suggests delirium until proven otherwise. Infection (especially urinary), dehydration, drug effects, and electrolyte changes are common, treatable causes. Older adults often show depression and physical illness through vague somatic and cognitive complaints. Treating depression (A) or placing the patient (B) before ruling out physical causes is unsafe. Intelligence tests (D) are rarely used in older adults, and orientation or judgment changes are not normal aging.

cards.prompt: During the admission interview a client describes the recent death of his mother while smiling and chuckling. How should the nurse document the client's affect? A. Flat B. Labile C. Euphoric D. Inappropriate
cards.promptHtml:
During the admission interview a client describes the recent death of his mother while smiling and chuckling. How should the nurse document the client's affect?

  • A. Flat
  • B. Labile
  • C. Euphoric
  • D. Inappropriate
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Affect is the observed emotional expression, and it is judged by range, intensity, appropriateness, and stability. Smiling while describing a death does not fit the content, so it is inappropriate (incongruent). Flat affect (A) shows almost no expression. Labile affect (B) shifts rapidly and intensely. Euphoric (C) describes a sustained elated mood, which is mood, not affect.

cards.prompt: A nurse is completing the mental status exam. Which findings belong under content of thought? Select all that apply. A. The client believes the neighbors are sending signals through the wall. B. The client reports hearing a voice telling him to leave. C. The client describes repeated, unwanted thoughts that the stove is on. D. The client cannot state today's date or location. E. The client's speech is rapid and pressured.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is completing the mental status exam. Which findings belong under content of thought? Select all that apply.

  • A. The client believes the neighbors are sending signals through the wall.
  • B. The client reports hearing a voice telling him to leave.
  • C. The client describes repeated, unwanted thoughts that the stove is on.
  • D. The client cannot state today's date or location.
  • E. The client's speech is rapid and pressured.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C

Content of thought covers delusions, hallucinations, obsessions, compulsions, phobias, and preoccupations. Beliefs about signals through walls (A) are delusions. A voice that others cannot hear (B) is a hallucination. Intrusive unwanted thoughts (C) are obsessions. Not knowing the date or place (D) is a problem of orientation, and rapid pressured speech (E) belongs under speech.

cards.prompt: During an intake assessment a client answers "yes" when the nurse asks, "Have you wished you were dead or wished you could go to sleep and not wake up?" Which question should the nurse ask next? A. "What has been going well for you lately?" B. "Have you been sleeping well?" C. "Have you actually had any thoughts about killing yourself?" D. "Do you think your family would be upset if something happened to you?"
cards.promptHtml:
During an intake assessment a client answers "yes" when the nurse asks, "Have you wished you were dead or wished you could go to sleep and not wake up?" Which question should the nurse ask next?

  • A. "What has been going well for you lately?"
  • B. "Have you been sleeping well?"
  • C. "Have you actually had any thoughts about killing yourself?"
  • D. "Do you think your family would be upset if something happened to you?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Suicide screening follows a direct, stepwise sequence: wish to be dead, then actual thoughts of killing oneself, then any action or preparation. Asking directly does not plant the idea and identifies risk. If answers continue to be yes, the nurse asks about plan and intent, does not leave the client alone, notifies the supervisor, and documents. Changing the subject (A, B) or asking an indirect question (D) delays the safety assessment, which takes priority.

cards.prompt: A client with severe vision loss who cannot hold a pen is admitted with suspected cognitive decline. Which approach is best? A. Give the Mini-Mental State Exam in the standard way and score the written items as zero. B. Use the mental status exam, because the MMSE requires the client to see and write. C. Skip cognitive assessment until the vision problem is treated. D. Ask the daughter to complete the exam for the client.
cards.promptHtml:
A client with severe vision loss who cannot hold a pen is admitted with suspected cognitive decline. Which approach is best?

  • A. Give the Mini-Mental State Exam in the standard way and score the written items as zero.
  • B. Use the mental status exam, because the MMSE requires the client to see and write.
  • C. Skip cognitive assessment until the vision problem is treated.
  • D. Ask the daughter to complete the exam for the client.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

The MMSE (maximum 30) screens cognition when time is limited, but reading and writing items require sight and the ability to write. If the client cannot do an activity, the nurse uses the mental status exam, which tests orientation, memory, attention, and judgment verbally. Scoring items as zero (A) would give a false picture of cognitive decline. Delaying (C) leaves a safety concern unassessed, and a proxy cannot complete the client's exam (D).

cards.prompt: A nurse prepares to interview an 84-year-old client for a mental health assessment. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Confirm the hearing aid is in place and turn off the television. B. Use simple, childlike language so the client will understand. C. With the client's permission, ask family members for additional information. D. Move quickly through the questions to avoid tiring the client. E. Allow a slower pace than with a younger adult.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse prepares to interview an 84-year-old client for a mental health assessment. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Confirm the hearing aid is in place and turn off the television.
  • B. Use simple, childlike language so the client will understand.
  • C. With the client's permission, ask family members for additional information.
  • D. Move quickly through the questions to avoid tiring the client.
  • E. Allow a slower pace than with a younger adult.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

Remove noise, make sure hearing aids work, and face the client, because deafness can be mistaken for cognitive impairment. Family often notice changes the client misses, but the nurse needs the client's permission first. The pace should follow the client's ability, which is usually slower. Childlike language (B) signals ageism and harms communication. Rushing (D) reduces accuracy and rapport.
