cards.prompt: A client's Global Assessment of Functioning score was 32 at admission and 58 at discharge. Which interpretation is most accurate? A. Functioning improved from marked impairment toward moderate symptoms or difficulty. B. Functioning worsened because the score no longer reflects serious symptoms. C. Symptoms resolved and the client has returned to a baseline of superior functioning. D. The scores cannot be compared because the scale is used only once.
cards.promptHtml:
A client's Global Assessment of Functioning score was 32 at admission and 58 at discharge. Which interpretation is most accurate?

  • A. Functioning improved from marked impairment toward moderate symptoms or difficulty.
  • B. Functioning worsened because the score no longer reflects serious symptoms.
  • C. Symptoms resolved and the client has returned to a baseline of superior functioning.
  • D. The scores cannot be compared because the scale is used only once.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

The GAF runs from 0 to 100, and a lower score means greater impairment. A score in the 31 to 40 range reflects major impairment or impaired reality testing, and 51 to 60 reflects moderate symptoms or difficulty. A rise of about 26 points shows improvement. It is measured at the initial assessment so progress can be evaluated. A score of 58 is not superior function, which is 91 to 100 (C). Current charts use WHODAS 2.0 instead (general knowledge).

cards.prompt: A nursing student reviews the move from DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5. Which statement shows correct understanding? A. "The five axes are still required, and the GAF is recorded on Axis V." B. "The axes were combined into one list of diagnoses, and the WHODAS 2.0 measures disability." C. "The GAF was replaced by Axis IV, which now measures functioning." D. "Psychosocial stressors are no longer assessed."
cards.promptHtml:
A nursing student reviews the move from DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5. Which statement shows correct understanding?

  • A. "The five axes are still required, and the GAF is recorded on Axis V."
  • B. "The axes were combined into one list of diagnoses, and the WHODAS 2.0 measures disability."
  • C. "The GAF was replaced by Axis IV, which now measures functioning."
  • D. "Psychosocial stressors are no longer assessed."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

DSM-5 removed the multiaxial system. Former Axes I to III are listed together as diagnoses, psychosocial and environmental problems are recorded with codes, and disability is measured with the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0, which Boyd names. The syllabus still asks about the five axes, so know both systems. The GAF is no longer in the DSM (A, C), and psychosocial factors are still assessed (D).

cards.prompt: A nurse interviews a 14-year-old who has been withdrawn and tearful. Which approach best fits the assessment of an adolescent? A. Use clinical terms such as "major depression" so the teen understands the seriousness. B. Interview the teen only with a parent in the room for the entire session. C. Rely only on the teen's self-report because parents are not reliable. D. Ask, "Have you been feeling sad or down lately?" and, when needed, gather information from a parent or teacher.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse interviews a 14-year-old who has been withdrawn and tearful. Which approach best fits the assessment of an adolescent?

  • A. Use clinical terms such as "major depression" so the teen understands the seriousness.
  • B. Interview the teen only with a parent in the room for the entire session.
  • C. Rely only on the teen's self-report because parents are not reliable.
  • D. Ask, "Have you been feeling sad or down lately?" and, when needed, gather information from a parent or teacher.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

The lecture directs the nurse to grade language to the patient's development, for example using "sad" instead of "depressed" with adolescents, and to verify information with trusted parties when needed. An adult-child power imbalance can reduce honesty, so discretion about separate interviews is also needed. Clinical terms (A) may be confusing. A parent present the whole time (B) may inhibit answers, and ignoring collateral sources (C) loses useful data.

cards.prompt: A patient admitted voluntarily to the inpatient unit tells the nurse, "Nobody here listens to me. I don't know why I have to stay." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "Everyone here wants to help you, so try to be patient." B. "Why do you feel that nobody is listening to you?" C. "It sounds like you feel unheard and frustrated about being here." D. "The doctor decided you need to stay, so we should follow the plan."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient admitted voluntarily to the inpatient unit tells the nurse, "Nobody here listens to me. I don't know why I have to stay." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "Everyone here wants to help you, so try to be patient."
  • B. "Why do you feel that nobody is listening to you?"
  • C. "It sounds like you feel unheard and frustrated about being here."
  • D. "The doctor decided you need to stay, so we should follow the plan."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Reflecting the feeling behind the statement shows acceptance and invites the patient to continue. Option A is false reassurance that also dismisses the concern. Option B is a "why" question, which sounds like a demand to justify feelings and puts the patient on the defensive. Option D defends the team and shuts down the patient's concern. The patient is communicating frustration, so respond to the emotion rather than the literal words.

cards.prompt: A student nurse reviews a recorded role-play of a patient interview. Which nurse statements are nontherapeutic communication techniques? Select all that apply. A. "You should stop seeing him; he isn't good for you." B. "Tell me more about how things have been at home." C. "Don't worry, everything will work out fine." D. "I know exactly how you feel." E. "You mentioned your sister twice. I'd like to hear more about that."
cards.promptHtml:
A student nurse reviews a recorded role-play of a patient interview. Which nurse statements are nontherapeutic communication techniques? Select all that apply.

  • A. "You should stop seeing him; he isn't good for you."
  • B. "Tell me more about how things have been at home."
  • C. "Don't worry, everything will work out fine."
  • D. "I know exactly how you feel."
  • E. "You mentioned your sister twice. I'd like to hear more about that."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

Giving advice (A) removes the patient's autonomy and implies the nurse knows best. False reassurance (C) may be untrue and blocks exploration of feelings. A cliche such as "I know exactly how you feel" (D) is not credible and breaks trust. Option B is an open-ended general lead, and option E is focusing; both are therapeutic because they keep the patient as the topic and invite elaboration.

cards.prompt: A patient who was recently told that a family member has died states, "I'm fine, really. I don't need to talk about it," while looking at the floor, slumped in the chair, with tears running down the face. Which response should the nurse make first? A. "Good, then I'll let you rest and check on you later." B. "You must be in denial. Crying shows you are not fine." C. "Would you like me to call your doctor to prescribe something?" D. "I notice you are tearful and quiet. I'd like to sit with you for a few minutes."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient who was recently told that a family member has died states, "I'm fine, really. I don't need to talk about it," while looking at the floor, slumped in the chair, with tears running down the face. Which response should the nurse make first?

  • A. "Good, then I'll let you rest and check on you later."
  • B. "You must be in denial. Crying shows you are not fine."
  • C. "Would you like me to call your doctor to prescribe something?"
  • D. "I notice you are tearful and quiet. I'd like to sit with you for a few minutes."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

When verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, rely on the nonverbal message. Stating the observation and offering presence respects the patient's pace without forcing disclosure. Option A accepts the words at face value and leaves a grieving patient alone. Option B interprets and labels the patient, which is presumptuous and likely to cause defensiveness. Option C moves to medication before exploring the patient's feelings, which changes the subject and avoids the emotion.

cards.prompt: A patient on the unit asks the nurse, "Are you married? Do you have kids?" Which response best maintains the therapeutic relationship? A. "I'm wondering what made you curious about that. This time is for you. How are things with your own family?" B. "Yes, I'm married with two children, and they keep me very busy." C. "That's too personal. Nurses are not allowed to answer that." D. "Why do you want to know about my family?"
cards.promptHtml:
A patient on the unit asks the nurse, "Are you married? Do you have kids?" Which response best maintains the therapeutic relationship?

  • A. "I'm wondering what made you curious about that. This time is for you. How are things with your own family?"
  • B. "Yes, I'm married with two children, and they keep me very busy."
  • C. "That's too personal. Nurses are not allowed to answer that."
  • D. "Why do you want to know about my family?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

The nurse should look for the reason behind a personal question, avoid unnecessary self-disclosure, and redirect to the patient. Option A does all three. Option B gives personal information with no therapeutic purpose and shifts the focus to the nurse. Option C is abrupt and may feel like rejection. Option D is a "why" question that can sound accusing. Disclosure is used only when it has a therapeutic purpose.

cards.prompt: A nurse realizes that she has been spending extra time with one patient, has defended the patient's behavior in team meetings, and feels that she is the only person who understands the patient. What is the nurse's best action? A. Continue as is, since the patient is making progress with her. B. Discuss the situation with the clinical supervisor and consider transferring the patient's care. C. Tell the patient she needs to spend less time with them and say nothing to the team. D. Ask the patient to keep their conversations private to avoid jealousy among other patients.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse realizes that she has been spending extra time with one patient, has defended the patient's behavior in team meetings, and feels that she is the only person who understands the patient. What is the nurse's best action?

  • A. Continue as is, since the patient is making progress with her.
  • B. Discuss the situation with the clinical supervisor and consider transferring the patient's care.
  • C. Tell the patient she needs to spend less time with them and say nothing to the team.
  • D. Ask the patient to keep their conversations private to avoid jealousy among other patients.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

These are warning signs that the relationship is moving outside professional boundaries. Clinical supervision, with transfer of care if needed, is the recommended response. Option A ignores the warning signs. Option C handles the boundary alone and abruptly, which could feel like rejection and leaves the pattern unexamined. Option D asks for secrecy, which is itself a boundary violation.

cards.prompt: Which nurse behaviors suggest that professional boundaries are becoming blurred? Select all that apply. A. Accepting a gift from a patient and keeping it secret from the team B. Telling the patient a personal worry about the nurse's own marriage C. Introducing the topic of confidentiality and meeting times during the first session D. Thinking about the patient frequently while away from work E. Telling the team about countertransference feelings during supervision
cards.promptHtml:
Which nurse behaviors suggest that professional boundaries are becoming blurred? Select all that apply.

  • A. Accepting a gift from a patient and keeping it secret from the team
  • B. Telling the patient a personal worry about the nurse's own marriage
  • C. Introducing the topic of confidentiality and meeting times during the first session
  • D. Thinking about the patient frequently while away from work
  • E. Telling the team about countertransference feelings during supervision
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D

Gift giving, secrecy, and frequent thoughts about the patient outside work are listed indicators of boundary drift. Sharing the nurse's own personal problems shifts the focus to the nurse and meets the nurse's needs. Explaining confidentiality and the meeting structure (C) sets boundaries during orientation. Bringing countertransference to supervision (E) is the correct way to prevent a boundary problem.

cards.prompt: A patient who has schizophrenia tells the nurse, "The kitchen staff are putting poison in my food." Which response is most therapeutic? A. "That is not true. The kitchen staff would never do that." B. "Yes, I will make sure they stop." C. "Why do you think they would want to hurt you?" D. "It sounds like you feel very unsafe right now. I'll stay with you while you eat."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient who has schizophrenia tells the nurse, "The kitchen staff are putting poison in my food." Which response is most therapeutic?

  • A. "That is not true. The kitchen staff would never do that."
  • B. "Yes, I will make sure they stop."
  • C. "Why do you think they would want to hurt you?"
  • D. "It sounds like you feel very unsafe right now. I'll stay with you while you eat."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

The course tool says not to agree with a delusion and not to argue or reason it away; instead, acknowledge the feeling behind it. Option D names the fear and offers presence, which supports eating without debating the belief. Option A challenges the belief, which increases distrust. Option B agrees with the delusion and reinforces it, which is clinically unsafe. Option C asks "why," invites elaboration of the delusion, and may feel like an interrogation.

cards.prompt: A nurse tells a patient that their therapeutic relationship will end in two weeks. In the next session the patient brings up a problem that was resolved weeks ago and says, "I'm not sure I can handle this." Which response is best? A. "Let's go over that problem again in detail so you feel ready." B. "We already worked through that. It may be hard to think about our meetings ending. Let's talk about the skills you have learned." C. "I'm sure you will be fine. You don't need to worry about it." D. "I can give you my number so you can call if it comes back."
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse tells a patient that their therapeutic relationship will end in two weeks. In the next session the patient brings up a problem that was resolved weeks ago and says, "I'm not sure I can handle this." Which response is best?

  • A. "Let's go over that problem again in detail so you feel ready."
  • B. "We already worked through that. It may be hard to think about our meetings ending. Let's talk about the skills you have learned."
  • C. "I'm sure you will be fine. You don't need to worry about it."
  • D. "I can give you my number so you can call if it comes back."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Raising old, resolved problems during termination is a common way to prolong the relationship. The nurse should avoid reopening the problem, acknowledge the likely anxiety about ending, and redirect to strengths and new skills. Option A reopens the problem and delays resolution. Option C is false reassurance. Option D breaks the boundary; the nurse should not agree to contact outside the relationship.

cards.prompt: During the third session of an outpatient closed group, two members openly criticize the nurse leader's rules, and another member is repeatedly blamed for the group's lack of progress. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate? A. End the group early and meet with each member individually. B. Remove the blamed member from the group immediately. C. Agree with the members' criticism to rebuild trust. D. Stay neutral, avoid taking sides, and treat all members respectfully while the conflict is addressed.
cards.promptHtml:
During the third session of an outpatient closed group, two members openly criticize the nurse leader's rules, and another member is repeatedly blamed for the group's lack of progress. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

  • A. End the group early and meet with each member individually.
  • B. Remove the blamed member from the group immediately.
  • C. Agree with the members' criticism to rebuild trust.
  • D. Stay neutral, avoid taking sides, and treat all members respectfully while the conflict is addressed.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Conflict after the early "honeymoon" stage is a normal part of group development and many believe it is needed to reach the working stage. The leader's task is to stay neutral, avoid siding with anyone, and protect a member who is being scapegoated. Ending the group (A) or removing the member (B) avoids the process rather than guiding it. Agreeing with the criticism (C) takes sides and weakens the leader's role.

cards.prompt: During the second session of a new outpatient coping-skills group, one member talks at length and cuts in whenever someone else starts to speak. The member's hands are trembling and the member glances often at the door. Which approach by the nurse leader is best? A. Treat the behavior as likely anxiety about the new group: acknowledge the member's point, then invite another member to speak. B. Treat the behavior as a bid for control: confront it in front of the group so the members see the rules enforced. C. Treat the behavior as a lack of social skills: move the member to individual therapy before the next session. D. Treat the behavior as attention seeking: stop responding to the member's comments until the talking stops.
cards.promptHtml:
During the second session of a new outpatient coping-skills group, one member talks at length and cuts in whenever someone else starts to speak. The member's hands are trembling and the member glances often at the door. Which approach by the nurse leader is best?

  • A. Treat the behavior as likely anxiety about the new group: acknowledge the member's point, then invite another member to speak.
  • B. Treat the behavior as a bid for control: confront it in front of the group so the members see the rules enforced.
  • C. Treat the behavior as a lack of social skills: move the member to individual therapy before the next session.
  • D. Treat the behavior as attention seeking: stop responding to the member's comments until the talking stops.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Monopolizing is common early in a group and usually reflects anxiety; it often eases within a few sessions. The leader acknowledges the contribution and redirects the discussion to others, and becomes more directive or limits speaking time if it persists. Public confrontation (B) can shame an anxious member. Removing the member (C) is premature. Ignoring the behavior (D) leaves the group waiting on the leader, and irritated members may drop out.

cards.prompt: A nurse is leading a group on a psychiatric unit. Which member behaviors are examples of individual roles that can interfere with group progress? Select all that apply. A. A member boasts repeatedly about personal accomplishments. B. A member tries to control other members by interrupting and giving orders. C. A member helps settle a disagreement and relieves tension. D. A member takes minutes of the session and keeps track of what was said. E. A member disagrees with every suggestion, even after the group rejected an idea.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is leading a group on a psychiatric unit. Which member behaviors are examples of individual roles that can interfere with group progress? Select all that apply.

  • A. A member boasts repeatedly about personal accomplishments.
  • B. A member tries to control other members by interrupting and giving orders.
  • C. A member helps settle a disagreement and relieves tension.
  • D. A member takes minutes of the session and keeps track of what was said.
  • E. A member disagrees with every suggestion, even after the group rejected an idea.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, E

Individual roles meet a member's personal needs and work against teamwork: the recognition seeker boasts (A), the dominator controls others (B), and the blocker resists and brings back rejected ideas (E). The harmonizer who eases tension (C) is a maintenance role that helps keep the group together. The recorder (D) is a task role that helps the group stay on its purpose.

cards.prompt: During a group session for patients with schizophrenia, a new member says, "I thought I was the only one who heard voices. It helps to know you hear them too." Which therapeutic factor does this statement best illustrate? A. Catharsis B. Universality C. Imitative behavior D. Altruism
cards.promptHtml:
During a group session for patients with schizophrenia, a new member says, "I thought I was the only one who heard voices. It helps to know you hear them too." Which therapeutic factor does this statement best illustrate?

  • A. Catharsis
  • B. Universality
  • C. Imitative behavior
  • D. Altruism
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Universality is finding out that others have similar problems, which reduces isolation and shame. Catharsis (A) is the open expression of feeling. Imitative behavior (C) is copying the behaviors of the leader or another member. Altruism (D) is learning to give to others, such as supporting a new member. The statement is about recognizing shared experience.

cards.prompt: A nurse leader notices that three members of a unit group meet before sessions to plan how to embarrass another member whom they dislike. Which term best describes this behavior? A. Groupthink B. Group norm C. Hidden agenda D. Cohesiveness
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse leader notices that three members of a unit group meet before sessions to plan how to embarrass another member whom they dislike. Which term best describes this behavior?

  • A. Groupthink
  • B. Group norm
  • C. Hidden agenda
  • D. Cohesiveness
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

A hidden agenda is a goal outside the stated group goals that disrupts the group process; the lecture uses three members planning to embarrass a disliked member as its example. Groupthink (A) is the tendency to avoid conflict and adopt the leader's thinking. A group norm (B) is the group's accepted behavior, such as raising hands. Cohesiveness (D) is the group's ability to stick together.

cards.prompt: A nurse prepares to lead a new psychoeducation group about medication management. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Assess members' reading level and memory before choosing materials. B. Hold the group in a private room with chairs in a circle and no table. C. Start the group late so that members who arrive late do not miss anything. D. Explain the group rules, purpose, and confidentiality at the first meeting. E. Ask each member to state the names of their medications to the group.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse prepares to lead a new psychoeducation group about medication management. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Assess members' reading level and memory before choosing materials.
  • B. Hold the group in a private room with chairs in a circle and no table.
  • C. Start the group late so that members who arrive late do not miss anything.
  • D. Explain the group rules, purpose, and confidentiality at the first meeting.
  • E. Ask each member to state the names of their medications to the group.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D

People with mental illness may have trouble remembering information, so assessing cognition and literacy guides materials. A private circle without a table encourages interaction and protects confidentiality. The first meeting covers rules, purpose, and confidentiality. Starting late (C) rewards lateness and makes punctual members resentful. Members may share their medications if they choose, but requiring it (E) violates confidentiality.

cards.prompt: A patient with depression tells the nurse during a cognitive behavioral therapy session, "I got a B on one test, so I'm going to fail out of nursing school and my life will be ruined." Which nursing response best uses CBT principles? A. "You are being negative. Try to think positive thoughts." B. "Your grades are fine, so you have nothing to worry about." C. "Let's look at the evidence: what other grades have you earned, and what is the worst thing that could realistically happen?" D. "Why do you always think the worst about yourself?"
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with depression tells the nurse during a cognitive behavioral therapy session, "I got a B on one test, so I'm going to fail out of nursing school and my life will be ruined." Which nursing response best uses CBT principles?

  • A. "You are being negative. Try to think positive thoughts."
  • B. "Your grades are fine, so you have nothing to worry about."
  • C. "Let's look at the evidence: what other grades have you earned, and what is the worst thing that could realistically happen?"
  • D. "Why do you always think the worst about yourself?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

CBT helps the patient test an automatic thought by examining evidence for and against it, looking at alternative explanations, and considering realistic outcomes. This patient is catastrophizing. Option A dismisses the patient and gives no method. Option B is false reassurance. Option D is a "why" question that sounds critical and does not examine the belief.

cards.prompt: A patient with a severe fear of elevators has learned progressive muscle relaxation. The therapist plans to expose the patient step by step, starting with looking at a picture of an elevator, while the patient uses relaxation. Which therapy is being used? A. Flooding B. Aversion therapy C. Operant conditioning D. Systematic desensitization
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with a severe fear of elevators has learned progressive muscle relaxation. The therapist plans to expose the patient step by step, starting with looking at a picture of an elevator, while the patient uses relaxation. Which therapy is being used?

  • A. Flooding
  • B. Aversion therapy
  • C. Operant conditioning
  • D. Systematic desensitization
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Systematic desensitization is planned, progressive exposure to the feared stimulus paired with relaxation, and the patient must master relaxation first. Flooding (A) exposes the patient to a large amount of the stimulus at once. Aversion therapy (B) pairs an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus. Operant conditioning (C) uses reinforcement, such as rewards, to increase a target behavior.

cards.prompt: A client started phenelzine two days ago. At the clinic the client reports a sudden pounding occipital headache, a stiff neck, and a racing heart after eating a pepperoni pizza with extra aged cheese. The blood pressure is 214/118 mmHg. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Teach the client which foods contain tyramine B. Have the client lie down and notify the prescriber immediately C. Ask the client to rest and recheck the blood pressure in 30 minutes D. Give the next scheduled dose of phenelzine with water
cards.promptHtml:
A client started phenelzine two days ago. At the clinic the client reports a sudden pounding occipital headache, a stiff neck, and a racing heart after eating a pepperoni pizza with extra aged cheese. The blood pressure is 214/118 mmHg. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Teach the client which foods contain tyramine
  • B. Have the client lie down and notify the prescriber immediately
  • C. Ask the client to rest and recheck the blood pressure in 30 minutes
  • D. Give the next scheduled dose of phenelzine with water
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Severe headache, neck stiffness, tachycardia and a markedly elevated blood pressure after a tyramine-rich meal on an MAOI is a hypertensive crisis, which can cause hemorrhagic stroke. The priority is immediate medical evaluation and treatment, so the prescriber is notified now and the client is kept safe. Teaching (A) comes after stabilization. Waiting 30 minutes (C) delays treatment of an emergency. Giving more MAOI (D) would worsen the situation.

cards.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has just been prescribed lithium for bipolar disorder. Which statements by the client indicate that the teaching was effective? Select all that apply. A. "I will keep drinking my usual amount of water and not change my salt intake." B. "I will have my blood level drawn in the morning before I take my dose." C. "I will skip my dose and use ibuprofen if I get a headache." D. "I will call right away if I develop vomiting, diarrhea and a coarse hand tremor." E. "I will stop the medicine when my mood feels stable."
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is teaching a client who has just been prescribed lithium for bipolar disorder. Which statements by the client indicate that the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I will keep drinking my usual amount of water and not change my salt intake."
  • B. "I will have my blood level drawn in the morning before I take my dose."
  • C. "I will skip my dose and use ibuprofen if I get a headache."
  • D. "I will call right away if I develop vomiting, diarrhea and a coarse hand tremor."
  • E. "I will stop the medicine when my mood feels stable."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D

Lithium is cleared by the kidneys, so consistent sodium and fluid intake keeps the level steady (A). The trough level is drawn about 12 hours after the last dose, before the morning dose (B). Vomiting, diarrhea and coarse tremor are early signs of toxicity and need prompt reporting (D). NSAIDs such as ibuprofen raise lithium levels (C is unsafe), and stopping without guidance risks relapse (E).

cards.prompt: A client who takes haloperidol for schizophrenia develops a sustained twisting of the neck, upward eye deviation and difficulty swallowing within hours of an increased dose. The nurse recognizes this as an acute dystonic reaction. Which prescriber order should the nurse anticipate? A. Propranolol orally B. Valbenazine orally C. Benztropine intramuscularly D. Lithium carbonate orally
cards.promptHtml:
A client who takes haloperidol for schizophrenia develops a sustained twisting of the neck, upward eye deviation and difficulty swallowing within hours of an increased dose. The nurse recognizes this as an acute dystonic reaction. Which prescriber order should the nurse anticipate?

  • A. Propranolol orally
  • B. Valbenazine orally
  • C. Benztropine intramuscularly
  • D. Lithium carbonate orally
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, laryngospasm) responds to an IV or IM anticholinergic such as benztropine or diphenhydramine, because EPS reflects excess acetylcholine relative to blocked dopamine. Propranolol (A) is used for akathisia. Valbenazine (B) treats tardive dyskinesia and is not an emergency drug. Lithium (D) is a mood stabilizer and does not treat dystonia. Airway compromise is possible, so the nurse stays with the client.

cards.prompt: A nurse reviews the medication list of an older adult client with moderate Alzheimer disease who is newly confused and constipated, with a dry mouth. Which medications should the nurse question because of anticholinergic effects? Select all that apply. A. Diphenhydramine at bedtime B. Donepezil each morning C. Amitriptyline daily D. Oxybutynin for bladder urgency E. Memantine twice daily
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse reviews the medication list of an older adult client with moderate Alzheimer disease who is newly confused and constipated, with a dry mouth. Which medications should the nurse question because of anticholinergic effects? Select all that apply.

  • A. Diphenhydramine at bedtime
  • B. Donepezil each morning
  • C. Amitriptyline daily
  • D. Oxybutynin for bladder urgency
  • E. Memantine twice daily
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

Diphenhydramine, amitriptyline and oxybutynin all block acetylcholine and can worsen confusion, constipation, dry mouth and retention, and the lecture advises avoiding all anticholinergics in dementia. Donepezil (B) is a cholinesterase inhibitor that raises acetylcholine, and memantine (E) is an NMDA antagonist; both are appropriate Alzheimer treatments that slow decline but do not reverse it.

cards.prompt: A client who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily has been stable on clozapine. The client is admitted to a smoke-free unit and stops smoking. Two days later the client is very sedated and dizzy. What is the most likely explanation? A. Clozapine levels have risen because smoking no longer induces CYP1A2 B. The client has developed agranulocytosis C. The client is having an acute dystonic reaction D. Nicotine withdrawal always causes sedation
cards.promptHtml:
A client who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily has been stable on clozapine. The client is admitted to a smoke-free unit and stops smoking. Two days later the client is very sedated and dizzy. What is the most likely explanation?

  • A. Clozapine levels have risen because smoking no longer induces CYP1A2
  • B. The client has developed agranulocytosis
  • C. The client is having an acute dystonic reaction
  • D. Nicotine withdrawal always causes sedation
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Cigarette smoke induces CYP1A2 and speeds clozapine clearance. When smoking stops, clearance falls and the level rises, producing sedation, hypotension or seizures. The nurse reports this so the dose can be reviewed. Agranulocytosis (B) presents with fever and sore throat, and dystonia (C) with muscle spasm. Nicotine withdrawal (D) typically causes irritability, not predictable sedation.

cards.prompt: A client with schizophrenia has missed several outpatient appointments and stopped taking an oral antipsychotic. Which response by the nurse best supports the client's adherence? A. "You must take this medicine or you will be hospitalized again." B. "Most people do fine, so try not to worry about side effects." C. "I will tell your family to watch you swallow every dose." D. "What has made it hard to take the medicine, and what side effects are you having?"
cards.promptHtml:
A client with schizophrenia has missed several outpatient appointments and stopped taking an oral antipsychotic. Which response by the nurse best supports the client's adherence?

  • A. "You must take this medicine or you will be hospitalized again."
  • B. "Most people do fine, so try not to worry about side effects."
  • C. "I will tell your family to watch you swallow every dose."
  • D. "What has made it hard to take the medicine, and what side effects are you having?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Side effects are the most often cited reason for nonadherence, and recovery-oriented care supports the client's own decision without coercion. Open-ended exploration of barriers (D) lets the nurse assess and treat side effects, and consider options such as a long-acting injectable. Threats (A) and surveillance (C) are coercive, and dismissing concerns (B) blocks therapeutic communication.

cards.prompt: A client prescribed sertraline asks the nurse why it has not worked after one week. Which response is best? A. "Some improvement may begin in about 2 weeks, and full effect takes longer, so please keep taking it." B. "This medicine works right away, so we should increase the dose today." C. "You should stop it and ask for a benzodiazepine instead." D. "Antidepressants only work if taken as needed when you feel low."
cards.promptHtml:
A client prescribed sertraline asks the nurse why it has not worked after one week. Which response is best?

  • A. "Some improvement may begin in about 2 weeks, and full effect takes longer, so please keep taking it."
  • B. "This medicine works right away, so we should increase the dose today."
  • C. "You should stop it and ask for a benzodiazepine instead."
  • D. "Antidepressants only work if taken as needed when you feel low."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Antidepressants take about 2 weeks to begin working, with fuller benefit over several weeks, and are continued 6-12 months after remission and tapered, not stopped abruptly. Option A corrects the expectation and supports adherence. Early dose increases (B) are a prescriber decision and not based on one week. Benzodiazepines (C) are short-term rescue agents. PRN use (D) is incorrect for maintenance therapy.

cards.prompt: A client with a known family history of severe adverse reactions to several antidepressants asks what genetic testing could offer. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate? A. "It can confirm which psychiatric disorder you have." B. "It predicts exactly which medication will cure your depression." C. "It can show whether you metabolize certain medications slowly or quickly, which helps guide drug and dose selection." D. "It replaces the need for blood levels and monitoring."
cards.promptHtml:
A client with a known family history of severe adverse reactions to several antidepressants asks what genetic testing could offer. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?

  • A. "It can confirm which psychiatric disorder you have."
  • B. "It predicts exactly which medication will cure your depression."
  • C. "It can show whether you metabolize certain medications slowly or quickly, which helps guide drug and dose selection."
  • D. "It replaces the need for blood levels and monitoring."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Pharmacogenomic testing of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 identifies poor and rapid metabolizers. Poor metabolizers are more likely to have adverse reactions, and rapid metabolizers may not reach therapeutic levels. Testing is reasonable with a personal or family history of adverse reactions. It does not diagnose a disorder (A), guarantee a cure (B), or replace monitoring (D).

cards.prompt: A client with schizophrenia says, "The man on the news is sending me secret messages, and a chip in my head lets the neighbors hear my thoughts." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "There is no chip. That is only your illness talking." B. "Tell me how the chip works so I can understand your experience." C. "That sounds frightening. I do not believe there is a chip, but I will stay with you and help you feel safe." D. "Let's not talk about that. Come and play cards with me."
cards.promptHtml:
A client with schizophrenia says, "The man on the news is sending me secret messages, and a chip in my head lets the neighbors hear my thoughts." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "There is no chip. That is only your illness talking."
  • B. "Tell me how the chip works so I can understand your experience."
  • C. "That sounds frightening. I do not believe there is a chip, but I will stay with you and help you feel safe."
  • D. "Let's not talk about that. Come and play cards with me."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

The belief is real to the client, so the nurse acknowledges the feeling (fear), states honestly that the nurse does not share the belief, and offers safety. Flatly denying the belief (A) blocks communication and invites defending it. Asking for details (B) feeds the delusion. Abruptly changing the subject (D) dismisses the client. Do not argue, do not agree, and redirect to the here and now once the client feels understood.

cards.prompt: A client received intramuscular haloperidol decanoate 4 days ago. Which findings should lead the nurse to suspect neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Select all that apply. A. Temperature of 39.8 C (103.6 F) B. Severe generalized "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity C. Elevated creatine phosphokinase D. Rolling tongue movements and lip smacking E. Labile blood pressure, heart rate of 124, and heavy sweating
cards.promptHtml:
A client received intramuscular haloperidol decanoate 4 days ago. Which findings should lead the nurse to suspect neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Select all that apply.

  • A. Temperature of 39.8 C (103.6 F)
  • B. Severe generalized "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity
  • C. Elevated creatine phosphokinase
  • D. Rolling tongue movements and lip smacking
  • E. Labile blood pressure, heart rate of 124, and heavy sweating
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C, E

NMS is a medical emergency with hyperthermia, severe rigidity, autonomic instability (tachycardia, unstable blood pressure, diaphoresis), altered mental status, and laboratory changes such as high CPK and leukocytosis. Tongue rolling and lip smacking (D) are tardive dyskinesia, a late-appearing movement disorder that develops over months to years, not days, and does not cause fever or autonomic change. Hold the antipsychotic and notify the provider.

cards.prompt: Two hours after receiving the first dose of haloperidol, a 22-year-old man's eyes roll upward, his neck is twisted to one side, and he cannot speak clearly. He is frightened. What is the nurse's best first action? A. Stay with the client and call the prescriber for an order for IM benztropine or diphenhydramine B. Give an additional dose of haloperidol to calm him C. Reassure him that the muscle spasm will pass on its own D. Place him in seclusion until the spasms stop
cards.promptHtml:
Two hours after receiving the first dose of haloperidol, a 22-year-old man's eyes roll upward, his neck is twisted to one side, and he cannot speak clearly. He is frightened. What is the nurse's best first action?

  • A. Stay with the client and call the prescriber for an order for IM benztropine or diphenhydramine
  • B. Give an additional dose of haloperidol to calm him
  • C. Reassure him that the muscle spasm will pass on its own
  • D. Place him in seclusion until the spasms stop
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

This is an acute dystonic reaction (oculogyric crisis and torticollis), most common in young men early in treatment. It is frightening and can compromise swallowing and breathing, so it needs prompt treatment with an IM or IV anticholinergic such as benztropine or diphenhydramine, usually followed by daily anticholinergics or a dose change. More haloperidol (B) worsens it. Waiting (C) and seclusion (D) ignore a treatable emergency and increase fear.

cards.prompt: A client with schizophrenia is starting olanzapine. Which statement by the client shows the teaching was effective? A. "If I gain weight, I will stop the pills on my own." B. "I can stop the medicine once the voices go away." C. "I will not need blood sugar checks because this is a new drug." D. "I will weigh myself every week and tell my provider if my weight climbs fast or I feel very thirsty."
cards.promptHtml:
A client with schizophrenia is starting olanzapine. Which statement by the client shows the teaching was effective?

  • A. "If I gain weight, I will stop the pills on my own."
  • B. "I can stop the medicine once the voices go away."
  • C. "I will not need blood sugar checks because this is a new drug."
  • D. "I will weigh myself every week and tell my provider if my weight climbs fast or I feel very thirsty."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Olanzapine causes marked weight gain and can cause new-onset diabetes, so the client should self-monitor weight and report rapid gain or signs of hyperglycemia such as extreme thirst. Stopping because of weight gain (A) or because symptoms improved (B) risks relapse; medication is usually lifelong, and changes are made with the prescriber, gradually. Fasting glucose and A1C monitoring are needed with second-generation antipsychotics (C).

cards.prompt: A client with schizophrenia drinks water constantly from the unit fountain. Today the serum sodium is 124 mEq/L and the client seems more confused. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Monitor daily weights and fluid intake B. Measure urine specific gravity as ordered C. Encourage extra fluids to flush out the medication D. Assess for headache, worsening confusion, and seizure activity E. Redirect the client with one-to-one observation if the water seeking is severe
cards.promptHtml:
A client with schizophrenia drinks water constantly from the unit fountain. Today the serum sodium is 124 mEq/L and the client seems more confused. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Monitor daily weights and fluid intake
  • B. Measure urine specific gravity as ordered
  • C. Encourage extra fluids to flush out the medication
  • D. Assess for headache, worsening confusion, and seizure activity
  • E. Redirect the client with one-to-one observation if the water seeking is severe
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D, E

Compulsive water drinking (polydipsia) can dilute serum sodium and cause water intoxication, a medical emergency that shows as headache, confusion and seizures. Care includes monitoring intake, weight and urine specific gravity, assessing neurologic status, notifying the provider, and close observation for severe cases. Encouraging more fluids (C) would make hyponatremia worse.

cards.prompt: The nurse is making assignments on a psychiatric unit. Which client should the nurse assess first? A. A client on olanzapine who has gained 3 pounds this month B. A client who started clozapine 6 weeks ago and now has a sore throat and temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F) C. A client with flat affect who skipped lunch D. A client taking benztropine who reports a dry mouth
cards.promptHtml:
The nurse is making assignments on a psychiatric unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?

  • A. A client on olanzapine who has gained 3 pounds this month
  • B. A client who started clozapine 6 weeks ago and now has a sore throat and temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F)
  • C. A client with flat affect who skipped lunch
  • D. A client taking benztropine who reports a dry mouth
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Fever and sore throat on clozapine suggest agranulocytosis, which is most likely in the first weeks to months and can progress quickly to overwhelming infection. The nurse holds the dose, obtains a blood count (ANC), and notifies the prescriber. Weight gain (A), a skipped meal with negative symptoms (C), and anticholinergic dry mouth (D) need attention but are not immediately life-threatening.

cards.prompt: A client with schizophrenia has been mute, rigid, and holding a fixed posture for two days, and has taken no food or fluids. Which nursing concern has the highest priority? A. Teaching about the medication regimen B. Improving social skills C. Hydration and nutritional status D. Participation in group activities
cards.promptHtml:
A client with schizophrenia has been mute, rigid, and holding a fixed posture for two days, and has taken no food or fluids. Which nursing concern has the highest priority?

  • A. Teaching about the medication regimen
  • B. Improving social skills
  • C. Hydration and nutritional status
  • D. Participation in group activities
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Catatonic behavior (stupor, mutism, posturing) leaves the client unable to meet basic needs, so physiologic needs come first: fluids, nutrition, elimination, skin and joint care, and monitoring of vital signs. Teaching (A), social skills training (B), and group work (D) are for a later, lucid period, since new demands during active psychosis add stress.

cards.prompt: A 24-year-old client has had delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech for 3 months with a marked decline in work function. There are no manic or depressive episodes and no substance use. Which diagnosis best fits? A. Schizophreniform disorder B. Brief psychotic disorder C. Delusional disorder D. Schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml:
A 24-year-old client has had delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech for 3 months with a marked decline in work function. There are no manic or depressive episodes and no substance use. Which diagnosis best fits?

  • A. Schizophreniform disorder
  • B. Brief psychotic disorder
  • C. Delusional disorder
  • D. Schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

The symptoms match schizophrenia, but duration decides the label: continuous signs for less than 6 months but at least 1 month is schizophreniform disorder; about one third recover and two thirds progress to schizophrenia. Brief psychotic disorder (B) lasts less than 1 month. Delusional disorder (C) has stable delusions without hallucinations or disorganization and little functional decline. Schizophrenia (D) needs at least 6 months of continuous signs.

cards.prompt: A 45-year-old inpatient with major depressive disorder has been withdrawn and tearful for three weeks. This morning he is smiling, joking with staff and says, "Everything is going to be fine now." He asks to be discharged today, and the nurse learns he gave his watch and wallet to his roommate last night. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Document the improved mood and recommend discharge planning. B. Ask him directly about thoughts of suicide, a plan, and the means. C. Ask his family whether they also think he seems better. D. Lower his observation level because his mood has lifted.
cards.promptHtml:
A 45-year-old inpatient with major depressive disorder has been withdrawn and tearful for three weeks. This morning he is smiling, joking with staff and says, "Everything is going to be fine now." He asks to be discharged today, and the nurse learns he gave his watch and wallet to his roommate last night. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Document the improved mood and recommend discharge planning.
  • B. Ask him directly about thoughts of suicide, a plan, and the means.
  • C. Ask his family whether they also think he seems better.
  • D. Lower his observation level because his mood has lifted.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Sudden calm or new energy after deep depression, plus giving away possessions, can mean the patient has decided to die; energy returns before mood and risk rises. The nurse must assess intent, plan, and means directly before anything else. Documenting improvement and discharge planning (A) and lowering observation (D) misread the change as recovery. Family input (C) is useful later but delays the priority assessment, which only the patient can answer.

cards.prompt: A patient is starting phenelzine (Nardil). The nurse is reviewing lunch choices with the patient. Which foods are acceptable on a low-tyramine diet? Select all that apply. A. Fresh grilled chicken breast B. Pepperoni pizza with aged cheese C. Fresh cottage cheese D. Tap beer E. A fresh apple
cards.promptHtml:
A patient is starting phenelzine (Nardil). The nurse is reviewing lunch choices with the patient. Which foods are acceptable on a low-tyramine diet? Select all that apply.

  • A. Fresh grilled chicken breast
  • B. Pepperoni pizza with aged cheese
  • C. Fresh cottage cheese
  • D. Tap beer
  • E. A fresh apple
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

MAOIs block the enzyme that breaks down dietary tyramine, so tyramine-rich foods can cause a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, stiff neck, palpitations, stroke). Freshly cooked, properly stored meat, fresh cottage and cream cheese, and fresh fruit are allowed. Aged or processed cheese, cured meats such as pepperoni, and tap or unpasteurized beer are restricted. The patient should also avoid decongestants and diet pills.

cards.prompt: An inpatient who is in a manic episode paces the hall, speaks rapidly, and tells the nurse, "I own this hospital and I'm firing you today." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "You do not own this hospital. You are a patient here for treatment." B. "Why do you think you have the authority to fire me?" C. "If you keep talking like this, I will have to give you medication." D. "You have a lot on your mind. Lunch is ready, so let's walk to the dining room together."
cards.promptHtml:
An inpatient who is in a manic episode paces the hall, speaks rapidly, and tells the nurse, "I own this hospital and I'm firing you today." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "You do not own this hospital. You are a patient here for treatment."
  • B. "Why do you think you have the authority to fire me?"
  • C. "If you keep talking like this, I will have to give you medication."
  • D. "You have a lot on your mind. Lunch is ready, so let's walk to the dining room together."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

In mania, the nurse stays calm, avoids arguing about grandiose beliefs, uses simple, direct statements, and redirects. Walking together suits the patient's need to move and meets the nutrition need. Contradicting the belief (A) and asking "why" (B) invite argument and are hard for a patient with flight of ideas to answer. Threatening medication (C) is punitive and escalates agitation.

cards.prompt: A patient who takes lithium for bipolar I disorder is being taught about the medication. Which statements by the patient indicate that teaching was effective? Select all that apply. A. "I will cut back on salt to help my blood pressure." B. "I will keep my fluid intake steady and drink more when I sweat a lot." C. "I can take ibuprofen for my headaches." D. "I will call my prescriber if I have vomiting or diarrhea." E. "I will keep my blood level appointments even when I feel well."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient who takes lithium for bipolar I disorder is being taught about the medication. Which statements by the patient indicate that teaching was effective? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I will cut back on salt to help my blood pressure."
  • B. "I will keep my fluid intake steady and drink more when I sweat a lot."
  • C. "I can take ibuprofen for my headaches."
  • D. "I will call my prescriber if I have vomiting or diarrhea."
  • E. "I will keep my blood level appointments even when I feel well."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B, D, E

Lithium and sodium compete in the kidney, so low salt intake, dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, and heavy sweating raise the lithium level and can cause toxicity. Steady salt and fluid intake, calling for fluid losses, and scheduled levels keep the level in range (0.6-1.2 mEq/L). NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce lithium clearance and raise the level, so option C is unsafe; option A is wrong for the same sodium reason.

cards.prompt: A patient who has taken lithium for six months comes to the clinic after two days of vomiting and diarrhea. The nurse observes a worsening hand tremor, slurred speech, and an unsteady gait. The lithium level is 1.9 mEq/L. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Withhold the next dose and notify the prescriber. B. Give the dose with food and recheck the level tomorrow. C. Restrict fluids to slow the diarrhea. D. Document the tremor as an expected side effect of lithium.
cards.promptHtml:
A patient who has taken lithium for six months comes to the clinic after two days of vomiting and diarrhea. The nurse observes a worsening hand tremor, slurred speech, and an unsteady gait. The lithium level is 1.9 mEq/L. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Withhold the next dose and notify the prescriber.
  • B. Give the dose with food and recheck the level tomorrow.
  • C. Restrict fluids to slow the diarrhea.
  • D. Document the tremor as an expected side effect of lithium.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

A level between 1.5 and 2.5 mEq/L with increasing tremor, ataxia, and slurred speech is moderate toxicity, often triggered by fluid and sodium loss. The nurse withholds further lithium and contacts the prescriber immediately for direction (a stat level and fluids if the patient can drink). Giving the dose (B) worsens toxicity. Fluid restriction (C) is dangerous because dehydration raises lithium levels. A fine resting tremor is an expected mild effect below 1.5 mEq/L (D), but a worsening tremor with neurologic signs at this level is not.

cards.prompt: A patient returns to the unit drowsy after an electroconvulsive therapy treatment. Which nursing action has the highest priority? A. Orient the patient to the date and place using a calendar. B. Offer a meal now because the patient has been NPO. C. Position the patient on the side, keep the airway open, and monitor vital signs and oxygenation. D. Review follow-up appointments with the patient's family.
cards.promptHtml:
A patient returns to the unit drowsy after an electroconvulsive therapy treatment. Which nursing action has the highest priority?

  • A. Orient the patient to the date and place using a calendar.
  • B. Offer a meal now because the patient has been NPO.
  • C. Position the patient on the side, keep the airway open, and monitor vital signs and oxygenation.
  • D. Review follow-up appointments with the patient's family.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

ECT uses short-acting anesthesia and a muscle relaxant, so recovery is managed like any postanesthesia recovery: airway, breathing, and vital signs come first. Reorientation (A) is needed because confusion is common but follows airway safety. A meal (B) is unsafe until the patient is awake and alert. Family follow-up teaching (D) can wait; supervision continues for at least 12 hours and observation for 48.

cards.prompt: A nurse is assessing a 62-year-old woman whose husband died eight months ago. Which finding most strongly suggests major depression rather than uncomplicated grief? A. Waves of sadness triggered by photographs of her husband. B. Tearfulness around the anniversary of his death. C. Difficulty sleeping on some nights since the funeral. D. Persistent feelings of worthlessness and a belief that she would be better off dead.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is assessing a 62-year-old woman whose husband died eight months ago. Which finding most strongly suggests major depression rather than uncomplicated grief?

  • A. Waves of sadness triggered by photographs of her husband.
  • B. Tearfulness around the anniversary of his death.
  • C. Difficulty sleeping on some nights since the funeral.
  • D. Persistent feelings of worthlessness and a belief that she would be better off dead.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

In uncomplicated grief, pain comes in waves, there is gradual movement, and self-esteem and competence stay intact. Persistent worthlessness and thoughts of death point toward a major depressive episode and require immediate suicide risk assessment. Sadness at reminders (A), anniversary distress (B), and some sleep disruption (C) are expected in the first year after a loss. Intense yearning beyond six months also suggests complicated grief and needs follow-up.

cards.prompt: A patient with severe depression has sat silently in the dayroom for two days and has eaten little. Which nursing approach is most appropriate? A. "I'll sit with you for a few minutes. You don't have to talk." B. "You'll feel better if you join the group this afternoon." C. "Everyone gets sad sometimes. Try to look on the bright side." D. "Why won't you talk to me?"
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with severe depression has sat silently in the dayroom for two days and has eaten little. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?

  • A. "I'll sit with you for a few minutes. You don't have to talk."
  • B. "You'll feel better if you join the group this afternoon."
  • C. "Everyone gets sad sometimes. Try to look on the bright side."
  • D. "Why won't you talk to me?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Depressed patients tend to be withdrawn and slow to respond; a calm, quiet, empathic presence builds trust without demanding conversation. Cheerleading, reassurance that minimizes the illness (C), pressure to participate (B), and "why" questions (D) block communication and can increase the patient's sense of failure. After trust develops, the nurse can break tasks into small steps and encourage meals and group attendance.

cards.prompt: A nurse enters the room of a client who is pacing rapidly, saying "I'm going to pieces, what is happening to me?" The client is breathless, cannot follow simple directions, and repeats the same detail about a phone call. Which nursing action is the priority? A. Stay with the client, speak in short simple phrases, and allow pacing B. Explain the relaxation technique of progressive muscle relaxation step by step C. Have the client recount, step by step, the events before this episode D. Place a hand on the client's shoulder to provide comfort
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse enters the room of a client who is pacing rapidly, saying "I'm going to pieces, what is happening to me?" The client is breathless, cannot follow simple directions, and repeats the same detail about a phone call. Which nursing action is the priority?

  • A. Stay with the client, speak in short simple phrases, and allow pacing
  • B. Explain the relaxation technique of progressive muscle relaxation step by step
  • C. Have the client recount, step by step, the events before this episode
  • D. Place a hand on the client's shoulder to provide comfort
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

The client is in panic: the perceptual field is reduced to a detail, learning is impossible, and the client perceives a threat to survival. The nurse stays present, uses few direct words, and allows pacing, keeping the environment safe. Teaching relaxation (B) and detailed history (C) require thinking the client cannot do yet. Touch (D) is often misread as an invasion by a panicking client.

cards.prompt: A student nurse who is about to take an examination says, "I'm a little nervous, but it's helping me focus and review more." The nurse recognizes this as which level of anxiety? A. Panic B. Severe C. Mild D. Moderate
cards.promptHtml:
A student nurse who is about to take an examination says, "I'm a little nervous, but it's helping me focus and review more." The nurse recognizes this as which level of anxiety?

  • A. Panic
  • B. Severe
  • C. Mild
  • D. Moderate
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

In mild anxiety the perceptual field widens, the person is alert, and learning is enhanced; the person can easily name the feeling. Moderate anxiety narrows the field with selective inattention. Severe anxiety greatly reduces the field and distorts inference, and panic makes learning impossible. The nurse can use the energy of mild anxiety to promote learning.

cards.prompt: A client with moderate anxiety is preparing for discharge teaching. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Encourage the client to describe one experience fully B. Direct the client's attention to the content being taught C. Postpone all teaching until the anxiety resolves completely D. Ask the client to name how anxious they feel E. Use long, detailed explanations covering every topic at once
cards.promptHtml:
A client with moderate anxiety is preparing for discharge teaching. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Encourage the client to describe one experience fully
  • B. Direct the client's attention to the content being taught
  • C. Postpone all teaching until the anxiety resolves completely
  • D. Ask the client to name how anxious they feel
  • E. Use long, detailed explanations covering every topic at once
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D

Moderate anxiety narrows the perceptual field slightly, but the person can attend to more when directed and can usually state "I am anxious now." Having the client talk about one experience, directing attention to key content and naming the feeling help the client learn. Postponing everything (C) is unnecessary because learning is still possible. Long, broad explanations (E) overload a narrowed field; use short, focused teaching.

cards.prompt: A client who was criticized by a supervisor goes home and snaps at the spouse over a minor issue. Which defense mechanism is the client using? A. Projection B. Rationalization C. Reaction formation D. Displacement
cards.promptHtml:
A client who was criticized by a supervisor goes home and snaps at the spouse over a minor issue. Which defense mechanism is the client using?

  • A. Projection
  • B. Rationalization
  • C. Reaction formation
  • D. Displacement
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Displacement discharges feelings onto a safer, less threatening target (the spouse) instead of the real source (the supervisor). Projection (A) attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to another. Reaction formation (C) expresses the opposite of the real feeling. Rationalization (B) offers a logical-sounding excuse for behavior.

cards.prompt: Which statements by clients indicate use of an ineffective or maladaptive coping response? Select all that apply. A. "I keep telling myself it was my fault that he hit me, so I stay." B. "After a stressful day I have a few drinks to calm down." C. "I made a list of the problems and called the clinic to ask for help." D. "I cannot recall anything about the assault, and I have not needed to." E. "I talk with my sister every week about how I'm feeling."
cards.promptHtml:
Which statements by clients indicate use of an ineffective or maladaptive coping response? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I keep telling myself it was my fault that he hit me, so I stay."
  • B. "After a stressful day I have a few drinks to calm down."
  • C. "I made a list of the problems and called the clinic to ask for help."
  • D. "I cannot recall anything about the assault, and I have not needed to."
  • E. "I talk with my sister every week about how I'm feeling."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D

Reinterpreting abuse as one's own fault is emotion-focused coping used when a problem-focused response (leaving or seeking help) is needed. Alcohol is a negative coping strategy that raises health risk. Unconscious repression of a traumatic event can prevent the person from addressing it. Problem solving and seeking help (C) and drawing on social support (E) are positive coping.

cards.prompt: Six weeks after a divorce, a client reports feeling sad, tearful and unable to concentrate at work. The client has no history of depression, does not meet criteria for major depression, and says the symptoms started a month ago. Which diagnosis does the nurse expect? A. Adjustment disorder B. Generalized anxiety disorder C. Panic disorder D. Borderline personality disorder
cards.promptHtml:
Six weeks after a divorce, a client reports feeling sad, tearful and unable to concentrate at work. The client has no history of depression, does not meet criteria for major depression, and says the symptoms started a month ago. Which diagnosis does the nurse expect?

  • A. Adjustment disorder
  • B. Generalized anxiety disorder
  • C. Panic disorder
  • D. Borderline personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Adjustment disorder (stress response syndrome, "situational depression") involves significant emotional or behavioral symptoms that follow an identifiable stressor within about 3 months, impair functioning, and ease as the situation resolves. The clear stressor, short time course, and absence of criteria for another disorder fit. The other diagnoses require different symptom patterns or a long-standing pattern. The nurse also screens for suicidal thinking.

cards.prompt: A nurse teaching about stress explains that cortisol released over a long period of stress has which effect on the body? A. It strengthens the immune response to infection B. It decreases allostatic load C. It lowers blood glucose D. It suppresses the immune system
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse teaching about stress explains that cortisol released over a long period of stress has which effect on the body?

  • A. It strengthens the immune response to infection
  • B. It decreases allostatic load
  • C. It lowers blood glucose
  • D. It suppresses the immune system
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

The HPA axis releases cortisol through CRH and ACTH. Cortisol helps in acute stress but, when sustained, is immunosuppressive: lymphocytes and natural killer cell function fall, so the person is more prone to illness. Allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear, increases rather than decreases. Cortisol tends to raise, not lower, blood glucose (general knowledge).

cards.prompt: During an assessment of a client who reports persistent stress, which question best shows how the client is appraising what is happening? A. "How many hours of sleep do you get each night?" B. "What does this situation mean to you, and do you feel you can handle it?" C. "Have you ever been told you have an anxiety disorder?" D. "Why can't you just relax and stop worrying?"
cards.promptHtml:
During an assessment of a client who reports persistent stress, which question best shows how the client is appraising what is happening?

  • A. "How many hours of sleep do you get each night?"
  • B. "What does this situation mean to you, and do you feel you can handle it?"
  • C. "Have you ever been told you have an anxiety disorder?"
  • D. "Why can't you just relax and stop worrying?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Appraisal is how the person judges an event: as harm, threat or challenge (primary) and the evaluation of available coping resources (secondary). An open question about meaning and ability to cope elicits both. Sleep (A) assesses physical functioning, not appraisal. A history question (C) is closed. "Why" and "just relax" (D) is judgmental and blocks therapeutic communication.

cards.prompt: A patient arrives at the emergency department gripping his chest, breathing rapidly and saying, "I'm dying." Cardiac enzymes and ECG are normal and the nurse suspects a panic attack. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Explain the physiology of the fight-or-flight response in detail B. Stay with the patient and speak in short, calm sentences in a low-stimulation area C. Hold the patient's hand and encourage him to talk about what triggered the attack D. Tell the patient his tests are normal and nothing is wrong
cards.promptHtml:
A patient arrives at the emergency department gripping his chest, breathing rapidly and saying, "I'm dying." Cardiac enzymes and ECG are normal and the nurse suspects a panic attack. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Explain the physiology of the fight-or-flight response in detail
  • B. Stay with the patient and speak in short, calm sentences in a low-stimulation area
  • C. Hold the patient's hand and encourage him to talk about what triggered the attack
  • D. Tell the patient his tests are normal and nothing is wrong
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

During panic the patient cannot process complex information, and the nurse's calm presence lowers anxiety. Brief, direct phrases and reduced stimulation are the priority. Detailed teaching (A) and exploring triggers (C) come after the attack subsides. Touch is avoided because a panicking patient may perceive it as an invasion. "Nothing is wrong" (D) dismisses very real distress; the physical symptoms mimic a cardiac event and the patient needs recognition of their seriousness.

cards.prompt: A nurse teaches a patient who is starting clonazepam (Klonopin) for panic disorder. Which statements by the patient show correct understanding? Select all that apply. A. "I should not drink wine while I am taking this medicine." B. "If I feel a panic attack coming, I can take a second dose right away to be safe." C. "I will not drive until I know how drowsy this makes me." D. "I can stop the medicine whenever I feel better." E. "My provider will lower the dose slowly when it is time to stop."
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse teaches a patient who is starting clonazepam (Klonopin) for panic disorder. Which statements by the patient show correct understanding? Select all that apply.

  • A. "I should not drink wine while I am taking this medicine."
  • B. "If I feel a panic attack coming, I can take a second dose right away to be safe."
  • C. "I will not drive until I know how drowsy this makes me."
  • D. "I can stop the medicine whenever I feel better."
  • E. "My provider will lower the dose slowly when it is time to stop."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

Alcohol adds to CNS depression (A). Sedation and dizziness make driving unsafe until the response is known (C). Benzodiazepines cause dependence, so they are tapered over weeks to prevent rebound anxiety and withdrawal, including seizures (E). Taking extra doses (B) risks oversedation and dependence, and stopping abruptly (D) can trigger withdrawal.

cards.prompt: A hospitalized patient with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes his hands for about 40 minutes before every meal, and the skin is now red and cracked. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate? A. Remove the soap from his room until the skin heals B. Tell him that the ritual is irrational and he must stop C. Schedule his hand washing after meals only and refuse any other washing D. Agree on a time-limited washing schedule, provide tepid water and moisturizing soap, and apply hand cream after washing
cards.promptHtml:
A hospitalized patient with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes his hands for about 40 minutes before every meal, and the skin is now red and cracked. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

  • A. Remove the soap from his room until the skin heals
  • B. Tell him that the ritual is irrational and he must stop
  • C. Schedule his hand washing after meals only and refuse any other washing
  • D. Agree on a time-limited washing schedule, provide tepid water and moisturizing soap, and apply hand cream after washing
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Early in treatment the ritual is not blocked, because stopping it abruptly raises anxiety sharply. The nurse protects skin integrity and works toward gradual reduction through a negotiated, time-limited schedule. Removing soap (A) or rigid prohibition (C) provokes panic and distrust, and telling him it is irrational (B) is critical and ineffective since he often already knows this.

cards.prompt: A veteran with PTSD tells the nurse, "I can't stand loud noises. I was in a bad place over there." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "It sounds like those experiences still affect you. I'll go at whatever pace is comfortable for you." B. "Tell me everything that happened over there so I can understand." C. "That was a long time ago. You are safe now." D. "Many veterans feel that way. Have you tried just ignoring the noises?"
cards.promptHtml:
A veteran with PTSD tells the nurse, "I can't stand loud noises. I was in a bad place over there." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "It sounds like those experiences still affect you. I'll go at whatever pace is comfortable for you."
  • B. "Tell me everything that happened over there so I can understand."
  • C. "That was a long time ago. You are safe now."
  • D. "Many veterans feel that way. Have you tried just ignoring the noises?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Trauma-informed care respects when and how the patient chooses to talk, acknowledges the impact and builds trust and a sense of control. Demanding the full story (B) risks retraumatization. Minimizing (C) and advising him to ignore symptoms (D) dismiss his experience and block communication.

cards.prompt: A nurse is teaching a patient with generalized anxiety disorder who has a new prescription for buspirone (BuSpar). Which statement by the patient indicates that teaching was effective? A. "I'll take it only when I feel very anxious, like a sedative." B. "I should feel completely calm after the first dose." C. "I need to take it every day, and it may take a few weeks to work fully." D. "I can have grapefruit juice with breakfast."
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is teaching a patient with generalized anxiety disorder who has a new prescription for buspirone (BuSpar). Which statement by the patient indicates that teaching was effective?

  • A. "I'll take it only when I feel very anxious, like a sedative."
  • B. "I should feel completely calm after the first dose."
  • C. "I need to take it every day, and it may take a few weeks to work fully."
  • D. "I can have grapefruit juice with breakfast."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Buspirone is non-sedating and non-habit-forming, but its effect builds slowly (first effects in about 1 week, full effect in 2 to 6 weeks) and it must be taken on a schedule, not as needed (A and B are wrong). Grapefruit juice increases buspirone levels and should be avoided (D).

cards.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient newly admitted with posttraumatic stress disorder after a sexual assault. Which actions are consistent with trauma-informed care? Select all that apply. A. Screen for suicidal thoughts and substance use B. Ask the patient to describe the assault in full detail during the first interview C. Explain each procedure and ask permission before touching the patient D. Place the patient in a room away from loud, unpredictable activity E. Plan to use a benzodiazepine as the primary long-term treatment
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is caring for a patient newly admitted with posttraumatic stress disorder after a sexual assault. Which actions are consistent with trauma-informed care? Select all that apply.

  • A. Screen for suicidal thoughts and substance use
  • B. Ask the patient to describe the assault in full detail during the first interview
  • C. Explain each procedure and ask permission before touching the patient
  • D. Place the patient in a room away from loud, unpredictable activity
  • E. Plan to use a benzodiazepine as the primary long-term treatment
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

PTSD carries increased risk of suicide and substance misuse, so screening comes first (A). Explaining and asking before touch preserves control and prevents retraumatization (C). Reducing triggering stimuli supports safety (D). Pressing for details (B) can retraumatize. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD; SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) plus therapy are used (E).

cards.prompt: An 82-year-old patient with generalized anxiety disorder is prescribed lorazepam (Ativan). Which nursing concern has the highest priority? A. Risk for falls and confusion B. Risk for weight gain C. Risk for hypertensive crisis D. Risk for sexual dysfunction
cards.promptHtml:
An 82-year-old patient with generalized anxiety disorder is prescribed lorazepam (Ativan). Which nursing concern has the highest priority?

  • A. Risk for falls and confusion
  • B. Risk for weight gain
  • C. Risk for hypertensive crisis
  • D. Risk for sexual dysfunction
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Benzodiazepines are generally not recommended for older adults because sedation, dizziness, confusion and respiratory depression increase the risk of falls and injury. Hypertensive crisis (C) is associated with MAOI interactions, and sexual dysfunction (D) is an SSRI effect. Weight gain (B) is not a characteristic concern with lorazepam.

cards.prompt: A patient with panic disorder started paroxetine (Paxil) 10 days ago and says, "I feel more jittery and my attacks seem worse. I want to stop it." What is the nurse's best response? A. "Stop it today and call your provider tomorrow." B. "Jitteriness is a sign the drug is toxic, so we will lower the dose now." C. "You will be switched to a benzodiazepine permanently." D. "A temporary increase in jitteriness can occur early, and the full benefit takes 4 to 6 weeks. Please do not stop it on your own; I will tell your provider."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with panic disorder started paroxetine (Paxil) 10 days ago and says, "I feel more jittery and my attacks seem worse. I want to stop it." What is the nurse's best response?

  • A. "Stop it today and call your provider tomorrow."
