  • B. "Jitteriness is a sign the drug is toxic, so we will lower the dose now."
  • C. "You will be switched to a benzodiazepine permanently."
  • D. "A temporary increase in jitteriness can occur early, and the full benefit takes 4 to 6 weeks. Please do not stop it on your own; I will tell your provider."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

SSRIs can briefly increase anxiety at the start, and the antianxiety effect appears after about 4 to 6 weeks. Abrupt discontinuation causes withdrawal symptoms and loses the benefit. The nurse acknowledges the concern, teaches expected effects and informs the prescriber, who may adjust the dose or add short-term help. Jitteriness is not toxicity (B), and a permanent benzodiazepine (C) is not recommended.

cards.prompt: A man comes to an urgent-care clinic the morning after a tornado destroyed his house. He has not slept or eaten since, has a blistered, untreated burn on his forearm, and keeps repeating, "I don't know what to do next." Which nursing action is the priority? A. Ask how he has handled major losses in the past B. Dress the burn and arrange food and a safe place to rest C. Give him a list of disaster-relief agencies to contact this week D. Teach him progressive muscle relaxation
cards.promptHtml:
A man comes to an urgent-care clinic the morning after a tornado destroyed his house. He has not slept or eaten since, has a blistered, untreated burn on his forearm, and keeps repeating, "I don't know what to do next." Which nursing action is the priority?

  • A. Ask how he has handled major losses in the past
  • B. Dress the burn and arrange food and a safe place to rest
  • C. Give him a list of disaster-relief agencies to contact this week
  • D. Teach him progressive muscle relaxation
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Boyd and the lecture rank the physical consequences of a crisis first: treat the injury and meet basic needs such as food, shelter and sleep. Screening for suicidal or homicidal thoughts comes next, before emotional work. Exploring past coping (A) and teaching relaxation (D) are later steps, once he is stable enough to focus. A referral list alone (C) leaves his immediate needs unmet, and a person this disorganized is unlikely to act on it.

cards.prompt: A nurse says to a patient who recently lost her spouse, "Everything will be all right, and he is in a better place." Which is the best analysis of this statement? A. It is therapeutic because it reduces the patient's anxiety quickly B. It is non-therapeutic only if the patient is crying C. It is therapeutic because it respects the patient's religious beliefs D. It is non-therapeutic because false reassurance blocks communication and expression of grief
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse says to a patient who recently lost her spouse, "Everything will be all right, and he is in a better place." Which is the best analysis of this statement?

  • A. It is therapeutic because it reduces the patient's anxiety quickly
  • B. It is non-therapeutic only if the patient is crying
  • C. It is therapeutic because it respects the patient's religious beliefs
  • D. It is non-therapeutic because false reassurance blocks communication and expression of grief
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Giving false reassurance such as "It will be all right" blocks communication, and the outcome is not under the nurse's control. The lecture advises normalizing grief, sadness and yearning rather than reassuring. Reflection, silence and allowing the expression of emotion are better. The remark would not be justified by the patient's beliefs unless she introduced them, and crying is not the criterion.

cards.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient who is hospitalized after a suicide attempt and is at imminent risk. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Remove sharps, cords, belts and other hazards from the room and search belongings B. Ask the patient to sign a no-suicide contract and then reduce observation C. Use the observation level ordered and interact with the patient during observation D. Work with the patient on a list of people and crisis resources to use when suicidal urges arise E. Promise the patient that thoughts of suicide will be kept confidential
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is caring for a patient who is hospitalized after a suicide attempt and is at imminent risk. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Remove sharps, cords, belts and other hazards from the room and search belongings
  • B. Ask the patient to sign a no-suicide contract and then reduce observation
  • C. Use the observation level ordered and interact with the patient during observation
  • D. Work with the patient on a list of people and crisis resources to use when suicidal urges arise
  • E. Promise the patient that thoughts of suicide will be kept confidential
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

Imminent risk calls for a safe environment, observation that becomes therapeutic through interaction, and helping the patient build a personal list of resources for safer choices when distressed. No-suicide contracts have no proven efficacy and must not replace observation (B). The nurse never promises secrecy about suicidal thoughts, because the team must be told to protect safety (E).

cards.prompt: A nurse asks a patient who says, "I can't go on," whether he is thinking of killing himself. He answers yes. What is the nurse's next best question? A. "Do you know how selfish that would be to your family?" B. "You don't really mean that, do you?" C. "Have you thought about how you would do it, and do you have the means?" D. "Why would you want to do something like that?"
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse asks a patient who says, "I can't go on," whether he is thinking of killing himself. He answers yes. What is the nurse's next best question?

  • A. "Do you know how selfish that would be to your family?"
  • B. "You don't really mean that, do you?"
  • C. "Have you thought about how you would do it, and do you have the means?"
  • D. "Why would you want to do something like that?"
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

After ideation is confirmed, assess risk: plan, intent, availability and lethality of means. Asking directly does not cause suicide. Judgmental or leading responses (A, B) and "why" questions (D) block communication and may lead the patient to conceal thoughts. Concrete plan and access to means drive the level of precautions.

cards.prompt: A nurse caring for a patient on a psychiatric unit notes that the patient is pacing, staring at staff and speaking louder. Which approach is best? A. Approach calmly from a non-threatening position, keep distance and an exit, listen and offer choices B. Stand close and tell him firmly that he must stop or lose privileges C. Call for staff to place him in restraints immediately D. Ignore the behavior to avoid reinforcing it
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse caring for a patient on a psychiatric unit notes that the patient is pacing, staring at staff and speaking louder. Which approach is best?

  • A. Approach calmly from a non-threatening position, keep distance and an exit, listen and offer choices
  • B. Stand close and tell him firmly that he must stop or lose privileges
  • C. Call for staff to place him in restraints immediately
  • D. Ignore the behavior to avoid reinforcing it
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

De-escalation uses nonthreatening body language, respects personal space, keeps the nurse's exit open, and uses listening, validation and concrete choices. Threats (B) escalate; restraint (C) is a last resort after de-escalation has failed in an emergency; ignoring escalating behavior (D) misses the chance to meet the unmet need that the behavior communicates.

cards.prompt: Which factors increase a patient's risk of aggression on an inpatient unit? Select all that apply. A. History of violent behavior B. A crowded, noisy day room C. Intoxication with alcohol or drugs D. Meal times, medication times and shift change E. Being a patient with a psychiatric diagnosis alone
cards.promptHtml:
Which factors increase a patient's risk of aggression on an inpatient unit? Select all that apply.

  • A. History of violent behavior
  • B. A crowded, noisy day room
  • C. Intoxication with alcohol or drugs
  • D. Meal times, medication times and shift change
  • E. Being a patient with a psychiatric diagnosis alone
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C, D

The patient's history is the most important predictor of aggression; crowding, noise, substances and busy times (meals, medications, shift change) raise risk. Having a psychiatric diagnosis alone does not make a person more likely to be violent than other patients (E).

cards.prompt: A patient with intermittent outbursts at work is referred to an anger management group. Which statement by the nurse best describes the group? A. "You will learn to control your body's arousal, change thoughts that fuel anger and practice new behaviors." B. "The leader will act as your therapist and explore your childhood." C. "This group is the best treatment for people who are violent." D. "You will vent your anger so it doesn't build up inside."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with intermittent outbursts at work is referred to an anger management group. Which statement by the nurse best describes the group?

  • A. "You will learn to control your body's arousal, change thoughts that fuel anger and practice new behaviors."
  • B. "The leader will act as your therapist and explore your childhood."
  • C. "This group is the best treatment for people who are violent."
  • D. "You will vent your anger so it doesn't build up inside."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Anger management is psychoeducational: it teaches arousal control, correcting irrational thoughts and replacing blaming or suppressing behaviors, with practice and homework. The leader is a teacher and coach, not a therapist (B). It is not effective for violent behavior (C) and the catharsis or venting model is discredited (D).

cards.prompt: A nurse working on a unit has just been struck by a patient. Which action by the nurse shows appropriate follow-up? A. Say nothing, as nurses are expected to handle aggression B. Confront the patient in the day room to set a firm limit C. Avoid that patient for the rest of the shift without telling anyone D. Document the incident and report it, and use a debriefing or support resource
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse working on a unit has just been struck by a patient. Which action by the nurse shows appropriate follow-up?

  • A. Say nothing, as nurses are expected to handle aggression
  • B. Confront the patient in the day room to set a firm limit
  • C. Avoid that patient for the rest of the shift without telling anyone
  • D. Document the incident and report it, and use a debriefing or support resource
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Documentation is critical to protect nurses, and assault can cause lasting consequences, including PTSD. Nurses may suppress feelings because they feel they must stay professional; support, debriefing and counseling help. Silence (A) and secret avoidance (C) leave the patient and staff unprotected and unsupported, and a public confrontation (B) risks escalation.

cards.prompt: A 78-year-old client is on day 2 after hip fracture repair. The night nurse reports that the client was calm and oriented yesterday but is now picking at the sheets, drifts in and out of alertness, and cannot follow a conversation. The family says this is "not like Mom at all." Which action should the nurse take first? A. Document that the client has developed dementia and request a neurology consult B. Check vital signs, oxygen saturation and blood glucose, and review recent medications C. Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the surgical site D. Give a PRN benzodiazepine to help the client sleep
cards.promptHtml:
A 78-year-old client is on day 2 after hip fracture repair. The night nurse reports that the client was calm and oriented yesterday but is now picking at the sheets, drifts in and out of alertness, and cannot follow a conversation. The family says this is "not like Mom at all." Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Document that the client has developed dementia and request a neurology consult
  • B. Check vital signs, oxygen saturation and blood glucose, and review recent medications
  • C. Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the surgical site
  • D. Give a PRN benzodiazepine to help the client sleep
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

A sudden change from baseline with a fluctuating level of consciousness is delirium, a medical emergency whose cause must be found fast. Hypoxia, infection, hypoglycemia, pain and new medications are common, reversible causes, so physiologic assessment comes first. Dementia develops gradually, so option A mislabels the problem. Restraints worsen agitation and are avoided. Benzodiazepines can deepen confusion and are suspect drugs in delirium, except when delirium is due to alcohol withdrawal.

cards.prompt: The nurse is planning care for a hospitalized older adult with delirium due to a urinary tract infection. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Update a whiteboard with the date and the nurse's name, and arrange family phone calls B. Keep the room dark and silent at all times and remove clocks and calendars C. Offer a cup of water every time a staff member enters the room D. Apply soft wrist restraints so the client does not pull out the IV E. Ask the family to bring in the client's glasses and hearing aids
cards.promptHtml:
The nurse is planning care for a hospitalized older adult with delirium due to a urinary tract infection. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Update a whiteboard with the date and the nurse's name, and arrange family phone calls
  • B. Keep the room dark and silent at all times and remove clocks and calendars
  • C. Offer a cup of water every time a staff member enters the room
  • D. Apply soft wrist restraints so the client does not pull out the IV
  • E. Ask the family to bring in the client's glasses and hearing aids
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

Evidence-based delirium care combines orientation cues, hydration, and sensory aids, with early mobilization and sleep and pain control. A whiteboard, family contact, frequent fluids, and glasses and hearing aids all reduce confusion and misperception. A dark, silent room with no orientation cues increases disorientation; the room should be adequately lit with clocks and calendars. Physical restraint should be avoided because it raises agitation and injury risk.

cards.prompt: A nurse is teaching the husband of a client with early Alzheimer disease who has a new prescription for donepezil. Which statement by the husband shows that the teaching was effective? A. "This medicine should bring back her memory within a few weeks." B. "If she gets nauseated or has diarrhea, I will stop giving it." C. "It may slow her decline, but it will not cure her, and stomach upset is the most common side effect." D. "I can give her an over-the-counter diphenhydramine at night so she sleeps."
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is teaching the husband of a client with early Alzheimer disease who has a new prescription for donepezil. Which statement by the husband shows that the teaching was effective?

  • A. "This medicine should bring back her memory within a few weeks."
  • B. "If she gets nauseated or has diarrhea, I will stop giving it."
  • C. "It may slow her decline, but it will not cure her, and stomach upset is the most common side effect."
  • D. "I can give her an over-the-counter diphenhydramine at night so she sleeps."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Cholinesterase inhibitors delay cognitive decline but generally do not improve function once it is lost; the main adverse effects are nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, which the provider can manage by titration, so the drug should not be stopped without advice. Diphenhydramine is anticholinergic and works against the drug and can worsen confusion; anticholinergics should be avoided in AD. Early treatment gives the best chance of slowing decline.

cards.prompt: A client with moderate Alzheimer disease tells the nurse, "Someone has been in my room and taken my purse." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "That sounds upsetting. Let's check your room together for your purse." B. "Nobody has been in your room. You probably misplaced it again." C. "Who do you think took it? Let's call security right now." D. "You have Alzheimer disease, so your memory plays tricks on you."
cards.promptHtml:
A client with moderate Alzheimer disease tells the nurse, "Someone has been in my room and taken my purse." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "That sounds upsetting. Let's check your room together for your purse."
  • B. "Nobody has been in your room. You probably misplaced it again."
  • C. "Who do you think took it? Let's call security right now."
  • D. "You have Alzheimer disease, so your memory plays tricks on you."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Suspicion in AD often follows a changed routine or a room that was cleaned or rearranged, and the patient cannot remember it. The principle is nonconfrontation: offer to search together, which takes the worry seriously and avoids an argument. Flat denial and blaming memory loss are confrontational and embarrassing. Calling security reinforces the delusion and escalates fear.

cards.prompt: Which findings would lead the nurse to suspect delirium rather than dementia in an older adult? Select all that apply. A. Confusion that developed over several hours B. Alert, clear level of consciousness with a decline over several years C. Symptoms that fluctuate during the day and are worse at night D. Asterixis or a coarse tremor along with a fever E. Gradual personality change with stable vital signs
cards.promptHtml:
Which findings would lead the nurse to suspect delirium rather than dementia in an older adult? Select all that apply.

  • A. Confusion that developed over several hours
  • B. Alert, clear level of consciousness with a decline over several years
  • C. Symptoms that fluctuate during the day and are worse at night
  • D. Asterixis or a coarse tremor along with a fever
  • E. Gradual personality change with stable vital signs
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

Delirium has a sudden onset, a fluctuating 24-hour course, reduced consciousness, and usually a physical illness or drug toxicity; asterixis or coarse tremor and unstable vital signs support it. Dementia is insidious and progressive with clear consciousness, stable vital signs unless another illness is present, and gradual personality change. Options B and E describe dementia.

cards.prompt: An older client with neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies reports seeing children in the room at night. The prescriber orders haloperidol. What is the nurse's best action? A. Give the dose, since hallucinations always require an antipsychotic B. Give the dose and ask the family to leave so the client can rest C. Hold the dose and reorient the client to place and time D. Question the order and ask the prescriber about the risk of severe sensitivity to antipsychotics
cards.promptHtml:
An older client with neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies reports seeing children in the room at night. The prescriber orders haloperidol. What is the nurse's best action?

  • A. Give the dose, since hallucinations always require an antipsychotic
  • B. Give the dose and ask the family to leave so the client can rest
  • C. Hold the dose and reorient the client to place and time
  • D. Question the order and ask the prescriber about the risk of severe sensitivity to antipsychotics
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Lewy body disease is marked by visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and fluctuating cognition, and these clients are very sensitive to psychotropic drugs, especially antipsychotics, and can react severely. The nurse should clarify the order and nonpharmacologic options before giving it. Not all hallucinations need drugs; calm reassurance and environmental changes come first. Asking the family to leave removes a calming support. Holding a dose without informing the prescriber is not the nurse's role.

cards.prompt: A 74-year-old widow, widowed 2 months ago, tells the nurse, "I can't remember anything and I'm useless." She is oriented, answers many screening questions with "I don't know," and has lost 8 pounds. Which action is the priority? A. Begin teaching about cholinesterase inhibitors B. Screen for depression with the Geriatric Depression Scale and assess suicide risk C. Place a bed alarm and move her next to the nurses' station D. Request an order for a CAM assessment
cards.promptHtml:
A 74-year-old widow, widowed 2 months ago, tells the nurse, "I can't remember anything and I'm useless." She is oriented, answers many screening questions with "I don't know," and has lost 8 pounds. Which action is the priority?

  • A. Begin teaching about cholinesterase inhibitors
  • B. Screen for depression with the Geriatric Depression Scale and assess suicide risk
  • C. Place a bed alarm and move her next to the nurses' station
  • D. Request an order for a CAM assessment
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Clear orientation, poor effort, self-deprecation, weight loss and a recent loss point to depression that mimics dementia (pseudodementia). Depression is the greatest risk factor for suicide in older adults, who account for a disproportionate share of suicides, so screen with the GDS and ask directly about suicidal thoughts. Cholinesterase inhibitors treat AD, which is not established. A bed alarm and CAM address delirium and fall risk, which are not suggested.

cards.prompt: A client with a long history of heavy alcohol use is admitted confused, with an unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which medication does the nurse anticipate giving first to prevent a chronic amnestic syndrome? A. Donepezil B. Haloperidol C. Thiamine D. Memantine
cards.promptHtml:
A client with a long history of heavy alcohol use is admitted confused, with an unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which medication does the nurse anticipate giving first to prevent a chronic amnestic syndrome?

  • A. Donepezil
  • B. Haloperidol
  • C. Thiamine
  • D. Memantine
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

These findings suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by thiamine deficiency. Thiamine is given before or with glucose in at-risk patients, and untreated Wernicke can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia, inability to learn new information, confabulation). Donepezil and memantine treat Alzheimer disease. Haloperidol does not correct the deficiency.

cards.prompt: A client with somatic symptom disorder says to the nurse, "Every doctor says nothing is wrong, but I am in agony and nobody believes me." Which response is most therapeutic? A. "The tests are all normal, so the pain is probably stress." B. "You need to stop seeing so many doctors and talk to a counselor." C. "I will ask the doctor to order more tests so we can find the cause." D. "It sounds exhausting to hurt this much and not feel believed. Tell me more about the pain."
cards.promptHtml:
A client with somatic symptom disorder says to the nurse, "Every doctor says nothing is wrong, but I am in agony and nobody believes me." Which response is most therapeutic?

  • A. "The tests are all normal, so the pain is probably stress."
  • B. "You need to stop seeing so many doctors and talk to a counselor."
  • C. "I will ask the doctor to order more tests so we can find the cause."
  • D. "It sounds exhausting to hurt this much and not feel believed. Tell me more about the pain."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

The cornerstones of care are trust and believing. The nurse accepts that the pain is real, uses an open-ended invitation, and can later link stress to symptoms and shift to coping. Telling the client the pain is "probably stress" or that they see too many doctors feels dismissive and ends communication. Ordering more tests on request reinforces provider shopping and unnecessary workups; the care plan should keep one provider and conservative treatment.

cards.prompt: A nurse is planning care for a client with somatic symptom disorder who sees many providers. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Arrange brief, regularly scheduled visits with one primary provider B. Tell the client that the symptoms are imaginary so unnecessary tests can stop C. Assess for depression and suicidal thoughts at each contact D. Ask the client to keep a symptom journal and bring it to appointments E. Request a long-term benzodiazepine to relieve the pain and anxiety
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is planning care for a client with somatic symptom disorder who sees many providers. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Arrange brief, regularly scheduled visits with one primary provider
  • B. Tell the client that the symptoms are imaginary so unnecessary tests can stop
  • C. Assess for depression and suicidal thoughts at each contact
  • D. Ask the client to keep a symptom journal and bring it to appointments
  • E. Request a long-term benzodiazepine to relieve the pain and anxiety
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

One provider and scheduled visits reduce provider shopping and unscheduled care. Suicide risk is raised in this disorder, and these clients are usually seen outside mental health settings where assessment is not routine, so screen each time. A journal helps the client and nurse link stress to symptoms. Symptoms are real to the client, so calling them imaginary breaks trust. Benzodiazepines are avoided because of dependence and because they complicate care.

cards.prompt: A 24-year-old client suddenly cannot move the left leg after witnessing a serious car crash. The neurologic exam, MRI and labs are normal, and the client appears calm about the paralysis. Which nursing approach is best? A. Accept the symptom as real and explore the stress connected to its onset B. Tell the client the paralysis is not real and ask them to walk C. Assign a full bed bath to rest the leg and avoid questions about the accident D. Explain that the symptom is being produced on purpose to avoid trauma care
cards.promptHtml:
A 24-year-old client suddenly cannot move the left leg after witnessing a serious car crash. The neurologic exam, MRI and labs are normal, and the client appears calm about the paralysis. Which nursing approach is best?

  • A. Accept the symptom as real and explore the stress connected to its onset
  • B. Tell the client the paralysis is not real and ask them to walk
  • C. Assign a full bed bath to rest the leg and avoid questions about the accident
  • D. Explain that the symptom is being produced on purpose to avoid trauma care
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Conversion disorder (functional neurologic symptom disorder) is loss of voluntary function with negative testing, tied to psychological conflict and not under conscious control. The nurse treats the symptom as real, ensures safety, and helps the client name the trigger and learn new coping skills; calm unconcern (la belle indifference) can occur. Confronting the client or implying faking is wrong, because faking is malingering or factitious disorder. Avoiding the topic prevents recovery and encourages dependence.

cards.prompt: The nurse is comparing clients on a medical unit. Which client most likely has factitious disorder? A. A client who reports back pain only on days a disability evaluation is scheduled and moves normally when unobserved B. A client who secretly injects insulin to cause hypoglycemia and repeated admissions, with no financial or legal gain C. A client who has had daily stomach pain for 8 months and spends hours worrying that it signals cancer D. A client who became unable to speak after a violent argument and cannot be cured by speech therapy
cards.promptHtml:
The nurse is comparing clients on a medical unit. Which client most likely has factitious disorder?

  • A. A client who reports back pain only on days a disability evaluation is scheduled and moves normally when unobserved
  • B. A client who secretly injects insulin to cause hypoglycemia and repeated admissions, with no financial or legal gain
  • C. A client who has had daily stomach pain for 8 months and spends hours worrying that it signals cancer
  • D. A client who became unable to speak after a violent argument and cannot be cured by speech therapy
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Factitious disorder is intentional production of illness to assume the sick role, with no external reward, usually covert, and often involves health care knowledge. Option A is malingering (an external goal; not a psychiatric disorder). Option C fits somatic symptom disorder (real symptoms with excessive worry over 6 months). Option D fits conversion disorder (aphonia without conscious control).

cards.prompt: Which findings are consistent with dissociative identity disorder? Select all that apply. A. Two or more distinct identity states that take control of behavior B. Gaps in memory for everyday events and personal information C. Persistent fear of having a serious illness despite negative tests D. A history of severe childhood trauma or abuse E. Deliberately fabricated symptoms to avoid legal consequences
cards.promptHtml:
Which findings are consistent with dissociative identity disorder? Select all that apply.

  • A. Two or more distinct identity states that take control of behavior
  • B. Gaps in memory for everyday events and personal information
  • C. Persistent fear of having a serious illness despite negative tests
  • D. A history of severe childhood trauma or abuse
  • E. Deliberately fabricated symptoms to avoid legal consequences
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D

DID is defined by two or more distinct identities ("alters") that take control, with memory gaps beyond ordinary forgetfulness, and it is strongly tied to chronic childhood trauma, with dissociation as a defense against overwhelming events. Fear of serious illness describes illness anxiety disorder. Fabricating symptoms to avoid consequences describes malingering, which is not a psychiatric disorder.

cards.prompt: A client with a dissociative disorder suddenly stares blankly, does not respond to their name, and then says, "None of this feels real." What should the nurse do first? A. Ask the client to describe the childhood abuse in detail B. Leave the client alone until the episode passes C. Speak calmly using the client's name, and use grounding such as naming objects in the room or touching a solid object D. Give a PRN benzodiazepine and darken the room
cards.promptHtml:
A client with a dissociative disorder suddenly stares blankly, does not respond to their name, and then says, "None of this feels real." What should the nurse do first?

  • A. Ask the client to describe the childhood abuse in detail
  • B. Leave the client alone until the episode passes
  • C. Speak calmly using the client's name, and use grounding such as naming objects in the room or touching a solid object
  • D. Give a PRN benzodiazepine and darken the room
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

During dissociation the client is detached from the present. Grounding techniques (clapping hands, touching an object, describing what is seen and heard) re-anchor the client in current surroundings. Pushing for trauma details raises anxiety and can trigger more dissociation. Leaving the client alone is unsafe and misses the chance to help. Sedation and a dark room reduce orientation cues and are not first-line.

cards.prompt: A client with somatic symptom disorder and depression is starting duloxetine for pain and mood. Which statement by the client shows that further teaching is needed? A. "I should report any new thoughts of hurting myself right away." B. "My blood pressure will be checked while my dose is adjusted." C. "If my pain eases, I will stop the capsules on my own." D. "I will tell the prescriber about any aspirin or ibuprofen I take."
cards.promptHtml:
A client with somatic symptom disorder and depression is starting duloxetine for pain and mood. Which statement by the client shows that further teaching is needed?

  • A. "I should report any new thoughts of hurting myself right away."
  • B. "My blood pressure will be checked while my dose is adjusted."
  • C. "If my pain eases, I will stop the capsules on my own."
  • D. "I will tell the prescriber about any aspirin or ibuprofen I take."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Stopping an SNRI abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, nausea, anxiety); the client should taper only with the prescriber. Duloxetine carries a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts, can raise blood pressure, and increases bleeding risk with NSAIDs or aspirin, so options A, B and D are correct statements. Duloxetine also helps pain, so it is a reasonable choice when no drug is specifically indicated for SSD.

cards.prompt: In the emergency department, a nurse notes that a 3-year-old has had repeated admissions for unexplained seizures and vomiting. The symptoms stop when the child is away from the mother, who is very attentive and knowledgeable about medical care. What is the nurse's best action? A. Confront the mother in front of the child and ask her to admit to causing the illness B. Wait until the next admission to see whether the pattern continues C. Discuss the concern with the mother and ask her to leave the child's room D. Share objective observations with the health care team and follow policy for suspected child abuse so the child is protected
cards.promptHtml:
In the emergency department, a nurse notes that a 3-year-old has had repeated admissions for unexplained seizures and vomiting. The symptoms stop when the child is away from the mother, who is very attentive and knowledgeable about medical care. What is the nurse's best action?

  • A. Confront the mother in front of the child and ask her to admit to causing the illness
  • B. Wait until the next admission to see whether the pattern continues
  • C. Discuss the concern with the mother and ask her to leave the child's room
  • D. Share objective observations with the health care team and follow policy for suspected child abuse so the child is protected
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Factitious disorder imposed on another (formerly by proxy) is a severe form of child abuse in which a caregiver induces illness, often by poisoning, smothering or inducing seizures, to gain attention. The mother rarely admits it and the child is often removed from her care. The nurse's priority is the child's safety: document facts, communicate with the team, and report per mandatory-reporting policy. Confrontation or delay puts the child at risk.

cards.prompt: The nurse on a substance use unit receives report on four patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first? A. A patient brought in after heroin use who is difficult to arouse, with a respiratory rate of 6 and pinpoint pupils B. A patient on day 3 of methadone detoxification reporting nausea and muscle aches C. A patient two days after stopping cocaine who is sleeping most of the day and says he feels flat D. A patient trying to quit smoking who is irritable and asking for a nicotine patch
cards.promptHtml:
The nurse on a substance use unit receives report on four patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

  • A. A patient brought in after heroin use who is difficult to arouse, with a respiratory rate of 6 and pinpoint pupils
  • B. A patient on day 3 of methadone detoxification reporting nausea and muscle aches
  • C. A patient two days after stopping cocaine who is sleeping most of the day and says he feels flat
  • D. A patient trying to quit smoking who is irritable and asking for a nicotine patch
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Airway and breathing come first. A respiratory rate of 6 with pinpoint pupils and decreased arousal indicates opioid overdose with respiratory depression, which can end in hypoxic death within minutes and needs naloxone and ventilatory support. Opioid withdrawal (B) is miserable but not life-threatening. Cocaine crash sleepiness (C) is expected, though depression and suicide risk need follow-up soon. Nicotine withdrawal irritability (D) is the least urgent.

cards.prompt: A nurse is assessing a patient who stopped using heroin 12 hours ago. Which findings are consistent with opioid withdrawal? Select all that apply. A. Yawning and rhinorrhea B. Pinpoint pupils C. Gooseflesh and muscle aches D. Respiratory rate of 8 with drowsiness E. Abdominal cramping and diarrhea
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is assessing a patient who stopped using heroin 12 hours ago. Which findings are consistent with opioid withdrawal? Select all that apply.

  • A. Yawning and rhinorrhea
  • B. Pinpoint pupils
  • C. Gooseflesh and muscle aches
  • D. Respiratory rate of 8 with drowsiness
  • E. Abdominal cramping and diarrhea
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

Opioid withdrawal is a rebound hyperexcitable state: yawning, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, dilated pupils, gooseflesh, muscle and bone aches, cramps, diarrhea, nausea, sweating, insomnia, and irritability. Pinpoint pupils (B) and slow, shallow breathing with drowsiness (D) are signs of opioid intoxication or overdose. Withdrawal is not life-threatening, but it is distressing and drives relapse, so assess with a tool such as the COWS.

cards.prompt: A patient found unresponsive after an opioid overdose receives naloxone intravenously and becomes alert with a respiratory rate of 16. Forty minutes later he is drowsy and his respiratory rate is 8. Which action by the nurse is best? A. Document that the overdose has resolved and encourage him to rest B. Give a second dose of the same medication only if he reports pain C. Notify the provider, support ventilation, and prepare to repeat naloxone D. Start naltrexone to provide longer-lasting protection
cards.promptHtml:
A patient found unresponsive after an opioid overdose receives naloxone intravenously and becomes alert with a respiratory rate of 16. Forty minutes later he is drowsy and his respiratory rate is 8. Which action by the nurse is best?

  • A. Document that the overdose has resolved and encourage him to rest
  • B. Give a second dose of the same medication only if he reports pain
  • C. Notify the provider, support ventilation, and prepare to repeat naloxone
  • D. Start naltrexone to provide longer-lasting protection
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Naloxone is active for roughly 30 to 81 minutes, which is often shorter than the opioid it reversed, so re-sedation and respiratory depression can return. The patient needs continued monitoring, ventilatory support as needed, and repeat dosing per order. Resting without monitoring (A) risks respiratory arrest. Pain is irrelevant to the dose (B). Naltrexone (D) is a maintenance drug, not a rescue drug, and can trigger severe withdrawal.

cards.prompt: A patient is starting once-daily naltrexone for alcohol use disorder. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective? A. "This medicine will make me violently ill if I have a drink." B. "I should wear a medical ID so emergency staff know opioid pain medicine will not work normally for me." C. "I can take it in the morning on the same day I finish my last opioid dose." D. "I need to stop taking it as soon as I plan to drink at a party."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient is starting once-daily naltrexone for alcohol use disorder. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

  • A. "This medicine will make me violently ill if I have a drink."
  • B. "I should wear a medical ID so emergency staff know opioid pain medicine will not work normally for me."
  • C. "I can take it in the morning on the same day I finish my last opioid dose."
  • D. "I need to stop taking it as soon as I plan to drink at a party."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Naltrexone blocks opioid (mu) receptors, so a medical ID alerts emergency staff that narcotic analgesics will be blocked. The violent-illness reaction (A) describes disulfiram. The patient must be opioid-free for about 7 to 10 days before starting, or withdrawal may be precipitated (C). Stopping around drinking (D) invites relapse, and nurses should reinforce continued adherence.

cards.prompt: A 68-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted 10 hours after his last drink. The nurse reviews his alcohol withdrawal plan. Which elements are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Lorazepam doses guided by the CIWA-Ar score B. Seizure precautions, especially over the first 48 hours C. Thiamine as prescribed D. Disulfiram started today to discourage drinking while he is hospitalized E. Chlordiazepoxide chosen because his liver disease calls for a long-acting benzodiazepine
cards.promptHtml:
A 68-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted 10 hours after his last drink. The nurse reviews his alcohol withdrawal plan. Which elements are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Lorazepam doses guided by the CIWA-Ar score
  • B. Seizure precautions, especially over the first 48 hours
  • C. Thiamine as prescribed
  • D. Disulfiram started today to discourage drinking while he is hospitalized
  • E. Chlordiazepoxide chosen because his liver disease calls for a long-acting benzodiazepine
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C

Withdrawal usually starts within 12 hours and seizures cluster in the first 48 hours, so seizure precautions belong in the plan. Benzodiazepines substitute for alcohol and are tapered by symptom score; lorazepam is preferred for older adults and people with liver impairment, so E has the reasoning backward (chlordiazepoxide and diazepam give smoother tapers in other patients). Thiamine prevents and treats Wernicke encephalopathy. Disulfiram (D) is a relapse-prevention drug for people in recovery and needs informed consent; it is not a withdrawal treatment.

cards.prompt: A patient admitted for pancreatitis says, "I only drink on weekends. My wife is exaggerating." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic? A. "Pancreatitis is almost always caused by heavy drinking, so you are in denial." B. "Most people with alcohol problems say the same thing." C. "Your lab values show a pattern that does not match weekend drinking." D. "Tell me what a typical weekend of drinking looks like for you."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient admitted for pancreatitis says, "I only drink on weekends. My wife is exaggerating." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

  • A. "Pancreatitis is almost always caused by heavy drinking, so you are in denial."
  • B. "Most people with alcohol problems say the same thing."
  • C. "Your lab values show a pattern that does not match weekend drinking."
  • D. "Tell me what a typical weekend of drinking looks like for you."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Motivational, nonjudgmental, open-ended questions explore the pattern of use without triggering defensiveness. Arguing, labeling denial, or lecturing with evidence (A, B, C) usually fails to produce an admission and damages the therapeutic relationship. Use a caring, matter-of-fact, direct approach and look for discrepancies the patient can notice for himself.

cards.prompt: While preparing medications, a nurse notices that a coworker has slurred speech and the smell of alcohol and is about to give medications to a patient. What should the nurse do first? A. Wait until the end of the shift and then privately ask the coworker about drinking B. Notify the charge nurse or supervisor immediately so the coworker is kept from patient care C. Offer to give the coworker's medications to avoid an error D. Tell the coworker to take a break and promise to say nothing if it stops
cards.promptHtml:
While preparing medications, a nurse notices that a coworker has slurred speech and the smell of alcohol and is about to give medications to a patient. What should the nurse do first?

  • A. Wait until the end of the shift and then privately ask the coworker about drinking
  • B. Notify the charge nurse or supervisor immediately so the coworker is kept from patient care
  • C. Offer to give the coworker's medications to avoid an error
  • D. Tell the coworker to take a break and promise to say nothing if it stops
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Patient safety is the priority. Nurses are obligated to report a colleague's impaired practice through proper channels, and the supervisor can remove the nurse from patient care and start the facility process. Peer assistance programs support recovery while protecting the public. Waiting (A), covering (C), or promising silence (D) all enable the impairment and leave patients at risk. Document objective behaviors, not a diagnosis.

cards.prompt: A nurse is teaching the family of a patient with alcohol use disorder. Which behaviors by family members are examples of enabling? Select all that apply. A. Telling the employer the patient has the flu after a binge B. Attending an Al-Anon meeting to learn about boundaries C. Paying the patient's overdue rent and an impaired-driving fine D. Taking over the patient's household chores and bills E. Declining to give the patient money and allowing him to face the consequences
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is teaching the family of a patient with alcohol use disorder. Which behaviors by family members are examples of enabling? Select all that apply.

  • A. Telling the employer the patient has the flu after a binge
  • B. Attending an Al-Anon meeting to learn about boundaries
  • C. Paying the patient's overdue rent and an impaired-driving fine
  • D. Taking over the patient's household chores and bills
  • E. Declining to give the patient money and allowing him to face the consequences
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

Enabling means shielding the user from consequences, which inadvertently reinforces use: making excuses, paying debts or fines, and taking over responsibilities. Attending Al-Anon (B) and setting limits while allowing natural consequences (E, when safety is maintained) are healthy responses and goals of family teaching. Teach families that enabling usually comes from fear and love, not malice.

cards.prompt: At a follow-up visit, which statement by a patient in early recovery from alcohol use disorder best indicates progress? A. "I promise I will never drink again." B. "I have not had a drink, so I no longer need meetings." C. "I can handle a few beers at parties, since wine was my real problem." D. "Friday evenings are my trigger, so I call my sponsor and go to a meeting then."
cards.promptHtml:
At a follow-up visit, which statement by a patient in early recovery from alcohol use disorder best indicates progress?

  • A. "I promise I will never drink again."
  • B. "I have not had a drink, so I no longer need meetings."
  • C. "I can handle a few beers at parties, since wine was my real problem."
  • D. "Friday evenings are my trigger, so I call my sponsor and go to a meeting then."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Recognizing personal triggers and carrying out a specific coping and support plan is a strong recovery indicator. Global promises (A) are unspecific, and stopping supports (B) or substituting another form of alcohol (C) signals continued denial and relapse risk. Recovery is a lifelong, "one day at a time" process that relies on coping skills and ongoing support.

cards.prompt: A patient was admitted 2 days ago after stopping cocaine. He sleeps most of the day, appears tearful, and tells the nurse that nothing matters anymore. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Assess for suicidal thoughts, plan, and intent B. Encourage him to attend the afternoon group C. Explain that excessive sleep is a normal part of the crash D. Teach him about contingency management programs
cards.promptHtml:
A patient was admitted 2 days ago after stopping cocaine. He sleeps most of the day, appears tearful, and tells the nurse that nothing matters anymore. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Assess for suicidal thoughts, plan, and intent
  • B. Encourage him to attend the afternoon group
  • C. Explain that excessive sleep is a normal part of the crash
  • D. Teach him about contingency management programs
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Cocaine withdrawal causes a prolonged "crash" with hypersomnia (12 to 18 hours), intense depression, anhedonia, craving, and possible suicidality. A statement that nothing matters is a cue to assess suicide risk first, because safety takes priority. Group attendance (B), reassurance (C), and teaching (D) may all be appropriate later, but none addresses the immediate risk.

cards.prompt: Which findings should the nurse expect in a patient with long-term methamphetamine use? Select all that apply. A. Severe tooth decay B. Skin sores from picking or scratching C. Constipation with pinpoint pupils D. Paranoia and hallucinations E. Weight loss
cards.promptHtml:
Which findings should the nurse expect in a patient with long-term methamphetamine use? Select all that apply.

  • A. Severe tooth decay
  • B. Skin sores from picking or scratching
  • C. Constipation with pinpoint pupils
  • D. Paranoia and hallucinations
  • E. Weight loss
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, D, E

Prolonged methamphetamine use causes tooth decay, intense itching that leads to skin sores, weight loss, addiction psychosis with paranoia and hallucinations, mood disturbance, cardiac arrhythmias, and stroke. Constipation and pinpoint pupils (C) are opioid effects. Because meth has a long duration of action, high body temperature and seizures are also risks.

cards.prompt: A patient is prescribed disulfiram. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching? A. "I need to read labels for hidden alcohol in vinegars, cough syrups, and baked goods." B. "I have to agree to this treatment, and I understand it can cause a serious reaction." C. "My alcohol-based mouthwash is fine, since I only swish it and spit it out." D. "This will not cure my drinking problem, but it may help me stay away from alcohol."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient is prescribed disulfiram. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

  • A. "I need to read labels for hidden alcohol in vinegars, cough syrups, and baked goods."
  • B. "I have to agree to this treatment, and I understand it can cause a serious reaction."
  • C. "My alcohol-based mouthwash is fine, since I only swish it and spit it out."
  • D. "This will not cure my drinking problem, but it may help me stay away from alcohol."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Disulfiram plus even small amounts of alcohol causes severe nausea and vomiting, and serious reactions can include arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse, and death. Hidden alcohol sources (foods, cough preparations, and alcohol-containing aftershaves and lotions that are absorbed through the skin) must be avoided, so mouthwash containing alcohol is unsafe. Informed consent is required (B), and the drug deters drinking but is not a cure (D).

cards.prompt: A patient who has received daily methadone at an opioid treatment program for 8 months says, "I feel great, so I'm done with the clinic as of tomorrow." Which response by the nurse is best? A. "That makes sense, since methadone does not cause physical dependence." B. "Stopping all at once can bring on withdrawal much like heroin withdrawal. Let's talk with your prescriber about tapering if you want to stop." C. "You can start naltrexone tomorrow so you stay protected from relapse." D. "Methadone leaves your body within a few hours, so you won't notice any change."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient who has received daily methadone at an opioid treatment program for 8 months says, "I feel great, so I'm done with the clinic as of tomorrow." Which response by the nurse is best?

  • A. "That makes sense, since methadone does not cause physical dependence."
  • B. "Stopping all at once can bring on withdrawal much like heroin withdrawal. Let's talk with your prescriber about tapering if you want to stop."
  • C. "You can start naltrexone tomorrow so you stay protected from relapse."
  • D. "Methadone leaves your body within a few hours, so you won't notice any change."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Methadone is a full opioid agonist and is physiologically addicting; quitting treatment can cause withdrawal similar to heroin, so discontinuation is done by gradually reducing the dose. It does cause dependence (A). Naltrexone (C) cannot start until the patient has been opioid-free for 7 to 10 days, or it precipitates withdrawal. Methadone's half-life is long, 15 to 30 hours, and its withdrawal can last several weeks (D) (the syllabus calls the half-life "low"; Boyd's value is current).

cards.prompt: A 54-year-old man with a long history of heavy drinking is brought in confused, with an unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which medication should the nurse anticipate giving first? A. Disulfiram B. Naltrexone C. Acamprosate D. Thiamine
cards.promptHtml:
A 54-year-old man with a long history of heavy drinking is brought in confused, with an unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which medication should the nurse anticipate giving first?

  • A. Disulfiram
  • B. Naltrexone
  • C. Acamprosate
  • D. Thiamine
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Confusion, ataxia, and visual or eye-movement abnormalities in a patient with alcohol use disorder suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, an acute, life-threatening thiamine-deficiency brain disorder. Thiamine (oral, IM, or IV) is the treatment, and early treatment can reverse symptoms. Disulfiram, naltrexone, and acamprosate are relapse-prevention drugs started later, after withdrawal and abstinence, and none treats the deficiency.

cards.prompt: A patient who used phencyclidine (PCP) is pacing, paranoid, and shouting that people are trying to hurt him. Which intervention is most appropriate? A. Move him to a low-stimulation area, keep a safe distance, and use short, clear instructions in a firm, nonthreatening tone B. Confront him with the fact that his beliefs are not real C. Ask several relatives to stay and reassure him D. Encourage him to talk through his fears in the busy day room
cards.promptHtml:
A patient who used phencyclidine (PCP) is pacing, paranoid, and shouting that people are trying to hurt him. Which intervention is most appropriate?

  • A. Move him to a low-stimulation area, keep a safe distance, and use short, clear instructions in a firm, nonthreatening tone
  • B. Confront him with the fact that his beliefs are not real
  • C. Ask several relatives to stay and reassure him
  • D. Encourage him to talk through his fears in the busy day room
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

During acute hallucinogen or PCP intoxication, goals are to reduce stimuli, keep everyone safe, manage behavior, and watch for medical and psychiatric complications. PCP can cause aggression, psychosis, and an adrenergic crisis, so keep instructions brief and simple and approach calmly. Arguing with delusions (B), crowding the room (C), and a stimulating setting (D) increase agitation and risk.

cards.prompt: Which statements about groups at risk for substance use disorders are accurate? Select all that apply. A. Cisgender males have higher rates of illicit drug and alcohol use than cisgender females. B. Cisgender males and females are equally likely to develop a substance use disorder. C. Cisgender women are less likely to seek treatment unless the substance is a sedative, sleep medication, or anxiety agent. D. LGBTQ+ teens are more likely to experience violence and suicide risk. E. A single genetic marker reliably identifies who will develop an addiction.
cards.promptHtml:
Which statements about groups at risk for substance use disorders are accurate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Cisgender males have higher rates of illicit drug and alcohol use than cisgender females.
  • B. Cisgender males and females are equally likely to develop a substance use disorder.
  • C. Cisgender women are less likely to seek treatment unless the substance is a sedative, sleep medication, or anxiety agent.
  • D. LGBTQ+ teens are more likely to experience violence and suicide risk.
  • E. A single genetic marker reliably identifies who will develop an addiction.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, B, C, D

The F25 lecture describes higher use among males but equal likelihood of developing an SUD, women with comorbid mood, anxiety, and eating disorders and trauma histories who seek help mainly for sedatives or anxiety agents, and higher stigma, violence, and suicide risk in LGBTQ+ youth. Genetics may account for up to about half of the risk, but no specific genetic marker has been identified (E).

cards.prompt: A 74-year-old widow is admitted after a fall with new confusion. Her daughter reports she drinks wine every evening. Which nursing action is best? A. Attribute the confusion to dementia and notify social services B. Ask her to rate her mood on a scale from 1 to 10 C. Ask about the amount and time of her last drink, screen with CAGE, review medications, and monitor for withdrawal D. Hold her next scheduled medications until she is oriented
cards.promptHtml:
A 74-year-old widow is admitted after a fall with new confusion. Her daughter reports she drinks wine every evening. Which nursing action is best?

  • A. Attribute the confusion to dementia and notify social services
  • B. Ask her to rate her mood on a scale from 1 to 10
  • C. Ask about the amount and time of her last drink, screen with CAGE, review medications, and monitor for withdrawal
  • D. Hold her next scheduled medications until she is oriented
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Alcohol is the substance of choice in older adults, who feel its effects at lower doses and are prone to falls, delirium, and withdrawal, especially with chronic illness and multiple medications. Substance effects and polypharmacy must be ruled out before confusion is called dementia (A). The last-drink time predicts withdrawal risk. A mood rating alone (B) misses the problem, and holding all medications (D) is unsafe without a provider's direction.

cards.prompt: A nurse is admitting a patient with severe gambling disorder who says, "I am due for a big win, and one more bet will fix everything." Which assessment is the highest priority? A. His credit card, loan, and debt history B. His family's attitudes toward gambling C. Suicidal thoughts, plan, and intent D. The number of hours he gambles each week
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse is admitting a patient with severe gambling disorder who says, "I am due for a big win, and one more bet will fix everything." Which assessment is the highest priority?

  • A. His credit card, loan, and debt history
  • B. His family's attitudes toward gambling
  • C. Suicidal thoughts, plan, and intent
  • D. The number of hours he gambles each week
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

This item tests safety over history-taking. People with gambling disorder have high rates of suicide, and the omnipotent belief that losses can be won back sustains denial. Assess suicidal thoughts, plan, and intent first; then address the belief, triggers, and relapse cues. Financial (A), family (B), and time-spent (D) assessments are important but secondary.

cards.prompt: Using the FRAMES model of brief intervention, which nurse statement best illustrates the "Responsibility" element? A. "Here is a list of programs you might choose from." B. "Your liver enzymes are higher than expected for your age." C. "I can see how hard this has been for you." D. "Whether you cut back is your choice to make, and only you can make it happen."
cards.promptHtml:
Using the FRAMES model of brief intervention, which nurse statement best illustrates the "Responsibility" element?

  • A. "Here is a list of programs you might choose from."
  • B. "Your liver enzymes are higher than expected for your age."
  • C. "I can see how hard this has been for you."
  • D. "Whether you cut back is your choice to make, and only you can make it happen."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Responsibility emphasizes the patient's freedom of choice and personal responsibility for change. Giving a list of options is the Menu (A), sharing lab results is Feedback (B), and showing warmth and understanding is Empathy (C). The remaining elements are Advice and Self-efficacy. FRAMES is the structure of brief interventions within SBIRT.

cards.prompt: A 14-year-old is brought to the emergency department after sniffing aerosol spray. He is drowsy and unsteady and has an irregular pulse. What is the nurse's first action? A. Assess airway, breathing, and oxygenation and apply a cardiac monitor B. Interview him about what he inhaled and how often C. Call his parents to discuss the incident D. Teach him about the dangers of inhalants
cards.promptHtml:
A 14-year-old is brought to the emergency department after sniffing aerosol spray. He is drowsy and unsteady and has an irregular pulse. What is the nurse's first action?

  • A. Assess airway, breathing, and oxygenation and apply a cardiac monitor
  • B. Interview him about what he inhaled and how often
  • C. Call his parents to discuss the incident
  • D. Teach him about the dangers of inhalants
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

Inhalants depress the CNS and can cause respiratory depression, coma, and fatal arrhythmias (sudden sniffing death), so airway, breathing, and cardiac status come first. History, family notification, and education are important but follow stabilization. Inhalant intoxication appears within minutes, and the fumes can displace oxygen and disrupt heart rhythm.

cards.prompt: A nursing student is sorting personality disorders by cluster for a unit review. Which disorders belong in Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional or erratic group? Select all that apply. A. Histrionic personality disorder B. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder C. Narcissistic personality disorder D. Schizotypal personality disorder E. Borderline personality disorder
cards.promptHtml:
A nursing student is sorting personality disorders by cluster for a unit review. Which disorders belong in Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional or erratic group? Select all that apply.

  • A. Histrionic personality disorder
  • B. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
  • C. Narcissistic personality disorder
  • D. Schizotypal personality disorder
  • E. Borderline personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

Cluster B includes antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic disorders, all marked by dramatic, emotional or erratic behavior. Schizotypal belongs to Cluster A (odd or eccentric), and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder belongs to Cluster C (anxious or fearful), together with avoidant and dependent. The instructor's reflective-practice table asks for three Cluster A, four Cluster B and three Cluster C disorders.

cards.prompt: A patient with borderline personality disorder who was admitted for depression walks to the nurses' station after an argument with her husband. Her forearm is bleeding from fresh cuts. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Ask her to explain what the argument was about B. Stay with her, apply pressure to the wound and get it treated C. Remind her of the unit's no-self-harm agreement D. Notify the therapist that she has relapsed
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with borderline personality disorder who was admitted for depression walks to the nurses' station after an argument with her husband. Her forearm is bleeding from fresh cuts. Which action should the nurse take first?

  • A. Ask her to explain what the argument was about
  • B. Stay with her, apply pressure to the wound and get it treated
  • C. Remind her of the unit's no-self-harm agreement
  • D. Notify the therapist that she has relapsed
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Physical safety comes first. The nurse stays with the patient, controls the bleeding and gets the wound assessed and treated, using a calm, nonjudgmental manner. Exploring the argument (A) and the triggers comes after the injury is treated. Reminding her of the agreement (C) is punitive and delays care. Calling the therapist (D) is appropriate later but is not the first action. Self-harm threats and acts are always taken seriously.

cards.prompt: During shift report, two nurses learn that a patient with borderline personality disorder asked each of them for an extra late-night phone call, telling each one that the other nurse had already said yes. Which action is most appropriate? A. Allow the call, since one of the nurses may have agreed B. Tell the patient that she lied to both nurses C. Bring the request to the team and give the patient one agreed answer D. Let each nurse decide the request on her own shift
cards.promptHtml:
During shift report, two nurses learn that a patient with borderline personality disorder asked each of them for an extra late-night phone call, telling each one that the other nurse had already said yes. Which action is most appropriate?

  • A. Allow the call, since one of the nurses may have agreed
  • B. Tell the patient that she lied to both nurses
  • C. Bring the request to the team and give the patient one agreed answer
  • D. Let each nurse decide the request on her own shift
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Playing staff members against each other is splitting, a defense typical of BPD that divides the team. The team counters it with open communication, team meetings and supervision so the patient gets one consistent response. Granting the call (A) rewards the split. Accusing the patient (B) is confrontational and invites a power struggle. Letting each nurse decide alone (D) keeps the inconsistency that splitting feeds on.

cards.prompt: A 35-year-old man with antisocial personality disorder is admitted under a court order. He becomes loud and says, "I do not need you telling me what to do." Which nursing goal has the highest priority? A. Protecting other patients and staff from harm B. Helping him develop empathy for others C. Teaching him about anger management D. Exploring his childhood attachment history
cards.promptHtml:
A 35-year-old man with antisocial personality disorder is admitted under a court order. He becomes loud and says, "I do not need you telling me what to do." Which nursing goal has the highest priority?

  • A. Protecting other patients and staff from harm
  • B. Helping him develop empathy for others
  • C. Teaching him about anger management
  • D. Exploring his childhood attachment history
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

For ASPD, patient and staff safety is the first priority because the patient may become verbally or physically aggressive when expectations are not met. Treating physical problems such as withdrawal comes second. Empathy, anger management and attachment work (B, C, D) are long-term psychological goals that follow once the environment is safe and a working plan is agreed upon.

cards.prompt: A patient with borderline personality disorder is starting dialectical behavior therapy. Which statement by the patient shows that the nurse's teaching was effective? A. "I will practice skills for managing emotions, handling distress and getting along with people." B. "This therapy will find out which childhood events caused my illness." C. "I will take a medication that cures my mood swings." D. "My therapist will tell me what to do when I feel overwhelmed."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with borderline personality disorder is starting dialectical behavior therapy. Which statement by the patient shows that the nurse's teaching was effective?

  • A. "I will practice skills for managing emotions, handling distress and getting along with people."
  • B. "This therapy will find out which childhood events caused my illness."
  • C. "I will take a medication that cures my mood swings."
  • D. "My therapist will tell me what to do when I feel overwhelmed."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A

DBT combines cognitive-behavioral strategies with acceptance. Skills groups teach emotional regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness and mindfulness, supported by weekly individual sessions. It is not an exploration of childhood causes (B), a medication program (C) or advice-giving (D). The patient is expected to practice skills actively.

cards.prompt: A nurse teaches a patient with borderline personality disorder and a history of substance use about the prescribed medications. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply. A. Each drug is chosen to ease a specific problem, such as mood swings or impulsive anger. B. Benzodiazepines are the preferred treatment for the anxiety of this disorder. C. Medication works best as an addition to psychotherapy. D. Taking several medications at once is encouraged. E. People with this disorder may be sensitive to side effects.
cards.promptHtml:
A nurse teaches a patient with borderline personality disorder and a history of substance use about the prescribed medications. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Each drug is chosen to ease a specific problem, such as mood swings or impulsive anger.
  • B. Benzodiazepines are the preferred treatment for the anxiety of this disorder.
  • C. Medication works best as an addition to psychotherapy.
  • D. Taking several medications at once is encouraged.
  • E. People with this disorder may be sensitive to side effects.
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, E

Drugs treat target symptoms or comorbid conditions and supplement therapy; they do not treat the disorder itself. Patients may react strongly to side effects, so doses may need adjusting. Benzodiazepines are avoided because of habituation and substance-use risk, and buspirone is the safer anxiolytic (B is wrong). Boyd advises limiting medications to target symptoms for short periods rather than adding many (D is wrong).

cards.prompt: A patient with paranoid personality disorder is admitted for an infection. He says the staff are "talking about him" and refuses the nurse's offered medication. Which response by the nurse is best? A. "Nobody here is talking about you. Please take this." B. Mix the medication into his food so he takes it without a struggle C. Explain what the medication is for in a calm, honest, matter-of-fact way D. Ask him why he does not trust anyone
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with paranoid personality disorder is admitted for an infection. He says the staff are "talking about him" and refuses the nurse's offered medication. Which response by the nurse is best?

  • A. "Nobody here is talking about you. Please take this."
  • B. Mix the medication into his food so he takes it without a struggle
  • C. Explain what the medication is for in a calm, honest, matter-of-fact way
  • D. Ask him why he does not trust anyone
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

Patients with paranoid personality disorder are suspicious and assume harm. The nurse builds trust through honesty, consistency and simple explanations, without arguing about the beliefs. Flat denial (A) will not change the belief. Hiding medication in food (B) is deceptive, violates his right to refuse and would confirm his suspicion if discovered. A probing question about trust (D) feels accusatory and invites defensiveness.

cards.prompt: A clinic nurse assesses a patient who wears mismatched, stained clothing, describes being able to "sense" when a neighbor will call, and believes that unrelated news broadcasts contain messages for her. She has no close friends and has never had a sustained psychotic illness. Which disorder does this most likely represent? A. Schizoid personality disorder B. Paranoid personality disorder C. Avoidant personality disorder D. Schizotypal personality disorder
cards.promptHtml:
A clinic nurse assesses a patient who wears mismatched, stained clothing, describes being able to "sense" when a neighbor will call, and believes that unrelated news broadcasts contain messages for her. She has no close friends and has never had a sustained psychotic illness. Which disorder does this most likely represent?

  • A. Schizoid personality disorder
  • B. Paranoid personality disorder
  • C. Avoidant personality disorder
  • D. Schizotypal personality disorder
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Magical beliefs, ideas of reference, odd appearance and social isolation, with brief or no psychosis, point to schizotypal personality disorder, which is more dramatically eccentric than schizoid. Schizoid patients are flat and indifferent, not odd in thought. Paranoid patients are suspicious of others' motives. Avoidant patients want closeness but fear rejection.

cards.prompt: A patient with avoidant personality disorder is reluctant to join the group on the unit and says, "Everyone will think I'm stupid." Which response by the nurse is best? A. "Everyone has to attend group; you will go with me now." B. "It sounds frightening to think others might judge you. Let's talk about starting with a small group." C. "You are being too sensitive; no one will think that." D. "I will excuse you from groups for the rest of your stay."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with avoidant personality disorder is reluctant to join the group on the unit and says, "Everyone will think I'm stupid." Which response by the nurse is best?

  • A. "Everyone has to attend group; you will go with me now."
  • B. "It sounds frightening to think others might judge you. Let's talk about starting with a small group."
  • C. "You are being too sensitive; no one will think that."
  • D. "I will excuse you from groups for the rest of your stay."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

Avoidant patients fear criticism and rejection and have low self-esteem. The nurse acknowledges the feeling, avoids criticism and builds trust with patience, then helps the patient try gradual, manageable social contact. Forcing attendance (A) and minimizing the fear (C) reinforce feelings of inadequacy. Excusing the patient entirely (D) feeds isolation, which care aims to decrease.

cards.prompt: The nurse is planning care for a man with antisocial personality disorder on an inpatient unit. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply. A. Apply unit rules consistently, with consequences for rule-breaking B. Agree to a later curfew if he promises to attend morning group C. Avoid lecturing and bargaining during teaching D. Include problem-solving and empathy-building group sessions E. Increase privileges before he has shown responsible behavior
cards.promptHtml:
The nurse is planning care for a man with antisocial personality disorder on an inpatient unit. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

  • A. Apply unit rules consistently, with consequences for rule-breaking
  • B. Agree to a later curfew if he promises to attend morning group
  • C. Avoid lecturing and bargaining during teaching
  • D. Include problem-solving and empathy-building group sessions
  • E. Increase privileges before he has shown responsible behavior
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: A, C, D

A structured milieu with consistently applied rules and consequences, direct teaching without lecturing, and groups (where peers challenge distorted views) are the recommended approaches. The patient reinforces self-responsibility when privileges follow accepted responsibility. Trading a privilege for a promise (B) is bargaining, which invites manipulation and power struggles, and unearned privileges (E) remove the link between behavior and consequences.

cards.prompt: A patient with dependent personality disorder asks the nurse, "What should I do about my discharge plan? Please just tell me what to do." Which response is most therapeutic? A. "Here is the plan that I think is best for you." B. "I can't help you with that." C. "Your doctor will decide that for you." D. "What choices have you considered so far? Let's review them together."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with dependent personality disorder asks the nurse, "What should I do about my discharge plan? Please just tell me what to do." Which response is most therapeutic?

  • A. "Here is the plan that I think is best for you."
  • B. "I can't help you with that."
  • C. "Your doctor will decide that for you."
  • D. "What choices have you considered so far? Let's review them together."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: D

Dependent patients look to others for decisions. The nurse supports growth by resisting the urge to decide, helping the patient list options and reinforcing the patient's own choices. Telling the patient what to do (A) and handing the decision to the prescriber (C) maintain dependency. A flat refusal (B) feels like abandonment and ends the discussion.

cards.prompt: A nursing student asks how obsessive-compulsive personality disorder differs from obsessive-compulsive disorder. Which statement by the nurse is accurate? A. "Both involve unwanted intrusive thoughts and rituals." B. "Only personality disorder begins in childhood." C. "The personality disorder is a pervasive preoccupation with order and control, and the person does not usually see it as a problem." D. "The personality disorder fluctuates with anxiety."
cards.promptHtml:
A nursing student asks how obsessive-compulsive personality disorder differs from obsessive-compulsive disorder. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

  • A. "Both involve unwanted intrusive thoughts and rituals."
  • B. "Only personality disorder begins in childhood."
  • C. "The personality disorder is a pervasive preoccupation with order and control, and the person does not usually see it as a problem."
  • D. "The personality disorder fluctuates with anxiety."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: C

OCPD is a pervasive pattern of perfectionism, orderliness and control, without true obsessions or compulsions, and patients usually do not see their behavior as problematic. OCD involves unwanted obsessions and compulsions that fluctuate with anxiety and distress the person. OCD often begins in childhood, whereas OCPD typically begins in adolescence or young adulthood.

cards.prompt: A patient with narcissistic personality disorder on a medical unit says, "I want the head nurse. You are obviously not qualified to care for me." Which nursing response is best? A. "I have been a nurse here for years and I am fully qualified." B. "I'll find out when the charge nurse is available, and I will check on you again. What are your main concerns today?" C. "Complaining like this will not get you better care." D. "You seem to need constant praise to feel good about yourself."
cards.promptHtml:
A patient with narcissistic personality disorder on a medical unit says, "I want the head nurse. You are obviously not qualified to care for me." Which nursing response is best?

  • A. "I have been a nurse here for years and I am fully qualified."
  • B. "I'll find out when the charge nurse is available, and I will check on you again. What are your main concerns today?"
  • C. "Complaining like this will not get you better care."
  • D. "You seem to need constant praise to feel good about yourself."
cards.answerHtml:
Answer: B

The nurse avoids a power struggle, remains courteous and steers toward concrete goals the patient can see as his own. Defending credentials (A) and threatening (C) start a battle. Interpreting the patient's need for admiration (D) is confrontational, and these patients often reject self-reflection. Care progresses slowly with measurable goals.

cards.prompt: A hospitalized patient with histrionic personality disorder compliments the nurse's appearance, touches the nurse's arm and says, "I feel we have a special bond." Which response best maintains the therapeutic relationship? A. Laugh it off and change the subject B. Ask the unit manager to reassign the patient permanently C.
